#8344. Xpedition NexLite 35 Bow Review: Accuracy and Speed Test

Published Oct 29, 2026 1:00 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

Late October is a great time to be a bowhunter. The bucks are chasing, and new bows seem to drop every week. One of them recently showed up on my front porch. (I’m still working on getting a buck to do that.) This one is a 35-inch featherweight from Xpedition, and on paper, its long axle-to-axle length and low mass weight make it a strong pick for anyone who wants one bow for both targets and the whitetail woods. I spent the last two weeks shooting the new Xpedition Nexlite 35 to find out if it lives up to that promise.

A typical 35-inch bow weighs 4.6 to 4.9 pounds. The NexLite 35 weighs 3.95 pounds. That weight savings comes from the Magnite riser material, which is a nanocomposite alloy that’s about 30 percent lighter than 6061 aluminum. Xpedition says it’s also stronger and absorbs vibration better than aluminum and carbon.

Low-profile arrow rest and sight mounting are now standard on premium and even budget compound bows. You’ll find Integrate rest mounting and a machined Picatinny sight mount on the NexLite 35. Xpedition also offers its XLOK accessories, such as a low-profile quiver and a bow stand.

The NexLite 35 uses the Tip-Shift tuning system. It’s a simple shimming system that doesn’t require a bow press. All you need is an Allen wrench to swap the shims and move your cams.

Before I fired my first shot from the NexLite 35, I was impressed with how light it is for a 35-inch bow. It’s only 4.9 pounds fully rigged with an XLOK stabilizer, Axcel Armortech sight, XLOK bow stand, and QAD arrow rest. Its low mass weight gives you the flexibility to run it as a lightweight hunting bow or rig it with long stabilizers for TAC and 3D competitions.

I paper tuned the NexLite without any drama. I didn’t need to use the Tip-Shift tuning system, but I did use it during the 2026 bow test. It’s a fantastically simple system. All you need to do is remove a screw with an Allen wrench and replace the spacer with the one that will fix your issue. The spacers have one, two, or three dots on them. The number of dots you install should always add up to four. I like that the Tip-Shift is a rigid system, so you don’t run the risk of an adjustment screw walking or accidentally moving a cam too far.

The NexLite 35’s draw cycle is smooth, but you can tell the cams were built for speed. The bow hits its peak weight early, evens out, and then there’s a final effort right before the valley. To me, it feels similar to drawing a Mathews Lift. The wall is solid with no give, and the valley is relatively short. If you come off the stops, the bow will let you know you’re creeping. But I found it very easy to keep the stops pinned, and the bow felt exceptionally comfortable and stable at full draw. It’s easy to drop the pin on the target and keep it there. At the shot, there is minimal vibration, which is impressive considering the bow’s low weight.

I quickly got used to the draw cycle while sighting in. Then I stepped back to 50 yards for accuracy testing and —— buddy, this bow is a shooter. I shot five five-shot groups at 50 yards that averaged 3.19 inches.

For the speed test, I shot a 430-grain arrow with the bow set at 61.2 pounds and a 31.5-inch draw length. The four-shot average was 281.6 fps. That’s pretty fast for a 35-inch bow.

The NexLite has nearly all the features you’d expect in a modern flagship bow, but there are three features I’d like to see added.

If you’re in the market for a long axle-to-axle bow, the NexLite 35 is definitely worth trying out at your local shop. It’s a top contender because its low mass weight makes it versatile as a combination target and hunting bow. It also has good performance, an easy-to-use tuning system, and high accuracy potential. I also really appreciate the NexLite 35’s build quality. It’s beautifully finished and masterfully machined — the type of workmanship I love to see in a premium bow.

Scott Einsmann is Outdoor Life’s gear editor. He oversees the gear team’s editors and writers who are subject matter experts in bows, knives, hunting, fishing, backpacking, and more. He lives in Richmond, Virginia with his wife and two bird dogs.

#8343. Why 5 Days of Heat Training May Be Enough

In a perfect world, we’d spend the month (or more) leading up to toasty races like the Javelina Jundred training to handle the heat. Actually, in a perfect world, we would heat train all year round to reap the potential physiological rewards, such as increased plasma volume, and maybe even improved Vo2 max and lactate threshold.

But we’re not all pros with flexible schedules and not everyone lives in the Arizona desert, where the average high is around 82 degrees Fahrenheit.

The last thing any of us want is to succumb to hot conditions, much less end up in the med tent, because we were too busy for heat training. But many heat training protocols call for weeks and even months of heat sessions to induce positive physiological adaptations; time we don’t often have to spare while juggling work, sleep, family obligations, and the ever-important logging of miles.

So when I found out that endurance gravel cyclist Metheven Bond claimed he managed to acclimate to the heat in only 5 days, I was curious: Can runners implement a similar protocol?

Off his 5-day protocol, Bond rode for 43 hours and 6 minutes with no sleep through the sweltering desert of Eastern Andalusia to finish sixth overall in The Badlands. If you’re unfamiliar with the gravel cycling race, Badlands runs some 507 miles across the Gorafe and Tabernas deserts in Spain,where temperatures regularly exceed 104 F.

To find out exactly what he did and how it may apply to runners, I spoke with Bond himself, as well as Aline Barre, a competitive ultra-cyclist and triathlete with a master’s degree in Sports Performance Analysis, and Daniel Snape, Ph.D., a performance physiologist, accredited sport and exercise scientist, and researcher in endurance and environmental physiology.

Earlier this year, Bond, who races for Ribble Outliers gravel cycling team, competed in some hot races in Spain and Switzerland. Temperatures reached nearly 97 degrees.

“I fell apart even though I thought I did everything right,” he told Trail Runner. “I froze all of my bottles and was drinking over a liter an hour for hydration, but my power still dropped off a cliff, my heart rate was through the roof, and I couldn’t think properly. I knew it was from the heat.”

Racing in hot conditions can compromise endurance capacity, and, as Bond discovered the hard way, it’s not always enough to rely on mid-race cooling. “I needed to find ways to adapt so the heat bothers me less, so I looked into heat acclimation.”

The goal of heat acclimation is to cause adaptations that allow the body to more effectively function in high temps. That process involves exposing the body to hot conditions that cause core body temperature to rise. Done long and consistently enough adaptations can include a lowered heart rate and body temperature, a higher sweat rate, improved performance, and better heat resilience.

“Before Badlands, I looked at the weather forecast and knew the heat was going to be bad. I’m in the North of England where it’s colder and somehow needed to get ready to be thrown into the heat,” Bond said. He visited the lab of Precision Fuel and Hydration, a sponsor of Ribble Outliers, for a focused heat training block. There, the Precision team implemented a protocol before Badlands consisting of five one-hour heat training sessions of cycling in a heat chamber set to 102 degrees over five consecutive days.

The team monitored Bond’s performance markers—such as heat transfer and skin temperature—throughout the block via sensors like the Core 2 Thermal Sensor, which mounts to any heart rate strap and transmits data in real-time to an app or wearable.

As the sessions progressed, Bond was able to push harder without a corresponding increase in cardiovascular effort. The result: Higher power output, lower average heart rate, and improved resistance to the fatigue of heat stress.

Aline Barre is a cyclist, triathlete, and endurance performance lead at Core. Like Bond, Barre had an equally unpleasant experience racing in the heat.

“My first endurance race was Ironman Frankfurt. For training, I didn’t do any running in the heat,” Barre said. “Race day was super hot and I was cooked. I was drinking a lot, but I felt horrible during the run. I was so afraid of the heat that I went to Finland for my second Ironman.”

Barre concluded the heat was holding her back—until she focused on acclimation. “Heat training is even more important for ultrarunners than endurance cyclists. In most cases, it’s easier to cycle in the heat than to run in the heat,” she said. “That’s because you move forward at a faster pace when riding a bike than running, creating substantially more airflow to help cool your skin through sweat evaporation.”

Combine this with the fact that running creates higher metabolic heat than cycling and it’s no wonder that medical teams see more cases of heat stroke at endurance running events than at cycling races. Additionally, some studies suggest that female athletes may require a slightly longer heat exposure period (10-14 days) or stronger heat stimulus relative to male athletes (seven days) to fully develop certain adaptations, particularly those related to sweating

“Most athletes see the majority of gains after 4-5 heat sessions and the full adaptation after doing 10 to 12 sessions within two to six weeks,” Barre said.

But for Bond, five days was enough. Performance physiologist and researcher Daniel Snape explains why.

“When you heat train, the main response you get is an increase in your blood plasma volume. For Bond to increase his plasma volume across those five days is a very normal and achievable response,” Snape said. Snape is part of a team of experts at the Health and Performance Hub at Leeds Beckett University. He works with professional ultrarunners like 2025 UTMB winners Tom Evans and Ruth Croft to develop specific heat acclimation strategies.

“Also you’re becoming more familiar with the heat, so your body doesn’t have that: ‘Oh no, I’ve got to increase my heart rate to cope with this stressor’ fight or flight response. That’s why five days straight was enough time for Bond to adapt and be able to hold a higher power output at a lower heart rate.”

While five days may be enough for a professional male endurance athlete who has a stellar baseline and access to a heat chamber, core body temperature sensor, and a team of experts, it might not be for many ultrarunners.

“Even I had to continue with three sessions per week of heat acclimation at home to maintain the adaptation, riding wrapped up in layers. I kept this up until a week before Badlands, when it was time to taper,” Bond said. He also points out that while significant adaptations can occur in five days, a few weeks is preferable for the mental preparation.

“The more times you train in the heat, the more confidence you have when you face it on race day,” he said. “You think: ‘Okay, it’s uncomfortable, but not as uncomfortable because I’ve been exposed to it. I’m used to this’.”

If you’re short on time and you want to have some semblance of conditioning going into Javelina or another toasty ultra, Core has a simple but mighty indoor heat training plan to build heat into your workouts with five sessions over 2 weeks. (See below.) It includes a long run where you start cool, then dress in warm layers for the last 75 minutes, as well as an easy 50-minute run where you run cool, but add a 30-minute passive heat session after.

The long run  is best done inside on a treadmill, but a smart trainer, stationary bike, or even a rowing machine will work as well. For your layers, you’ll need clothing that is non-permeable and traps heat against your body,  such as a heat suit, thermal top, down jacket, rain jacket, fleecy sweat suit, and/or wool hat. As a last resort, Bond recommends using a trash bag with holes cut out for your head and arms.

The passive heat session consists of time in a sauna, steam room, hot tub, or even the bathtub. If you’re preparing for a hot desert race, a sauna is the way to go if you can access one. Research shows that repeated post-exercise sauna sessions can enhance key components of heat adaptation, such as blood plasma volume and thermoregulatory efficiency. To prepare for a trail run in the tropics, a steam room or steamy bath are the best options.

Alternatively, you can do a micro heat training block that includes five days of only passive heat sessions immediately after your normal training runs, when your heart rate and core temperature are still elevated. According to Dr. Snape, even this can be effective at improving performance come race day.

The benefits of heat training extend beyond simply ramping up for a 100-miler under the desert sun, however.

“With the sauna for example, we know that if you do a hill workout, then go into the sauna, it has some muscle hypertrophy benefits, helping with recovery,” Snape said. “We also know that saunas improve your immune function. And if you do a sauna session late at night, it can actually improve sleep quality.”

Before starting a heat training plan, you should already be used to training for a minimum of four days per week and at least four hours of total weekly volume. You should also be able to complete a 60-to 75-minute run workout.

“You can do heat training right up until taper week. But don’t start heat training too close to your race. If you start two weeks before your race, the chance is quite high that you’ll expose your body to unnecessary fatigue because it’s not used to the heat,” Barre said. “We recommend starting four to five weeks out. During heat sessions, monitor your skin temperature, sweat rate, and heart rate so you don’t overdo it or get a heat illness, which can be life-threatening if you’re not careful. And hydrate before, during, and after heat sessions.”

It’s important to note that even if you use a Core sensor as part of your heat acclimation protocol, you can’t wear it into saunas or your bathtub at home, so there’s no way of knowing your internal body temperature during those passive sessions. As such, active and passive heat training should only be done when someone else is with you or in a nearby room.

“Any heat acclimation protocol will induce a training stress. Respect it as an additional thing to recover from,” Snape said. “That means you will have to take some training off the table elsewhere when undergoing a heat training block. That could mean cutting nine hours of running down to eight hours.”

Heat acclimation doesn’t have to be a part-time job. If you have time for 7-14 heat sessions during or after the run workouts on your training plan, you should experience full adaptations. But if you only have time for a 5-day heat adaptation block, it’s still more beneficial than not training for the heat at all, helping you develop a base adaptation that can make it mentally and physically easier to stay on pace when the heat is on.

#8338. The Biggest Archery Mistakes You’re Making This Bow Season

Published Oct 29, 2026 2:22 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

Over the past 20 years, I’ve shot, competed with and hunted with everything from selfbows to compounds. If there’s a mistake you can make while shooting a bow, I’ve done it. Luckily, I’ve also had the chance to learn from world-class coaches, Olympians, and the best archers in the world. So I’ve learned how to fix the worst errors and spot trouble in other bowhunters.

Here are five common archery mistakes that new and experienced bowhunters make that ultimately cost opportunities in the field.

The easiest archery flaw to fix is also one of the most common ones. When you grip your bow properly, it becomes easier to tune, and your accuracy will improve because you won’t induce inconsistent torque into the bow. To grip your bow, place your hand as high as it will go in the grip, turn your knuckles so they’re at a 45-degree angle to the riser and make sure the bow touches your hand only between your thumb pad and lifeline.

Read Next: How to Grip a Compound Bow for Better Hunting Accuracy

Have you ever used the wrong pin, forgotten to look through your peep or fired as soon as your pin was close to a deer’s kill zone? Those mistakes happen because you’re relying on your subconscious to shoot the bow.

In the backyard, you can let your subconscious run the shot. Heck, you could shoot half asleep and do all right. But shooting under pressure is a different story. You can’t trust your subconscious in those situations because it will take shortcuts to skip to the ultimate goal — firing the arrow. It’s a lot like AI: It finds the most efficient solution, and wiping you out might be mere collateral damage.

Instead of relying on autopilot, you need a firm shot process that you fully control. Make a list of the key steps of your shot and check them off one by one. This keeps you in the present and focused on the process, not the result.

Read Next: Target Panic! Joel Turner and Joe Rogan Talk Archery

With time and repetitions, your strings can move, which affects your bow’s tune and sight tape. Don’t be one of those hunters who misses an easy shot because their sight was off or their drop-away rest timing changed. Every month or so, check your sight and rest timing, shoot your bow through paper and make sure your broadheads are in tune.

When you first learned to shoot a bow, someone probably told you that you need a consistent anchor point. But that doesn’t mean you need to anchor the string into your face. Pressing your face or your nose against the string causes oscillation, which leads to left-and-right inconsistencies. The string can touch your face, but only lightly.

If you find yourself trying really hard to hold your bow steady, you’re approaching archery the wrong way. A steady aim is the result of your form and bow setup. There’s no muscling your way to it. You also can’t make your pin stop moving. The goal is for your pin to have a slow, consistent float around the spot. Once you achieve that, your next job is to focus on shot execution.

When you make a change to your archery form or your bow, it’s normal for your accuracy to suffer at first. Trust the process during that learning period, and shoot at a big target such as the Blackout Longshot 36. The goal during the period is to get used to your change and not care about accuracy until your shot feels good again.

Scott Einsmann is Outdoor Life’s gear editor. He oversees the gear team’s editors and writers who are subject matter experts in bows, knives, hunting, fishing, backpacking, and more. He lives in Richmond, Virginia with his wife and two bird dogs.

#8335. ‘It’s Trailer Park Chemistry.’ A Hybrid Bighorn Sheep Is on the Lam and That Could Be Bad News for Wild Herds

Published Oct 29, 2026 2:47 PM EDT

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

The two-paragraph Sept. 18 news release from Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks raised more questions than it may have intended.

The department “is seeking help from the public to locate a hybridized female rocky mountain bighorn sheep that went missing from a private alternative livestock facility near Vaughn in early September,” the release from FWP’s Region 4 office in Great Falls stated. “The bighorn ewe is described as weighing about 120 pounds and is primarily white in color with a red ear tag.”

The news release stressed wildlife officials’ concern that the ewe could come into contact with wild bighorn sheep in the vicinity. Domestic sheep are often vectors for pathogens that can fatally infect wild sheep.

What the news release didn’t disclose is that the “alternative livestock facility” in question is owned by Arthur “Jack” Schubarth, who was convicted in 2024 of violating the federal Lacey Act in his pursuit to create giant hybrid bighorn rams. Schubarth pleaded guilty to helping smuggle genetic material from Marco Polo argali sheep from Kyrgyzstan into the United States in order to clone the ram and create a “super sheep” with huge spiraling horns and resistance to the pathogens that infect North American wild sheep. His quest was enabled by Montana hunting outfitter John Lewton, who lopped off the testicles of his clients’ trophy wild bighorns, kept the gonads on ice, and later sold them to Schubarth.

The idea, Schubarth later told court officials, was to use the genetic material to incubate hybrid sheep with horns larger than any North American rams.

Lewton was sentenced last week in federal court in Billings and received a $20,000 fine and a year of probation for his part in the genetic alchemy. As a condition of his federal-court sentence, Lewton is prohibited from outfitting or guiding hunters for a full year.

The notion that a “Frankenram” could be produced with a combination of cloned embryos and artificial insemination isn’t an abstraction. In 2017, Schubarth actually produced what he called the Montana Mountain King, a pure cloned Marco Polo ram birthed to a surrogate bighorn ewe. Schubarth subsequently bred offspring of the Montana Mountain King to captive bighorn ewes on his farm west of Great Falls. It’s one of these ewes that has now gone missing, according to Fish, Wildlife & Parks.

Schubarth’s genetic hermetics has both baffled and impressed wildlife investigators, who told Outdoor Life that the sort of reproductive science that Schubarth practiced is normally limited to hospitals, universities, and other science centers with state-of-the-art facilities.

“The best way to describe his operation is trailer-park chemistry,” said a source familiar with the case who spoke on background. “He’s pulled off a pretty high-level genetics program with hardware-store gear and limited resources.”

Schubarth received probation for his guilty plea to the Lacey Act violations. In his petition to the federal court for leniency, Schubarth’s attorney, Jason Holden, noted his client’s contribution to the science of wildlife propagation.

“Jack is an 81-year-old non-violent man,” Holden wrote in 2024. “His crime, the cloning of a Marco Polo Sheep from Kyrgyzstan, has ruined his life, reputation and family. Jack did something no one else could, or has ever done. On a ranch, in a barn in Montana, he created Montana Mountain King. MMK is an extraordinary animal, born of science, and from a man who, if he could rewrite history, would have left the challenge of cloning a Marco Polo to only the imagination of Michael Crichton.”

Read Next: Montana Man Charged for Illegally Cloning and Breeding Marco Polo Sheep from Central Asia

The department’s all-points-bulletin asking the public to report a lone and roaming ewe may not produce any sightings. That’s because there’s a possibility that the ewe isn’t actually on the lam. She may have been sold to an out-of-state game farm, said sources who spoke to Outdoor Life on the condition that they wouldn’t be identified based on the speculative nature of their hunches.

Schubarth, who is on probation from the 2024 federal wildlife-trafficking charges, has been charged by FWP with failure to report the escape of an animal permitted in his commercial wildlife operation, according to charging documents at the Cascade County District Court in Montana.

The “game farm” permit requires that if anything escapes the permitted facility, owners must report within 48 hours to both FWP and the Montana Department of Livestock.

“According to our records, the ewe in question reportedly escaped on Sept. 2, and our game wardens heard about it the next week,” says Dave Hagengruber, FWP’s public information officer in the Great Falls regional office. “Wardens went out to talk with Schubarth in mid-September, and he basically said, ‘Oh yeah, I meant to tell you.’”

Schubarth told wardens the ewe likely escaped either over a fence damaged by a wind storm or through a gate accidentally left open at the end of his property, beyond lines of kennels of dogs that produce puppies sold in Schubarth’s pet store in Great Falls.

Assuming the ewe did leave Schubarth’s facility, it could pose a risk to the region’s wild sheep.

“Cascade is 30 miles from his farm, and there’s a sizeable band of [wild] bighorns there,” says Hagengruber. “The Birdtail Hills are 20 to 25 miles to the west, and there are bighorns in those hills. The Rocky Mountain Front, home to Montana’s most treasured bighorn sheep herd, is 60 or 70 miles west. Fortunately, this is not a ram, so it’s less likely to roam widely, but the threat of disease transmission is a significant concern. That’s why we want to hear of any sightings. It’s Jack’s property and his responsibility to locate and return to his facility, but we can’t have this hybrid sheep potentially contacting wild bands.”

Schubarth insists he did not sell the ewe, and suspects the fugitive sheep was killed by predators within a few miles of his facility in the Sun River Valley.

“I haven’t heard anything about her, and to my knowledge Fish and Game hasn’t heard anything for five weeks now,” Schubarth said in an interview. “With all the people out looking, we haven’t seen it and no one’s called me. I’m assuming, with her lack of experience with predators, that a coyote got her.”

“She’s mainly bighorn and probably three or four domestic crosses from the original cross that was 50 percent bighorn,” Schubarth said. “I added some more bighorn from that original [parentage]. So they’re probably 62.5 percent bighorn. They don’t have any experience of being wild. I’m pretty sure she would have watched coyotes walk right up to her” without trying to evade them.

Schubarth further confirmed that he still has “around 45 head of sheep, is all” remaining on his 200-acre game farm. “All my sheep are sold right now and just waiting to leave. I’ve kept them back because I just want the pleasure of birthing out the lambs. It’s something I like to do, and at 83 years old, I like to see new life.”

As for the descendants of the Montana Mountain King, Schubarth said that the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service required him to destroy progeny of the cloned ram back in 2024. The federal court also required Schubarth to dispose of all hybrid bighorn sheep by Dec. 31, 2025, and to stop “from engaging in breeding activity of big game stock while on supervision,” according to sentencing documents.

“We had 190 head of the hybrid Marco/bighorn here at the ranch and none of them got pneumonia in the three years I held them while waiting for a forever home for them. All were slaughtered,” he says. “I did sell some, 15 in all. There are some down in Texas, and every so often I see on Facebook somebody advertising a Marco Polo, but there’s no way they are more than about a quarter Marco” based on genetic dilution, he said.

As for the Montana Mountain King himself, Schubarth says the ram ended up at a zoological park in upstate New York. Indeed, last summer the Rosamond Gifford Zoo in Syracuse, New York, announced the acquisition of “Tilek,” the cloned argali at the center of Schubarth’s case. The ram had been held at an Oregon wildlife rehabilitation center for over three years before being moved to the Syracuse zoo.

Schubarth says “Tilek” would be about nine years old, but observed that he has not yet expressed the most distinctive trait of the Marco Polo subspecies of argali: its spiraling horns.

“He’s basically still 54 to 57 inches,” says Schubarth. “He ought to have 75 inches of horn on each side. But this year they put him in a larger grass pen so maybe he’ll grow more. For safety’s sake, they should have castrated him so no more genetics could get out there. Maybe they did, for all I know. I’ll never see him again. I don’t ever leave my ranch.”

Schubarth said that statements from prosecutors that he was motivated to create a hybrid ram with giant horns in order to upsell to commercial shooting operations are wrong. He was more interested in cross-breeding to create a bighorn race that might be resistant to what’s often called “M. ovi,” a respiratory disease that often results in catastrophic pneumonia-caused die-offs in wild sheep.

“My thinking was that here’s this wild sheep that has evolved with domestic sheep for thousands of years,” says Schubarth of the Marco Polo, native to the high alpine plateaus of central Asia. “The feds and Fish and Game made it out that I was selling to the hunt community and only motivated to create bigger horns. In actuality, I was after the immune system, and the reality is that even after several generations, these Marco hybrids still seem to be immune to pneumonia. I think that’s the real story.”

If he regrets anything about the misadventures of the Montana Mountain King, it’s that he trusted the lab that created the clone from genetic tissue smuggled from Kyrgyzstan.

“I’ve been happy all my life except for this last foolishness about the Marco Polo,” Schubarth says. “I wouldn’t have done it had the cloning company not told me it was legal. They lied after they took $32,000 from me. That was the cost of stockpiling the tissue and making the embryos for me.”

The rest of the genetic work was a cinch, he says. The surrogate bighorn ewes, most of which Schubarth bought from zoos in Canada and Colorado, were selected for their ability to carry the hybrid lamb.

“Laparoscopic work is easy,” he says, and artificial insemination is an established livestock practice. The trick is creating a genetically manipulated zygote.

“You take the egg and suck out the product and you put the material from the Marco Polo into the egg and implant it in a ewe. A little electricity, and poof, the thing starts to grow.”

Schubarth says he will be entirely out of the game-breeding business by 2027.

“Fish and Game has accomplished what they always wanted: to drive me out of business,” he says.

Meanwhile, he says the captive-shooting industry is thriving. He cites high-fence operations in Kansas and Texas that would pay top dollar for his hybrid bighorns while also insisting that he sold to fellow breeders, not trophy hunters.

“The feds made it out that I was the center of this industry based on shooting animals in pens,” he says, before acknowledging that most of his animals probably met that fate. “Without the interest of the hunting community, these animals would be worthless and only sold for meat. So yes, the industry revolves around the harvesting of these animals by collectors.”

Fish, Wildlife & Parks is less interested in the commercial than in the pathological outcome of the case. The state has struggled to establish bighorn sheep populations in prime habitat in the Missouri River Breaks and in the mountains of southwest Montana. Bands that thrive for years are often wiped out in a single season by pneumonia epizootics that often originate in domestic sheep.

State game wardens are authorized to shoot on sight wild bighorns that contact domestic sheep. The fear is that a traveling ram could become infected by a domestic sheep, and then take that pathogen back to the wild herd.

“We have spent many years and sportsmen’s dollars to restore and transplant wild sheep into available habitat in Montana,” says FWP’s Hagengruber. “We’ve had recent restorations in the Belts and the Breaks, and disease is always a big concern, and so is the ability of this hybrid ewe to breed with either domestic or wild sheep. So we take the possibility that there may be a hybrid domestic/wild sheep running around central Montana very seriously.”

Anyone who sees a lone sheep with a red ear tag in central Montana is urged to call FWP’s Region 4 office at 406-454-5840.

Andrew McKean is Outdoor Life’s hunting and conservation editor, drilling into issues that affect wildlife, wildlands, and the people who care about them. He’s also OL’s optics editor, helping readers to make informed buying decisions.

#8331. How to Field Dress a Deer Like a Pro: The Ultimate Step-By-Step Guide

Published Oct 30, 2026 9:10 AM EDT

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Learning (or remembering) how to field dress a deer can feel overwhelming, but if you have a sharp knife and a reasonably strong stomach, you’ll be able to figure it out. If you manage to do so without nicking the guts or yourself, that’s ideal.

Removing the guts is the bare minimum required for dropping a deer at a processor, and an essential skill every deer hunter should learn. A field-dressed deer is also a lighter deer, which makes dragging and loading it less cumbersome. And the sooner you gut a deer after shooting it, the better the venison will be. So, here’s a guide on how to field dress a deer in a few easy steps.

All you really need to gut a deer is a sharp knife and, if it’s getting dark, a good headlamp. Other deer hunters carry the kitchen sink with them and won’t field dress a deer without some or all of the following items:

Many experienced deer hunters can field dress a deer in minutes, while it can take new or casual deer hunters a half hour or more. The best way to gut a deer is to work slowly, use a sharp knife, and have adequate lighting.

Keep these gutting rules in mind before you get started:

Start by rolling the deer onto its back. It should be belly-up and evenly balanced on both shoulder blades. Adjust the rump and hips to ensure they’re as even as possible. If you’re working on a slope, rotate the deer so its rump points downhill and its head is uphill.

Ask a buddy to hold a leg. If you’re solo and the deer keeps slipping sideways or downhill, try wedging a log or stick under its rump or using paracord to tie a hind leg to a branch. Personally, I find paracord to be overkill, but will sometimes use my knee, shoulder, or armpit to anchor a hind leg or keep it out of the way as I work.

This step and the next can be done now or after opening the abdominal cavity. Grab a handful of the mammary gland, or testicles with your non-dominant hand and lift away from the deer’s body. Keeping your blade mostly parallel to the deer’s body, slice away at the base of the stretched hide until you’ve freed the reproductive organs, and toss aside. The goal is to avoid cutting into the organs and instead cutting under them.

This step can be done later or not at all, but I prefer to do this now (particularly when working alone) since it relaxes the tension between the hind legs and prevents your deer from rolling on you. It also creates more space to work while removing internal organs. I butcher my own deer and this does not sacrifice any of the meat on the hindquarters when done correctly.

Cut the muscle between the two back legs to expose the center of the pelvic bone. Find what looks like dead center on the meat between the two back legs and cut down (usually a few inches) from the top of the pelvis to the anus. Stay as close to the center as possible to avoid gouging the roasts on either leg. Don’t saw the muscle. Slice it instead, letting the downward pressure of your blade do the cutting.

Insert your knife tip into the side (not the center) of the anus. Keeping your blade pressed against the bone that encircles the rectum, cut around the rectum rather than through it. The goal is to cut the connective tissue so you can pull the tube of intestines out rather than dice it up.

This abdominal cut is often the most difficult for hunters, and the key here is not to puncture the deer’s stomach or bladder because you don’t want to get any bile or urine on the meat.

Prevent stabbing the guts by turning your knife blade up (toward the sky) and tilting it so the blade is more parallel to the deer’s belly rather than perpendicular. Working close to the base of the belly, grab a handful of hide and pull it up to create some space between the layer of hide and the organs beneath. Insert the tip of your knife and make an incision until you see (or more likely, feel with the knife tip) empty space below it. Keep the incision shallow and make the slit long enough to work a finger or two of your off-hand in the space. Take care to not insert the blade too far into the abdominal cavity.

Now that you’ve made an opening incision, apply even upward pressure with your knife blade to “unzip” the abdomen, or make a lengthwise cut along the deer from pelvis to breastbone. This is similar to using a pair of scissors to slice a piece of wrapping paper in a single, fluid motion. Don’t saw with your knife.

The organs you’re ultimately trying to remove lie in two groups: the guts (liver, stomach, intestines, bladder, kidneys, fat if present, etc.) and the vitals (heart and lungs). These two groups are separated by the diaphragm: a thin wall of purple muscle between the abdominal cavity and the rib cage.

Note: If you plan to shoulder mount your deer, do not split the ribs. You should only make your cut to the base of the lower ribcage (above) and stop there, since your taxidermist will need all that hide from the ribs to the tip of the nose (this is called the cape).

If you are planning on a skull mount or you aren’t mounting your deer at all, you can split the ribs if you want. Your blade will encounter some resistance once you hit the rib cage. If you center your knife, you can slice through cartilage in the breastplate before hitting bone. Some hunters use a hatchet or saw to split the rib cage open, but a stout fixed-blade knife will also work. Splitting the rib cage makes it easier to see (and therefore remove) the heart and lungs, but isn’t necessary if you are having trouble cutting through it. This step is especially useful if you suspect a broadhead is lodged in the rib cage.

Personally, I just carry a slim field-dressing knife when I hunt and skip this step altogether during rifle season. I don’t mind reaching into the rib cage to remove the lungs, heart, and windpipe by feel.

To access the heart and lungs in the rib cage (and ultimately free everything) you need to cut the diaphragm. Use the tip of your knife to puncture this thin layer of muscle, then circle the entire rib cage, keeping your knife close to the ribs. Once the diaphragm has been cut away, blood and jellied bits of lung usually slosh into the abdominal cavity. This is perfectly normal (and a sign of a good shot).

Work from the top of deer down toward the pelvis. If you split open the rib cage this part will be easier; if not, you’ll have to do it more by feel.

At the top of the chest cavity, you’ll see or feel a large ribbed tube. That’s the windpipe. Cut it crossways (perpendicular to the spine), then use a finger or two to grab ahold of it from the inside and begin pulling it up and away. This will begin to loosen the heart and lungs.

Grab hold of the heart and/or lungs with your off-hand and pull while continuing to cut connective tissue along the spine. Keep going all the way down to the pelvis and keep working until the stomach and guts come loose, too. Because all the organs are attached to the deer along the spine, it can be helpful to tilt the deer on its side for this part so the organs roll out of your way and reveal their connection point.

As everything loosens, just roll the guts and intestines out of the deer and onto the ground. Note: If you haven’t yet separated the rectum from the anus, the guts will still connect to the carcass by a single tube — that’s the lower large intestines, or colon. To free the guts and toss aside, slice the colon crossways just above the pelvis and tie it off (if it’s full) so pellets don’t spill inside your deer.

Read Next: How to Skin a Deer, Step by Step

To field dress big game with a hatchet, use it as you would a big belt knife, opening the paunch with a small incision at the base of the sternum. Then, tip the blade at right angles to the animal, with the handle up and your fingers spreading the skin close to the blade as you run it to the rectum. Do not try to cut the skin down into the animal; hair will collect on and dull the blade. Dump the entrails.

To quarter the carcass, hang it or set it belly-up on the ground. Loosen hams with careful strokes tight against the pelvis and through the ball joints. Don’t chop; use the blade like a knife, your fist around the hatchet head (inset). Remove the shoulders the same way, leaving the skin on unless you must remove it to let a big animal, like an elk or moose, cool in warm weather. The hatchet (or, better yet, a slim double-bit ax) excels at splitting the backbone. Hang the animal head down, rear legs spread, to facilitate this task. —Wayne Van Zwoll

It’s always best to gut your deer as soon as possible, but the window you have depends on the weather and the shot you made. If the weather is hot or even mild, the sooner you field dress your deer, the better. Within an hour of the shot is ideal in these conditions. If it’s cold, a deer can last longer before it needs to be gutted — hours or even overnight if you have to back out while blood trailing. It’s always easier to dress a deer when it’s warm and pliable.

The best knives for field dressing are usually a fixed-blade knife with a sharp blade. A smaller, handier blade makes certain tasks easier, like removing the colon and avoiding puncturing the guts. A larger, stouter blade is easier for heavy-duty tasks like splitting the ribs.

Field-dressing a deer isn’t difficult once you get the hang of it, and it’s usually easier with a buddy to help hold a leg or a light. Use a sharp knife, make slow, deliberate cuts at connective tissue. Do your best to avoid puncturing the stomach or bladder, but don’t panic if you do. More important is to avoid cutting yourself. The process may be messy or unpleasant, but ultimately you’ll end up with a cooling carcass ready for the skinning shed or processor.

Natalie Krebs is the Executive Editor of Outdoor Life, where she tackles everything from reporting digital features to producing podcast episodes. Originally from Missouri, she currently lives in northwest Arkansas with her bird dog, Hatchet.

#8330. Whatever You Think of Him, Mark Dowdle Is Built for the Backyard Ultra

At lap 87 of the Last Soul Backyard Ultra in Bornheim, Germany, this August, Mark Dowdle transformed (or regressed, he’s not entirely sure) into the football and lacrosse player he was in college.

To be fair, Ayyoub “Ello” El Osrouti pretty much started it. A backyard ultra, as you probably know by now, is a last-person-standing race not much different from “The Long Walk”—the movie about 100 boys who walk until there’s one left—except the runners in backyard races aren’t shot after they drop.

Now at 4 a.m. on August 18—three days and 15 hours into the race—it was just down to El Osrouti and Dowdle, who were engaged in a Hamilton-like duel to determine the winner. Ello busted out of the gate. The German had been trying to run faster laps to break Dowdle, but this was, by comparison, a sprint. Dowdle, deviating from his tactic of running his own race, decided to stay right with him.

Dowdle completed the lap in 38 minutes—his fastest of the race by over 5 minutes. El Osrouti got up and finished four minutes later, also his fastest lap.

But about half way through the lap, El Osrouti stopped and sat down. Dowdle stopped, too, and just stared at him in silence. It was both competitive and a little chilling, like Dowdle thought the Last Soul race was a literal invitation to collect his competitors’ souls along the way.

Dowdle’s behavior left many of his hundreds of thousands of followers on Instagram, Youtube, and TikTok a little stunned. The 29-year-old Minnesotan has become a wildly popular Internet figure through dishing out zen advice and positivity. Rich Roll, the addict turned endurance athlete who serves up mindfulness every week on his podcast, called Dowdle a “changemaker” when he had Dowdle on the show. There was a good reason for it: Basically every time Dowdle took a breath, he said something enlightening or inspiring about hard work, endurance, or self-improvement.

With two backyard ultra wins in 2026 alone, there’s little doubt that Dowdle is one of this year’s ultrarunning breakout stars, partly because of his success in the backyard format and partly because of his social media savvy. But he didn’t get that way by reading scripted platitudes on TikTok; Dowdle isn’t faking that zen.

When I told him about the Taco Bell 50K and how it attracted those who wouldn’t normally even consider running an ultra, he said, “people want to be challenged. Sometimes they just don’t know it yet.” Even when he was a football and lacrosse player at the University of St. Thomas in Saint Paul, Minnesota, drinking way too much and trying to please others at the expense of himself, he would think about the meaning of life and why people do the things they do. He attributes his personal growth to running, but also to journaling.

“These are the kinds of things I think about all the time,” Dowdle said. “I was constantly thinking about this connection between words and action and who I wanted to be.”

Dowdle works as a motivational speaker now. But deep down, he’s got an edge.

It’s that edge that makes him stand out (and ruffle feathers) in a sport known for its kumbaya positivity, especially the camaraderie-focused backyard ultra community. Dowdle likes being a little weird and competitive and even scary: He once made a YouTube video called “Ultrarunning Has A Mark Dowdle Problem.” He compares himself to Dennis Rodman, the wildly divisive and brilliant NBA player.

“I’m sure that some of these other guys who are competitive will want to put that competition right back on me,” Dowdle said. “I welcome that.”

His friend and rival Harvey Lewis seems like a golden retriever to Dowdle’s heeler. Dowdle sort of agrees with that comparison and sort of doesn’t. He points out that he and Lewis aren’t that different. (Lewis agrees with him, for what it’s worth.)

“I think Harvey Lewis is competitive in a way that’s much tricker to identify,” Dowdle said. “But I don’t hide it. There are times I don’t care. I’ll show everything on my sleeve.”

Lewis believes that Dowdle’s zen, more than his competitiveness, is what’s carried him to so much recent success. On October 17, 2026, they came together as teammates: Lewis, 50, and Dowdle lined up as part of a U.S. team of 15 against the world’s best at the 2026 Backyard Ultra World Team Championship. Team USA competed on the Big’s Backyard Ultra course in Beltbuckle, Tennessee, the original backyard ultra devised by Gary “Lazarus Lake” Cantrell. Dowdle went on to run 107 laps, or 446 miles—a personal best—to lead Team USA to victory over Australia. Lewis ran 83 laps.

The Backyard Ultra World Team Championship is held every two years, alternating with the individual world championship. The 2026 race began at 6 a.m. Mountain Time on Saturday, October 17, with 69 national teams competing simultaneously around the world.

The format is simple: Each team of 15 runners runs a 4.167-mile loop every hour, on the hour. The country with cumulatively the most loops completed across all 15 runners wins the team title. Team USA races on the original backyard ultra course in Gary “Lazarus Lake” Cantrell’s backyard in Bell Buckle, Tennessee.

Mark Dowdle led Team USA to the win with a cumulative 1,120 laps (yards) to defeat Australia by 51 yards. He was the last American standing with 107 laps, or 446 miles—a personal best. Belgium’s Ivo Steyaert and Merijn Geerts broke the individual backyard ultra world record by each running 124 yards (512 miles) before deciding to call it quits due to boredom, on-the-ground photographer Jacob Zocherman reports.

Since its inauguration in 2020, Belgium and the U.S. have each won two team titles.

Lewis said Dowdle’s “why” is perhaps the strongest he’s ever seen. It “cements his discipline and his unwavering desire to not give up.”

“Mark has a great energy force,” Lewis said. “He has a level of enthusiasm that’s immeasurable.”

But what, exactly, is an energy force? Is it zen or competitiveness? Dowdle likes to ask it another way: Why can’t it be both?

Take a wild guess who inspired Dowdle as a collegiate football and lacrosse player to turn his life around and start running. It wasn’t Joe Rogan, but if that was your first guess, you’re on the right track.

Feeling sorry for himself on the bus ride home after losing two of three lacrosse games his senior year, he listened to David Goggins on Joe Rogan’s podcast. Goggins talked about how running carved him into the person he was today. The way he bragged about pissing blood, shitting himself, and eating only saltine crackers during his long runs spoke to Dowdle. Dowdle already knew he needed to change.

He went for a run when they got back to campus—even though it was 2 a.m.

If Goggins lit the fire, James Lawrence, the Iron Cowboy, stoked it. Lawrence had completed the 50/50/50 challenge, or 50 Ironman-length triathlons in 50 days across 50 states. The way he leaned on his family during that journey spoke to Dowdle. Dowdle, to this day, gives all the credit to his wife, Lucy, for centering him and scolding him whenever he acts, for lack of a better description, too much like a bro.

Dowdle tried for many years to make it as a running guru—some might say influencer—and ultrarunner. He found some limited success. Runner’s World interviewed him in 2023 for his calendar challenge, when he ran the number of miles corresponding to the day of the month, for a full month. (For example, 26 miles on the 26th.) By the beginning of 2026, he had 40,000 Instagram followers and a modest apparel sponsorship that netted him $200 a month. And then he entered the BPN Go One More backyard ultra this April.

Dowdle had already won the Arrowhead 135-miler in January, finishing in 35:48:00—a four-hour improvement over his 2025 fourth-place finish. But he chalked that up to his ability to withstand the Minnesota winter conditions that dropped to minus 40 degrees Fahrenheit.

The BPN Go One More was another story; he hadn’t even made it to 100 miles in a backyard ultra before. He could sense other peoples’ doubts—they didn’t drive him, but they did irritate him a little. He mumbled at one point that they “had no fucking idea.”

Dowdle ended up running 306 miles in 73 hours of rainy and muddy conditions, and the way he did it captivated people: He looked fresh and happy most of the time, like he was playing tag on the playground. In a few days, his Instagram following jumped to 108,000, and brand deals were knocking at his door. He also began booking keynote speaking events, sometimes for conferences that he helped set up the year before for one of his odd jobs to get by while he pursued running.

He proved that BPN was no fluke two months later, finishing second to Lewis at the Mid-State Mile, a last-person standing event in Franklin, Tennessee.

But Last Soul sent him into a new stratosphere. After their fateful showdown on lap 87, Dowdle and El Osrouti dueled for another six hours. And despite the German banking a cumulative five hours of extra rest over the course of the race, after that 93rd lap he gave out. Dowdle ran the final lap solo to win the race with 94 loops, or 391.7 miles. The race attracted 10 million viewers to the livestream and more than 100,000 at any one time, attention that Lewis called “freakishly different” than any other ultra in history, even Western States or Rachel Entrekin’s historic overall win at the Cocodona 250.

After Last Soul, Dowdle’s Instagram following jumped from 108,000 to over 400,000.

“It’s been everything I’ve been trying to build for several years now,” Dowdle said. “But nothing really has changed. It’s sort of weird because I’ve been saying the same thing now that I have over the past seven years. But people are willing to listen more when I go 94 hours in a backyard.”

Dowdle, a Christian who has described his goal in races to experience suffering in a way that brings him closer to Jesus Christ and to others, says he’s handled his newfound success because of his wife. Everyone, he said, should get a Lucy. On the way home from the BPN race, Lucy saw his phone blowing up and reminded him that many of those people were loving him because of what he just did, but that she and his friends loved him for who he was.

Dowdle’s breakthrough would not be possible without the backyard ultra format, and not just because he’s one of the best in the world at it. The race, as Lewis alluded to, is insanely popular: What started as another one of Laz’s harebrained ideas with the Big’s Backyard Ultra in 2011 has ballooned to over 1,000 independent backyard ultras across the globe.

Lewis was perhaps the event’s first breakout star. He was known, he said, after winning Badwater in 2014, but the attention was far different after he won Big’s Backyard in 2023, his second victory, and set a backyard world record by running more than 450 miles. The format changed the high school teacher’s life.

“I was doing other cool stuff but never got noticed,” Lewis said. “But after the backyard, I was invited to all these running events, at no cost, places I’d never get to go to as a teacher. Australia, Botswana, all over the place. In Botswana, people knew who I was, and I was like, ‘really’? It just created so many more doors opening.”

Backyard ultras favor a unique skillset. Neither Lewis or Dowdle have the legspeed to compete for a top spot at a “fast” ultra like Western States. But, Lewis counters, a top contender at Western States may struggle at a backyard ultra.

“I’ve seen collegiate-type runners, and they get totally destroyed,” Lewis said. “It’s a different type of grit that’s required for running five straight days.”

Lewis and Dowdle possess that special mindset that doesn’t have much to do with a training plan. Lewis is writing a book on mindset, in fact, that will be released next fall. For Dowdle, the ultimate challenge (and intrigue) comes in the unknown.

“You have no opportunity to say ‘in 10 miles this race will be over,’” Dowdle said. “You just have to wrestle with the discomfort.”

Dowdle does that, he said, by using skills he learned from his parents. His relentless, even disturbing, will comes from his mother, and he got an addict’s penchant from his father. His dad, he said, has been sober for nearly 30 years by using his addictive personality for good, investing his energy in Alcoholics Anonymous and helping others overcome their itches.

But Dowdle also excels by finding out who he was as a person: “Running helped me figure out the person I was running away from and also running toward the person I wanted to be.”

There is a dual narrative in his head, one that every ultrarunner facing the highs and lows of a long race knows. The first tells him he’s not worthy. The other feels only elation. Neither, he said, is true.

“I know that the narrative playing in my head at that moment is not the full truth,” Dowdle said. “And the narrative that tells me I’m not good enough. As long as my feet are still moving forward, I can combat that thinking and know that’s not the full truth.”

Proving that imposter syndrome wrong is his part of his “why,” the magic power that he and Lewis seem to possess that helps them run much farther than just about anyone else. But that’s not his only motivation.

Dowdle was, at one point, a football coach. But when he examined his life, he didn’t think football was the right avenue for what he truly wanted to do. He wanted to connect with young men and try to help them crawl out of the same situation he was in years ago, before he began running and journaling. So he traveled across the country and hosted beer miles. He still does this, though he drinks non-alcoholic varieties now, or he simply challenges athletes to beat his beer mile time. (It’s 5:51.57.)

When the race is over, he sits down with athletes and talks with them about their lives. He tells them he was like them once, a little lost and full of doubt and pain, with only alcohol seeming to help. There are other ways, he tells them. Running could be one. A personal journey, like that of the Iron Cowboy, could be another.

“I watched the Iron Cowboy documentary, and it made me realize that I do have control, and that I can do hard things and I’m capable of more,” Dowdle said. “That’s the gift he gave me in that moment. Now I’ve been on a mission to try to give that gift to other people.”

#8329. Review: Mountain Equipment Switch Base Zip T

The Mountain Equipment Switch Base Zip T is an ultralight, close-fitting base layer designed for high-output cold-weather activities. It is made with Octa Fleece, a warm, highly breathable ultralight fleece similar to Polartec Alpha Direct, but much more durable, and pairs well with a windbreaker or winter shell jacket.

If you’re not familiar with Mountain Equipment, they’re a highly regarded British manufacturer that has designed technical outdoor gear for mountaineering and polar exploration since 1961. They make a wide range of products, including technical clothing, sleeping bags, and mountaineering backpacks. Backcountry.com carries their products in the United States. I’ve been recommending Mountain Equipment’s men’s Ibex and women’s Chamois softshell pants for winter hiking for years, and they’re still best in class.

The top uses 20-denier, 100% Octa Fleece, made from a specialized hollow polyester fiber with eight radial projections that give the yarn a gear- or octopus-like cross-section. The hollow center and projecting “fins” create insulating air spaces that trap warm air, letting water vapor escape. Octa Fleece has a similar warmth-to-weight ratio as Polartec Alpha Direct but is more durable, which is why larger clothing manufacturers such as Arc’teryx and Mountain Hardwear use it and are developing products with it. See our FAQ for a more detailed comparison of Octa Fleece and Polartec Alpha Direct.

The inside of the Switch Base Zip-T is a fuzzy, warm fabric that is a delight to wear next to the skin or over a thin base layer, while the outer surface is made of highly breathable, abrasion-resistant mesh.

The Switch Base Zip-T can be worn as a base layer or a mid-layer over a thin base. The interior has a fuzzy fleece texture that feels warm and comfortable. Flatlocked seams improve next-to-skin comfort by reducing bulk and minimizing potential irritation. The exterior is an open and breathable mesh that is much more abrasion-resistant. Thumbhole loops help keep the sleeves in place when adding a midlayer or waterproof shell.

Nylon shoulder overlays protect an area that sees regular friction from backpack straps.  This added reinforcement improves the top’s suitability for regular mountain use without significantly compromising its lightweight design.

A deep half-zip provides practical ventilation when body heat builds, making the Switch Base Zip T more adaptable than a standard crew-neck baselayer. Similarly, the loose wrists let you pull the sleeves up your arms to vent more heat. I’ve found the Switch to be a delightful base and mid-layer, worn by itself or under a windbreaker on a chilly morning. The fabric is more wind-resistant than a mid-layer hoodie made with Polartec Alpha Direct, and I like using a pullover like it in winter more than a hoodie because it’s easier to layer with the shells and headgear (hats) I typically wear.

The Switch Base Zip T is designed for a wide range of cold-weather activities, including:

It performs best during activities that involve frequent changes in effort and temperature since you can vent it so easily or layer it with a windbreaker or shell to increase wind resistance and heat retention. It also delivers warmth well above its weight, making it a lightweight midlayer that packs an outsized amount of warmth.

The Mountain Equipment Switch Base Zip T is a well-designed cold-weather or winter base layer for active users who prioritize low weight, quick drying, and effective ventilation. Its Octa Fleec fabric provides lightweight warmth while helping manage moisture, and the half-zip makes it easy to regulate temperature during demanding climbs and ski tours. It is not the best choice for maximum insulation when activity levels are low, but that is not its main purpose. For fast-moving winter adventures, the combination of comfortable seams, reinforced shoulders, and quick-drying performance makes the Switch Base Zip T a strong and practical choice.

#8328. Your Ski Gear Has Been Sitting All Summer. Here’s What to Check Before You Get on the Snow.

Welcome to the most impatient time of year—for skiers, at least. The dog days of summer are behind us and we’re eagerly awaiting the first lifts to start spinning. You don’t have to sit around twiddling your thumbs, though. Instead, put them to good use getting your gear prepped for the coming season

Ski shops have transitioned from summer to winter and are firing up their tuning machines and readying their bootfitting benches—without the long wait times of the regular season. So whether you need to update or maintain your gear, follow these six tips so all that’s left to do on opening day is load your gear into the car and drive.

Nothing ruins your first ski day like searching in vain for that one glove you swore was in your boot bag. And about those boots, didn’t you leave them in the downstairs closet back in April? The first item on your agenda is to make a shred list, literally. Work down from head to toe: Helmet, goggles, buff, jacket, gloves, pants, boots, skis, poles. Knowing where you left everything is half the battle. Taking a good look at their condition is critical.

“First thing’s first, if you need to stop by your local ski shop, go now before the season starts, and definitely before the holidays,” said Otto Gibbons, hardgoods supervisor for Sturtevants Ski Shope in Bellevue, Wash. Gibbons recommends taking a good look at your skis’ bases. “If there are any noticeable points of damage, like core shots or large gouges, get those skis tuned.” Look closely to see if there are different colors of base material in the core shot because if so, water can deteriorate your ski. “Large gouges will also slow you down on the hill and even affect how your ski hooks up at a lower edge angle,” Gibbons cautioned.

Next up, check your edges and sidewalls. “If you look along your skis’ sidewall and see any area where the edge is blown out, go to your local shop because sometimes those can be repaired and save the ski from a larger fail-point of separation,” Gibbons said. If you see rust, it’s the result of not drying your edges the last time you skied. A ski tech will tune both your side and base edges to remove the rust.

“If you cannot remember the last time you took your skis into the shop, do it now,” Gibbons said. “Skis should be waxed to keep the bases hydrated and fast.” If you are someone who holds on to gear forever, know that skis typically have a life expectancy of 300-400 days of hard skiing, so if your skis no longer have snap and response, it’s likely time to get a new pair.

When inspecting your boots, first make sure they are not missing any parts like buckles. Second, check the condition of the boot soles, because if you walked around the base area from morning through après last season, your soles may be ground down and therefore your binding may not release or retain your boot properly. “If you have replaceable soles, it is important to replace them if they have worn down close to the lug of the actual shell,” said Gibbons. A ski shop tech will help you figure out what replacement soles you need.

Now for the Cinderella approach: Put your boot on and make sure it still fits. It should feel like a firm handshake. “If your foot is different than it was before due to weight change, age, pregnancy or someone dropped a piano on it, then that might mean your boot fits differently,” cautioned Gibbons. “Remember you likely haven’t had your foot in constrictive footwear for a couple of months, so don’t panic; ‘a little tighter than I remember’ is common.” And make sure your liners are clear of foreign objects: “You’d be surprised what we find, including critters,” Gibbons told SKI.

The last thing to check is the condition of your liner. Stock liners have a life span of around 60 to 120 days of hard skiing before they get that packed-out feeling. “You can put a new aftermarket liner into a shell and breathe new life into the boot if you love your skiing experience in it,” said Gibbons. “If you are outperforming the boot, or the boot is old enough to vote, start looking for a new boot.”

If you took advantage of Labor Day sales and got new skis or boots, you still need to dial them in. Go now to mount your bindings on your new skis before the wait time increases at your local shop. Also, consider the compatibility of your setup if you made any changes. “If you got new Gripwalk soles on your boots, make sure your skis, including your powder boards, have bindings that are Gripwalk compatible, otherwise the binding will not function properly with the wrong soles in it,” Gibbons said.

If you have a new pair of boots, walk around the house in them to check for hot spots. “You’ll most likely have to get them punched or worked on,” said Ian Lochhead, head alpine ski coach for the University of Colorado. Lockhead recommends that recreational skiers prioritize comfort and an appropriate flex. “Ski racers often have boots that are too tight in the toe box, but you need that part of your foot to be able to move so you can be more athletic and control your edges better. If you’re into carving, get your canting and fit issues checked out by a boot fitter before you ski in new boots.”

Skis can perform great “out of the box,” but if you get a new pair, you might need to make some slight adjustments like de-tuning the sharp tips and tails. “Skis usually come good from the factory, but we always check them,” said Lochhead. “Any shop will be able to check the base and edge bevels of your new skis, and they can even tailor them to perform best for the drier snow in the Rockies or harder snow on the East Coast.”

Outerwear takes a hit every season—from rubbing up against your dirty car when loading your skis, to tears from your favorite glades. It would be a huge bummer if you find out there’s a large hole in the back of your pants on opening day, or that your jacket doesn’t repel water like it used to.

“It’s a good idea to wash your jacket in tech wash regularly, particularly with PFAS-Free DWRs,” said Will Dobrowski, materials coordinator for Stio. “These chemistries are affected more easily by oils and stains, so when the water on the outside of your jacket stops beading up, it’s time for a wash and dry. The dryer is actually what re-invigorates your DWR to help water bead more effectively, so if you need a quick fix in the morning, throw it in the dryer for 10 minutes on low heat.”

Dobrowski recommends checking for holes on the exterior of your outerwear, followed by interior seams to make sure the seam tape isn’t peeling away, which would allow water into the jacket. You can repair small holes with adhesive gear tape, but apply it to both sides. “I throw it in the dryer for 15 minutes after patching to help the glue adhere to the fabric,” he said. Lastly, check zippers, which are common places of wear. Some brands have programs to fix issues like replacing zippers, but keep in mind turnaround times vary.

Think back to last season: Did you hit your head? “As a rule of thumb, any fall that ‘rings your bell,’ even if you don’t get a concussion, would warrant getting a new helmet,” said Jon Jay, Sweet Protection’s North American brand manager. “It’s sort of like replacing a child’s car seat involved in any sort of car crash. Do you really want to risk a more serious injury because of unseen damage?”

Barring any crashes, it’s important to check the exterior shell for any warping or cracks because the outer shell of your helmet is your first line of defense, said Jay. Also make sure that the buckle is fully functional and the straps are not worn or frayed. You can remove the inner cloth liner and wash it, but don’t remove the Mips insert if your helmet has one.

“If you’re a skier who hasn’t taken a fall in a while, we recommend replacing your helmet every four to five seasons of regular use,” Jay told SKI. “Most modern helmets are built using very technically-engineered plastics, but they will lose strength and rigidity with regular use.”

Once you know which helmet you’ll use this season, make sure your goggles are compatible, because nothing says ice cream headache like goggle gap. Inspect the foam and strap to make sure there’s a good seal against your face and then check out the lens. “If your goggle lens has scratches, cracks, or cloudiness that interferes with your vision, it’s time to replace it,” said Grady Skelton, global snow marketing manager for Smith. “If you have interchangeable lenses, a damaged lens can be a quick, easy, and budget-friendly fix.”

Once you’ve checked these boxes, there’s only one thing to do: Refresh the forecast infinite times until you finally get the news you’ve been looking for.
