#8299. We Tested Survival Knives to Find the Best for Any Situation

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more

When you’re heading outdoors, you can never be too prepared—and that includes having the right survival knife on hand at all times. No one wants to find themselves in a life-or-death scenario in the wilderness. However, it can happen to anyone, even the most experienced hunters, anglers, hikers, and backpackers. This is where a good knife can help tip the scales in favor of one’s survival. Few success stories don’t include one at some point.

Whether used for shelter construction, fire starting, food preparation, or defense, knives are a catch-all tool. And while any knife could technically be a survival knife, some are better suited for emergency situations and extreme conditions than others. With that in mind, we put a handful of blades through extensive tests to find the best survival knives for every budget and every scenario.

When I previously tested bushcraft knives, I found the Tops Fieldcrafter to be the best. With bushcraft and survival so intertwined, it only made sense that this knife is also my top pick for this category. In short, this blade is a beast. Tops built it quite ruggedly with 150CM stainless steel. It has an extremely beefy feel in the hands. The blade shrugged off wood batoning tests as if it were nothing.

I used this knife to field dress a Wisconsin whitetail last November, and it handled the task easily. The sharp spine is also a great scraping and fire-starting tool. The only potential con is that the knife’s scaling feels a little slick to me. I haven’t had an issue with it slipping, but I would appreciate more of a texture to the handle. Fortunately, the finger groove and jimping make up for that shortcoming. It’s not a cheap knife, but this is one of those cases where the price of admission is worth it.

I’ve owned the Kansbol for a few years, and it never fails to impress despite its bargain basement price point. Because it weighs less than 4 ounces, this is an excellent option for backpackers. I sometimes forget I have this one in my pack because it’s so light. The versatility of the blade can’t be understated either. Morakniv gave it a unique modified combination of Scandi and flat grind. It will handle everything from light woodwork to food processing.

I love the spine on this knife. It is sharp and throws a huge spark for fire starting. This spine does it better than some of the $300+ knives that I own. The handle is simple and surprisingly ergonomic despite a plain appearance.

The only real downside of the Kansbol is that it is not a full tang. It’s not something to split wood or use on other heavy projects. However, the trade-off is worth it because this knife is practical for many other tasks. For under $40, it’s a true bargain. It’s worth consideration as a secondary knife, even if you already have a primary one. That’s how much I like this knife. Even seasoned survivalists will find a lot to like with the Kansbol.

Benchmade didn’t play around when they designed the Mini Bushcrafter. This rugged knife is beefy and ready for abuse in a survival situation. The CPM-S30V steel gives this knife some incredible edge retention qualities. I’ve been testing it for several months and haven’t worn down the factory edge yet. This knife is much lighter and more natural in the hands than the original Bushcrafter.

I love the balance of this blade. Despite a shortened blade length, it carves, notches, and slices on par with my best knives. It’s also just a great-looking knife. Benchmade paired it with an excellent Ferro-rod ready sheath. The knife might be slightly undersized for some tasks, like wood batoning. However, during my testing, I managed to split the wood with it. It just takes a little more awareness of the shorter blade length. There is no denying it’s thick enough for high-leverage jobs. The CPM-S30V steel also drives the price point up quite a bit. However, for situations where one’s life might be on the line, this is one knife where it’s worth not skimping.

Wargoat is an awesome name for a knife, and it has the performance to match. During my testing, this Montana Knife Company knife sliced through most materials like butter. This is technically a defense knife. However, it effortlessly carves and feathersticks wood without affecting the edge. The choice to use MagnaCut steel with a Cerakote finish is inspired. It’s meant to cut down on flash that could give away the user’s position. Consequently, it also gives the knife the perfect edge retention and corrosion resistance combination. This gives this knife some excellent peace of mind for survival scenarios. Maintenance is going to be minimal.

I love the handle on this knife. MKC added texturing to the G-10 handles, making it rock solid in the hands.  This knife is extremely expensive, at over $300. Part of that price comes from its being made in the USA. Its smaller size also limits it for some survival scenarios. This tactical knife is better as a secondary knife for defense in the wild. It will probably be a popular item for soldiers and game wardens who work outdoors frequently. Overall, I love the quality of the craftsmanship here. This knife was designed and manufactured with care, and it shows.

The Izula is an impressive little knife with a versatility factor that’s off the charts. When I think of tactical, I think concealable. That’s what the Izula does best. It’s an excellent neck knife but it also works well for horizontal carry. Because it weighs under 2 ounces, it’s a knife that’s easy to carry and forget until needed. This knife has the thinnest profile of any that I own. It’s great to slip in those narrow front pockets of a survival pack as a backup.

It amazes me that this knife sells for under $70. I like it for light carving, trap construction, and wild game preparation tasks.  This knife is a little undersized for some survival tasks. No one is going to baton wood with it. It also doesn’t come with scales, which can provide a better grip. However, I don’t think that’s a dealbreaker. Aftermarket scales are plentiful and cheap. This is also a great option for anyone who likes making paracord wraps. Ultimately, this knife has many uses in a survival scenario, making it worthy of consideration.

The Buck 119 is a classic knife design that never goes out of style. It features a versatile clip-point Bowie-style blade that excels in nearly every facet of bushcraft. Buck touts this one as a hunting knife. Subsequently, we like it best for survivalists who expect to clean game and fish frequently. However, the full-tang design is also beefy enough for wood splitting and shelter construction projects. The 6-inch length makes for an ideal, do-all type of knife. We also like the ergonomics of the handle. It has subtle finger grooves that conform to most hands perfectly.

The finish of this knife is easily scratched, but for survival purposes, it doesn’t matter much. Some users will like the sheath, and others will hate it. That feature is more a matter of preference than any other part of this knife. However, this knife does deliver something for everyone. Buck also builds variants in three different steel qualities. That gives it more versatility budget-wise than other fixed-blade survival knives.

This Uncharted Supply Co. knife isn’t well-known, which is a shame because it is a solid survival knife. I’m a sucker for ergonomics, and I love what it brings to the table. The rubberized grip has never slipped in my hands. Add a perfect finger groove and ramped-up jimping, and it fits my hand like a glove. It’s beefy enough for heavy tasks, too. I easily split wood with this knife. Uncharted includes a small whetstone and a decent fire starter. This knife is also my pick for the best with a fire starter. It throws a big spark with the included rod.

At $40, it’s incredibly affordable. It’s worth throwing one in the glovebox or boat as a backup. This knife has some serrations, which I know some survival enthusiasts shy away from. However, I think they have a case use here. It’s good for ice anglers and bush pilots who might need to cut their seatbelt quickly in an emergency. There is also a glass breaker on the end for exiting a sinking vehicle quickly.

The Hunter Pro Alox is a gorgeous and robust folding knife. During my testing, I found that the blade locks into place with a meaty snap. As a folder, it doesn’t have the ability to split wood, but it is still very capable. I noticed zero wiggle or play in the blade when locked into place. It handles light carving and bushcraft tasks quite admirably. I haven’t field-dressed a deer with this blade yet, but I can already tell it would be up for the task. A slight finger groove and subtle jimping give great control to the blade tip. I like the feel of the aluminum scaling. It’s not as tacky as I normally like my knife handles, but I’ve never had this knife slip.

I tested this knife on everything from wood to paracord and cardboard. It still has a great edge. The main downside of this knife is that the aluminum scaling won’t be ideal in a cold environment. It makes the knife a little difficult to grip in cold conditions. For every other scenario, it is more than capable. It’s a solid EDC knife that can easily transition to a survival situation in a pinch.

Fortunately, I haven’t found myself in a survival scenario. However, I have spent time testing various knives in survival tasks. These include starting fires, splitting wood, sticking feathers, carving, and more. Some of these knives were given heavy-duty cardboard ripping tests. Those tests were great for judging edge retention because of how quickly the material dulls an edge.   Additionally, I evaluated knives based on ergonomics, sheaths, and carrying ability. Some knives were chosen based on input from other outdoor enthusiasts I know and trust. Other factors that were considered during testing include:

Any knife is better than no knife in a survival situation. However, some types are better suited for different purposes. It depends on what one’s goals are for a survival situation. Knives best suited for light food prep are vastly different from shelter-building tools. These are some of the more popular options.

Fixed blades are the more popular choice for survival because of their versatility. With a full tang, a fixed-blade knife can seamlessly transition from wood splitting to food prep to shelter construction. With a proper sharp spine, it is the safest way to start a fire using a Ferro rod. This style is also excellent for field dressing and skinning wild game. The main downsides to a fixed blade are weight and ease of carry.

Folders offer a huge weight savings advantage over fixed blades. However, these knives aren’t robust enough for tasks like wood splitting. They are good for lighter tasks like food preparation or light trap construction. Some folding knives are also a good choice for cleaning game animals or fish.

The proper grind is essential for survival. Most survival experts prefer a Scandi, which is more of a wedge shape, for chopping and splitting. Flat grinds work better as an “all-purpose” type of grind. Consider the flat grind if planning to do food prep with the knife. When it comes to edges, a simple straight edge is best. Mainly because it’s the easiest to sharpen. I did include one partially serrated option on this list. That edge is handy for cutting heavy fabrics and fibers, like a seat belt.

In most instances, a slightly larger knife is better. Knives in the 8 to 10-inch overall length range are best. Blades in the 4.5 to 7-inch range are better for heavy tasks like wood batoning. Bigger isn’t always better, though. Knives that are too large can be a burden to carry.

Most experts agree that a drop point is usually best. These blades usually have a Scandi grind that’s easy to sharpen in the field. That grind is ideal for wood carving tasks. This knife shape usually has a deep belly, which is especially handy when skinning game animals.

#8298. Traversing the Saiga Silk Road

As we skidded off the main road and onto a mud path maintained only by tire treads, lines began to blur.

Flanking our two-track trail were a series of parallel lanes no more than a foot wide, which forked, merged, and crisscrossed our own. In the distance, I saw what looked like a ghost train, faintly visible and thrust forward by howling Siberian winds.

Through borrowed binoculars, I soon got my first glimpse of an ancient tableau, seemingly untouched since Neanderthals roamed the earth. On the far horizon, hundreds of nomadic travelers pierced the frigid air with their ringed horns, inhaling the brittle shards through Snuffleupagus snouts as they sprinted across the desolate steppe.

Watching them charge through the treeless plain at full bore, I was reminded of a saying I’d heard shortly before arriving in this remote corner of Kazakhstan: “The saiga is a freedom-loving animal.”

Since time immemorial, saiga antelope have blazed trails across Central Asia while other civilizations rose and fell around them. They once inhabited a world dominated by woolly mammoths, saber-toothed cats, and giant deer with antlers 12 feet across—and outlived them all. When pioneering human caravans first attempted to navigate this unforgiving land, they considered the saigas to be their guides.

Ahead of my arrival, seasonal rains transformed once-green grasslands into sludge punctuated by tufts of withering brush. Driving through such muck is, I would soon discover, akin to controlled hydroplaning. The steering wheel bucked wildly as our tires swerved, shredding deep into the gunk and desperately gripping anything remotely solid enough to push off from.

In the front seats were Alexandr and Albert, two team members from the Association for the Conservation of Biodiversity of Kazakhstan, or ACBK. Between them, they have more than twenty-five years of experience following saigas across the steppe, and I’d arranged to join them for the western leg of one of their field audits.

Our visit was timed to coincide with the rutting season, a critical part of the year for saigas. This is a gathering time, when antelope from across the region sprint together in massive single-file lines, before congregating for a series of competitive battles and subsequent mating rituals.

For males, it’s a time for strutting and headbutting to demonstrate one’s physical prowess to female onlookers—an activity so energy-intensive that many will forget to eat and keel over from extreme physical exhaustion. For females, this is a time of choosing. In addition to assessing fitness, they pay particular attention to one distinctive feature: a potential mate’s floppy, elongated nose. The saigas’ sniffers are essential for filtering out dust in the semidesert plains and for warming frigid winter air before it reaches their lungs. A large nose is the ultimate sign of virility, so as the males marched into these annual gatherings, they were doing everything they could to accentuate their schnozzes.

Because of the saigas’ preference for large-scale migrations across a landscape almost entirely devoid of trees, they have long been a favorite of global wildlife trackers. The isolation and starkness of the saiga world is a strength when it comes to GPS collars, which deliver a reliable stream of daily pings without risk of visual obstruction. Prior to such breakthroughs, conservationists would sometimes spend weeks roaming the boundless steppe unsuccessfully trying to locate the nomadic herds.

The wildlife sanctuary we were traveling through was created only a year prior, with its boundaries informed by tracking data that Albert and his team personally collected. He seemed pleased that the animals were continuing to use the newly designated space as intended. Standing along the roadside, Alexandr spotted a stream of the famously skittish ungulates wrapping around the contours of the earth. As he did, ripping wind and snow started blowing in sideways—the outer ring of an encroaching storm.

These were no fluffy flakes. This was the harsh, crunchy ice of a walk-in freezer, which instantly hardened our truck’s caked-on mud like liquid nitrogen.

Seemingly unperturbed by the dropping barometer, Albert chirped, “Who’s hungry?” Setting up an impromptu picnic, he and Alexandr dug into a prepared meal of fresh bread, tea, and dried meats of unknown provenance. In a muted attempt to thaw my face, I opted to guzzle spicy instant noodles.

A tradition of nomadism has loomed large in this corner of the world since at least the Early Iron Age. The very word kazakh is thought to be derived from the Turkic word qaz, which means “wanderer” or “vagabond.” For millennia, small human groups routinely migrated to higher altitudes in the hot summer months, where melting snow made for abundant water and greenery, before returning to sheltered valleys ahead of winter’s whipping winds. At various times of the year, disparate nomads would also congregate for formal meetings and large cultural festivals, complete with physical challenges like wrestling and tug-of-war. When the gatherings were finished, the nomads dispersed once again.

Historical analysis has shown that nomads’ seasonal migrations and time-honed transit corridors may have helped pave the way for portions of the Great Silk Road, which was less a singular route than an ever-evolving web of pathways and bypasses that linked together reliable stopovers. At the Silk Road’s peak, this corner of western Kazakhstan along the fertile banks of the Ural River became a vital transcontinental crossroads. To this day, the river still serves as a natural boundary between Asia and Europe, meaning this part of Kazakhstan is, quite literally, where East meets West.

The land above the Caspian Sea also served as a main artery that linked together key transit points. Strategic settlements along the riverbank allowed weary caravans to rest their heads, unwind in large public baths, exchange knowledge, stock up on essential supplies, and regroup before moving onward.

Among overland voyagers traversing the continental divide, saigas have long been spoken of with an almost mythical reverence. Cave paintings of the antelope created as far back as the seventh century BCE depict them as resilient, elusive, and charismatic. Expert navigators who embody the true spirit of a most inhospitable terrain.

In human society, traditional nomadic practices persisted even as the land itself was variously claimed and reclaimed by Turkic tribes, Genghis Khan, and the Russian Empire. Only with the rise of the Soviet Union in the twentieth century did mandatory sedentarization efforts successfully manage to lock nomadic people in place, force them to farm, and extinguish a cultural flame that had burned brightly for millennia. Denied the ability to live in perpetual motion, people’s navigational muscles began to atrophy.

This transition was viewed by many as an inevitable shift toward “modernization,” but it also represented a significant diversion from our own history as a species. Of the roughly 300,000 years that Homo sapiens have existed, we spent the first 288,000 of them living in small, mobile groups that followed the migratory patterns of other animals. Forcing nomads into agricultural plots was also a colossal failure because much of the steppe soil was unsuitable for growing crops, which is why so many people were nomadic in the first place. Iconic filmmaker Werner Herzog once remarked that “whatever went wrong and makes our civilization something doomed is the departure from the nomadic life.”

Whether by choice or necessity, most Kazakh people now lead stationary lives in urban centers. The world that nomads once freely roamed has also been feverishly transformed, not only by agriculture but through the construction of new roads and railways.

For the saigas, whose nomadic days never ceased, these new layers now represent an existential threat.

With the weather taking a turn for the worse, Albert and Alexandr ultimately decided to call it a day and start fresh in the morning. After a blistering drive through whiteout conditions, we hunkered down in a tiny village less than 10 miles from the Russian border, where Albert pulled out his laptop and showed me how saiga movements have changed over the years.

“They would routinely trek hundreds of miles as part of an expansive migratory route across the Eurasian steppe,” he said. “Saigas could be found from the Caucasus Mountains to Mongolia, and everywhere in between.”

For millennia, they lived with few barriers and obstructions on the landscape. Then, seemingly overnight, rattling railways and roaring roads began to crisscross the region, fragmenting the saigas into smaller, more isolated groups. As the interior steppe got more accessible to vehicles and passengers, development begat more development.

On his screen, Albert clicked open a recent map that showed how a population of GPS-collared saigas once routinely traveled deep into Uzbekistan before being unceremoniously clipped off by a new rail line in 2014. The data from the years prior to the railway’s construction showed a flurry of squiggly lines representing individual animals zipping back and forth with the seasons. The post-construction slide showed those same animals spinning around despondently on the northern side of the tracks, while the fresh grasses and water they had come to rely on withered away to the south.

Such interruptions can lead to a complete collapse in spatial knowledge—a loss that science writer Ben Goldfarb once wrote is “as thorough as the erasure of a language.” Just as human nomads forced to stay in one place eventually lost connection to the physical landmarks of their ancestors’ journeys, young saigas learn where they can reliably find food and shelter, as well as places to stay away from, through active participation and observation. This cultural exchange keeps their world in orbit and is one of the reasons they have been successful at navigating a terrain fatal to so many before them. As the land they know is cleaved and partitioned, whole stretches of the Saiga Silk Road begin to fade from memory.

To unwind this damage, Albert’s team has partnered with the Kazakh government to construct dozens of saiga-friendly crossing points, where slightly sloping dirt ramps rise up to match the height of the train tracks, making it appear from a distance as though there’s a natural gap in the rail line. Cattle-guard fences positioned far away from the crossings ensure that trains and saigas never actually run into each other at these intersections, which would shatter the illusion of safety.

ACBK has also worked with the Uzbek government to reshape its border fences from a barbed-wire wall to an X-shaped barricade that blocks vehicles from driving through but leaves just enough space for saigas to pass. Over time, Albert hopes such efforts can rebuild the trust necessary for them to confidently return to a plateau they once relied on.

The next morning, I was astonished by how austere the steppe looked compared with the day before. Gone was the slippery muck and browning grasses of shifting seasons, replaced by a blanket of crunchy snow. Against this stark black-and-white backdrop, the fresh crystals functioned like fingerprint dust, illuminating the only remaining pops of color: the rust-red streaks of human and nonhuman pathways in the dirt.

Parked in an otherwise empty tract of prairie land, we watched in stunned silence as thousands of saigas seized the day, flying like banshees across the periphery, their hooves gouging the frozen crust and stamping pigment into an earthen canvas.

As I gazed east toward the colorless horizon, I tried to envision how it might have looked in the thirteenth century, when this corner of the world boasted a vast network of caravanserai, or road inns, where exhausted travelers could rest and recover before continuing onward into the great unknown.

I pondered what it must have felt like for an intrepid merchant to know that they would not see another human being for many days, maybe weeks. To be fearful of what you may soon encounter, but take solace that the space between is not wholly empty. For there is life beyond humanity’s margins, and among nonhuman communities, that in-between space is the center of everything. That, I imagined, must have offered some measure of assurance that the road ahead, perilous though it may be, is well traveled.

This essay was adapted from the new nonfiction travelogue The Hidden Nations of Animals and is published here exclusively for Adventure Journal, with permission from Penguin Random House.

#8297. ‘There Was No Controlling that Fish.’ Two Buddies Land One of the Largest Blue Marlin Ever Caught in Southern California

Published Nov 2, 2026 12:56 PM EST

The hottest fishing news, tips, and tactics

California fishing buddies Mike Mackenback and Matt Mackinga headed their 20-foot fishing boat into the Pacific at about daybreak on October 25. They were targeting wahoo, which had been hitting off the coast of southern California, but they were about to catch something much bigger.

“We ran south, looking for water temperature breaks where we believed wahoo would be found,” Mackenback tells Outdoor Life. “We were trolling by about 8 a.m., with three lines out – one a deep diving plug, a surface-skipping ‘Black Bart’ lure on another line, and a far back shotgun line with a lure.

“We were about 12 miles from San Pedro, trolling on a beautiful slick-ocean with clear water about 1,500-feet deep.”

Mackenback is a veteran marine boatman, having worked on tugboats and as a merchant marine. He knows boats and fishing and trolled fast at 8 knots for wahoo along a water temperature break from 73 to 75 degrees.

“The fish came up and smashed the surface skipping Black Bart lure about 30 minutes after we started,” says Mackenback, 29, who is now a real estate agent in Redondo Beach. “I thought at first it was a striped marlin until it jumped, then I knew it was huge – there was no controlling that fish as it ran 400 yards of line off a reel in one minute.”

Mackenback held the trolling rod which was set with a Shimano 30 Tiagra reel. It was spooled with 80-pound test Spectra braided line, with a top-shot of 50-pound test monofilament, and a 25-foot 200-pound test fluorocarbon leader.

Mackenback quickly realized they had hooked a huge blue marlin that was rapidly taking all the line off his reel, which was rigged for wahoo and much smaller striped marlin.

“I gave the rod to Matt, he went to the bow to fight the fish, and I turned the boat to chase after it,” Mackenback says. “The marlin was jumping and racing away, and I chased it with the boat for a few minutes while Matt tried to gain some of the line it took on those blistering runs.”

Matt kept the line tight on the marlin, and Mackenback got closer to the fish with his boat.

Then the marlin dove deep as it got a second wind during the fight.

“It almost spooled us twice,” says Mackenback. “Matt would gain line fighting the fish. I’d stay over it with the boat, and then it would dive deep again, and again, and again.

“We traded back and forth fighting the fish with the rod. We had no fighting belt or harness – just a small slide on the rod butt cushion. I didn’t think there was a 10 percent chance we’d catch and release it. My wahoo tackle wasn’t built for a giant blue marlin.”

One hour into the epic battle, the anglers decided to just follow the blue with their boat, trying to tire it out over time.

Almost two hours into the marlin battle they gained enough line on the fish that they could see its shiny blue color deep below in clear water. Then it dove deep again, and it was another 45 minutes before they spotted the fish near their boat.

“Suddenly the line went slack, and I thought it was gone,” Mackenback says. “We saw the swivel to the leader, grabbed it, and hauled on the leader to get it close.

“The fish was whipped, I knew it was gone as I was holding 600-pounds of blue marlin beside my 20-foot boat.”

They tried multiple times to revive the marlin for release. But the big blue fought until it was dead. There was no way they could get the marlin pulled up into their Grady-White boat. So, they lashed it to the side of their boat and ran slowly back to San Pedro’s Cabrillo Way Marina where they’d left that morning.

They notified the marina they were coming in with a huge marlin, and a crane was waiting for the anglers to haul the fish up and weigh it.

Their blue marlin measured more than 13 feet and weighed 595 pounds. It’s one of the largest blues ever caught off Southern California. Giant blues are believed to have moved into the region due to unusual water and weather conditions in this El Nino year.

In September 2015, a 648-pound blue marlin was caught 40 miles off San Diego by anglers aboard the boat Pegasus. A 692-pound blue was caught also during an El Nino year off the coast of Southern California.

Read Next: My Outboard Died — Just as We Hooked Up with a Giant Marlin

Mackenback and Mackinga cleaned and processed their marlin, and had some of it for dinner that night.

“We spent hours processing the marlin into steaks, and gave a lot of it to neighbors and friends,” says Mackenback. “We grilled marlin steaks that night and had a great cookout.”

Bob McNally has been an outdoor writer since shortly after the earth’s crust cooled. He has written 12 outdoor books, more than 5,000 outdoor magazine stories (including many for Outdoor Life) and more newspaper outdoor columns and features than there are hairs on a grizzly bear.

#8296. How Two Bored Belgians Broke the Backyard Ultra World Record

Trail Runner contributing photographer Jacob Zocherman drove 15 hours from his home in Sweden to document the Belgian team at the 2026 Backyard Ultra World Team Championship in Retie, Belgium. Unlike a typical race with a predetermined finish and a predictable narrative arc within it, backyard ultras only end when there is one runner left. Zocherman spent the five days and four hours of what ended up being a world-record-breaking run on the course, sleeping in a camper van when he could. He spoke with managing editor Abby Levene during and shortly after the race.

Ivo Steyaert and Merijn Geerts had been running for 98 hours at the 2026 Backyard Ultra World Team Championship, and they were bored. Never mind they had each run over 400 miles on the same 4.167-mile course. Never mind they hadn’t gotten more than a few minutes of sleep at once in over four days. They looked fresh, the nights were long, and blah blah blah, on-the-ground photographer Jacob Zocherman reports. But with the 100th lap on the horizon, something clicked.

“You could see something happen to them, like a spring flower waiting through winter,” Zocherman tells Trail Runner. “Suddenly the sun comes and nothing happens, nothing happens, and then in a specific moment everything happens and the flower comes out in bloom. That’s what I saw in them—suddenly they were happy to be there, cheering with the audience, laughing with each other and joking.”

It was like colleagues going out to the bar on a Friday afternoon: They’ve found their happy place, Zocherman says. Except in this case, their happy place was a park in Retie, Belgium, aka the middle of nowhere.

“It’s very touching to see, because they are so humble and so easy to like,” Zocherman says. “At that point, I felt like the race would go on forever. But it also feels very fragile—when there are only two runners left, there is no room for error.”

Per backyard ultra rules, runners must run the 4.167-mile lap on the hour, every hour, until only one runner remains and is declared the winner. In case that isn’t nutty enough, the Backyard Ultra World Team Championship is an even nuttier spinoff of this format: Each participating country (of which this year there were 67) simultaneously conducts its own backyard race with 15 participants, and the country with the most cumulative laps wins. This backyard team world championship now alternates every other year with the individual championship, held on the original backyard ultra course in mastermind Gary “Lazarus Lake” Cantrell’s backyard in Bell Buckle, Tennessee.

Team USA would go on to win the team world title, with Mark Dowdle leading the stars and stripes to a collective 1,120 laps, also known as “yards,” for its second world title in six years. Australia took second, 51 yards behind, and Belgium took third, 11 yards off of them. While the team competition inherently shaped the dynamic of the race, with runners sacrificing their own best interests to slow down and pull teammates along, Steyaert and Geerts had several additional goals on their minds.

They’d each run over 100 laps multiple times—four times for Steyaert and six for Geerts. But neither had ever run through a fifth night. Belgium’s fourth-place runner Kenneth Vanthuyne was long gone after hallucinating that he was at work when Steyaert and Geerts put on their headlamps for the fifth time.

“That was the critical moment,” Zocherman says. “It was the one thing they had always wanted to do.”

As the sun rose over the dewy fields surrounding the dirt road of the race course, they both looked unscathed.

“I was like, ‘OK, nothing can stop them,” Zocherman says. They turned their attention to the Belgium national backyard ultra record of 115 laps, held by Jan Vandekerckhove. They checked that off and reset the goal to the world record of 119 laps, set by Australia’s Phil Gore at Dead Cow Gully in Queensland last year. That, too, proved to be seemingly no problem.

At 5:00 p.m. on Thursday, October 22—over five days after they started running—Zocherman heard rumors that Steyaert and Geerts were setting out on their final lap.

“I think they could have continued. They looked fresh, they looked really good,” Zocherman says. “But I also know they wanted to finish together. And the longer you go, the smaller the margins are that something will happen and one will finish over the other. And they wanted to avoid that. But they wanted to finish together.”

Sure enough, when the pair returned to the start/finish arch at 5:57 p.m., they did not go back out when the clock reached the top of the hour. Instead, the two friends, standing side-by-side in matching red shirts, grinned to the crowd of cheering onlookers, each raising a hand and joining them together over their heads in the shape of a heart.

Together, they had accomplished what no one had done before: Run 124 laps of a 4.167-mile course every hour, on the hour, for a total of 516.7 miles and a new backyard ultra individual world record.

“They are like brothers and have run many times as the two remaining runners,” Zochermans says. “So to them, it is not a competition that late in the race. They are doing it together. And they want it to remain like that. It’s kind of beautiful. It’s poetry.”

From the start at 2 p.m. local time on Saturday, October 17, until Steyaert and Geerts concluded their record-breaking run five days and four hours later, Zocherman was on the ground to document it all. It’s a stroke of good fortune that of the 67 backyard ultra team competitions happening around the world, Zocherman—who lives in his native Sweden—chose to go to Belgium. It’s also not a coincidence.

In fact, Zocherman almost didn’t make the 15 hour drive to Retie after his mother was unexpectedly diagnosed with an aggressive form of cancer two weeks before the race. The only reason he did go, Zocherman tells Trail Runner, is because that random campground in a foreign country is like home. Zocherman had been at the same course in April for the Legends Backyard Ultra, and the mini-universe environment of these events bring people together in a special way that’s hard to describe.

“It was an emotional rollercoaster and a logistical battle,” Zocherman says. “I wouldn’t have gone if it wasn’t this backyard ultra. It was a personal reason to be among people I know and like. I didn’t think it would be the crazy result that it was.”

Zocherman made the trek with his dog Balou, who he says keeps him grounded at these events with no predetermined end, or even rhythm. (She’s now witnessed three world records and could not be less impressed.) They did two laps of the course every day and got a decent amount of sleep for the first few nights before squeezing in 20 minutes at a time between loops by the end.

“I also know it will be a very long race and I have to drive home for 15 hours after so I can’t be crazy wasted,” he says. “Although you become crazy wasted anyway.”

Here’s how this world-record-setting run unfolded, through Zocherman’s eyes and words.

The first out of 372 whistles marks the start for the team world championships, by whistler Eilis Lanclus.

Matthias Pelgrims, one of the top runners the Belgian team is preserving his energy during the first loops of the competition.

Never a dull moment for the crews in between the loops. Always something to worry about.

The hula skirt. Once in a while there is a loop with someone wearing a hula skirt in order to break the monotony.

Resting runners in-between the loops with the watcher waiting to collect.

The puzzle. Whatever brings joy to the table and something to do during the early days is welcomed.

Approaching camp on day three. It’s a misty and cool morning after a very wet and challenging second night of the race.

The runners don’t fear the rain so much during the race, they say. It’s the wind ripping over the exposed night loop that they worry about.

Willem De Troyer is suffering from pain in his legs and is screaming out in pain at every step during what would be his last loop before timing out.

The emotions are rising as the race continues.

Jelle Tielemans is having a hard time during day three, moments before he quits. After 45 hours of racing, only 13 runners of the 990 who started in 67 countries remain.

As the race goes on, usually runners move closer to the start area in order to save time in between the loops.

Bert Verbist on his way back to the camp after yet another successful loop.

Common duties by different hands. Although the race is repetitive, the things that need to be done are endless and carried out by volunteers throughout all the hours of the day and night.

The remains of a celebration for Merijn Geerts, who turned 52 during the race.

Evariest Callens gets a massage on his throbbing legs after 69 hours of running.

Matthias Pelgrims, who just timed out after 68 loops, receives an emotional hug from his partner Jody.

Matthias Pelgrims, who just timed out after 68 loops, receives an emotional hug from his partner Jody.

The intersection of the two loops. The night loop is more open and exposed, while the day loop is more sheltered but also a bit more technical in the forest.

Merijn Geerts takes a micro-nap in between loops.

Tanja Steyaert crews her husband Ivo throughout the race.

The control center with the camera feeds from different parts of the loops, as well as the race broadcast and other tracking sites.

A tense wait for the remaining runners to finish their loops and go out for another.

Sleep is grabbed when you can and where you can. Nothing is certain in a backyard ultra, other than knowing you will get little sleep.

Ivo Steyaert and Merijn Geerts run through the fifth night. They are the only remaining runners of the 15 who started for Team Belgium.

The party is getting real in the Belgian countryside.

Ivo Steyaert and Merijn Geert’s backyard ultra world record is celebrated with the power cutting out (and the start/finish arch falling down) after heavy rain broke the electric circuits. But nothing, seemingly, can stop their progress.

The remains of the previous days. A lot of food, drinks, and beer.

Ultimately, Ivo Steyaert and Merijn Geert ran 124 loops—and set a new world record—before stopping.

In running and in life: Ivo Steyaert and Merijn Geerts celebrate with their wives as well as crews after setting the world record.

#8295. Counter Drone Technology Has Come to Deer Hunting and Landowners Are Starting to Fight Back

Published Nov 2, 2026 3:39 PM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

You’re five minutes into legal shooting with high hopes for your morning sit, then you hear it. A faint buzzing overhead. Eyes to the sky, you spot the drone hovering over your property. Suddenly, you’re less optimistic about your hunt.

[Insert neighbor] is up to no good again, you think. But is it actually who you think it is? How can you be sure? Basic, consumer-level drones can fly for miles. They can also spook deer and other wildlife on both public and private land.

Talk to landowners and deer hunters in Big Deer country and you’ll hear that drone usage has skyrocketed in recent years. Sure, there are a lot of folks flying drones legally during deer season. In many places it’s legal to fly a drone while attempting to recover a hit deer. Thermal drones are incredibly effective at this. But more and more, folks are using drones to scan other people’s properties in order to locate (and sometimes harass) big bucks.

Enter the drone defense system — a technology that defends against unwanted drones flying over a hunting property for all the wrong reasons.

Modern deer hunting and land management look vastly different than they did just a few years ago. Today, drones weave through several aspects of whitetail management and sometimes hunting and poaching, too. Drones are used for population surveys, property management, and deer recovery. These are common reasons deer hunters and land managers consult drone operators or fly their own drones. So long as laws are followed and ethical hunting is prioritized, there’s nothing wrong with any of that. In fact, when used properly, drones can be a net positive for whitetail herds, especially when sound management is the driving force.

But like with any new technology, some people are hellbent on using thermal drones for unethical purposes, namely, spying on the neighbor’s deer — and possibly even poaching them. That has sparked the need for the drone defense systems being promoted by Jack Huston, owner and operator of Midwest Deer Surveys.

“Most of the problem is people flying over property they don’t own or have permission to be on,” Huston says. “It’s not so much local landowners flying every day trying to know how to hunt a buck. It’s more people scouting the whole township, if you will.

“That’s a huge problem, and in my eyes, it’s trespassing,” Huston says. “People work so hard to have land to hunt. They work to make it ready for hunting season. Then, if somebody wants to just go fly a drone and buzz your deer, they can. And I don’t think that should be OK.”

The fast-growing popularity of drones in the hunting world creates a whole barrage of questions: What are the regulations around drones? Is it legal to fly over someone else’s property? Will wildlife agencies be using drone tracking tech to prevent poaching? Huston says the laws are very different from state to state.

“You know, Ohio is completely wide open — probably too much so,” Huston says. “Then there are some states that are what I call anti-drone.”

For example, Pennsylvania prohibits drone usage for any type of hunting, including tracking wounded deer.

Huston’s system allows a landowner to identify when a drone flies their property, and who the drone is registered to.

“I go all around the country doing deer surveys for landowners,” Huston said. “I talk to all of these people, and they are complaining about drones flying over their farms. A lot of times, these people are bigger landowners in the area, and people get curious.

“A lot of people pushed me to find a product that could essentially serve as a radar for drones. That is this product. People are setting them up at their house or barn and it just sits there and monitors the drone activity on that property, and all around it.”

The system picks up the transmission between the remote controller and the drone itself. It’s able to read that transmission and get the location of the pilot, location of the drone, the make of the drone, its serial number, and more. It records all of that and stores it for the user.

The collected drone detection information feeds back to an app on the landowner’s phone. It lets them know who’s flying, where they’re flying, and everything that’s going on in their airspace. It’s essentially a monitoring tool to alert landowners when someone is flying their property.

“With these drone detectors, we have real data of how many people are flying, and it’s certainly far more than I thought,” Huston says.

Huston says you can buy one of several drone defense system sizes and choose from options that cover roughly a 5-mile, 20-mile, or 40-mile radius.

“A lot of my customers are just geo-fencing their farm,” Huston says. “So, they’re creating a bit of a bubble around their property where they want to cover the skies.”

But as you can probably guess, setting up one of these systems isn’t cheap. Smaller stations start at about $5,000 while the bigger station will set you back about $12,000. Still, for a large property owner who has spent millions of dollars on owning the ground and implementing habitat work, the cost of a drone surveillance system is only a drop in the bucket.

While Huston doesn’t manufacture these himself (he works with a company on the manufacturing side), he helped establish and design the drone defense system.

Huston’s installations are already making positive impacts for some landowners who invest. He says there have been several instances where drones were detected, confirmations of illegal use were made, and law enforcement was called to intercept. Essentially, drones were being used to aid in poaching, and the drone defense systems assisted in prevention, and maybe eventual prosecution.

It does not take too much imagination to see how wildlife agencies and their game wardens might one day use similar drone detection systems to catch poachers and illegal fliers.

“Drones are the Wild West, right now,” Huston says. “I think, when the word gets out on these… It will push drones to be used how they’re supposed to be used.

Read Next: Drones Could Revolutionize How Hunters Recover Lost Deer … If They’re Not Banned First

“When I go out on my land, or my family’s land, I don’t want a drone bothering me,” Huston says. “And if there is one, I want to know who it is and solve that problem. This is the solution to that problem. Without it, people can get away with whatever they want.”

#8294. Swarovski NL Pure Binocular Review: The Best Glass Money Can Buy

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more

Let me tell you a story about how good the Swarovski NL Pure binocular is. On a combined elk and deer hunt in Montana, a fellow writer, two guides, and I were glassing a bedded whitetail buck from long way off, trying to figure out if he was worth a stalk. I was looking through the NL Pure, and the other guys were peering into various other high-end binos, none costing less than a grand and some costing much more than that.

Studying the deer, I said, “He’s got decent mass but isn’t super tall or wide. He might go 130 inches.” The other guys asked how I’d surmised all this from so far away. I handed him the NL Pure, and one after another, they said, “Oh!” and “Ah!” and “Holy sh*t!” Finally, they all agreed that the buck was somewhere between 125 and 130, and we tromped off to go look for another.

That’s what next-level resolution does for you. It doesn’t come cheaply, of course, but it makes a real difference in the field. And so, with that in mind, let’s take a close look at the Swarovski NL Pure, how it performed in my testing, and why I think it is the best hunting binocular you can buy today.

Related: The Best Binoculars of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

The NL Pure is not new. Not by a long shot. The first models in the series hit shelves way back in 2020, one of the few good things to happen in a no-good, rotten year. All the more impressive then that now, six years later, the NL Pure is still as good a binocular as you can find.

Not long after those first NL Pure offerings debuted, I awarded the 10×42 model our “Best Binocular at Any Price” award in F&S’s annual binocular test—and it has not relinquished that distinction since. Every year, I test the latest and the greatest glass, and I keep a 10×42 NL Pure handy to compare to the newest contenders. And for now, at least, it is still at the top of the heap.

I have written before that the gap between good and great binoculars is closing. That’s great news for hunters. But a handful of models still stand totally apart, and the NL Pure is the finest example of that. My 10×42 test model notched perfect scores in the resolution and image quality tests. With lots of binoculars, you have to look and look and strain your eyes to detect small differences in resolution. Not with these. The NL Pure’s advantage in resolving detail is immediately obvious, and the picture is as clean and bright as you could want, with virtually zero color shift, field curvature, or stray light. But it’s not enough to say that the binocular’s optical performance is the best or even perfect. It’s more like a revelation. You peer into it, and the world looks like a better place.

Meanwhile, the NL Pure’s innovative hour-glass, open-bridge design saves weight and balances perfectly in the hand, making it easy to stabilize the binocular on long glassing sessions, and an available forehead rest adds to the comfort. The focus wheel is large, precise, and silky. The diopter and eyecup adjustments are positive and exact.

Related: How to Use Your Binoculars and Spotting Scope to Hunt Elk, Mule Deer, and Antelope in the West

If you want to see exactly how I tested the NL Pure, you can go to our annual binocular test and look at the section called “How I Tested and Score Binoculars.” In a nutshell, I used a 1951 USAF Resolution Test Chart to test resolution in daylight and low-light conditions. I used a color-artifact chart to test for chromatic aberration. I also tested for edge-to-edge clarity, feeling of immersion (which we’ll get to), overall image quality, handling, ergonomics, build quality, and weather resistance.

In all of the optical categories, the NL Pure set the standard. Resolution was nothing short of astounding. But world-class glass like this offers more than just stunning detail; it immerses you in the image. An optics professor I used to test binoculars with calls this “feeling of immersion.” With the NL Pure’s huge field of view and field-flattening lenses, you get the sense that you’ve stepped into the picture and that everything there is brilliant and vivid and free of the little imperfections that otherwise distract you from the experience.

The quality of the construction is obvious the second you put this binocular in your hand, and everything from the focus wheel to the diopter functioned just as it should. All of that said, the NL Pure is not flawless. To my surprise, it pretty much bombed my weather-resistance test, which involved a half-hour submersion in a creek and then a half-hour visit to the deep freeze. After the submersion portion, the image was usable but not especially clear, and it was close to unusable coming out of the freezer. I should be clear that my test is obviously tougher than what most hunters will face in the outdoors. Still, it provides an apples-to-apples comparison, and only one binocular out of about 10 tested did worse.

That, however, is the NL Pure’s only flaw. In every other way, this binocular is spectacular. The other thing that is spectacular—as in breathtaking—is the price. The NL Pure now comes in seven configurations, from 8×32 to 14×52, and ranges in price from $2,799 to $3,849. For most of us, that’s a whole lot to spend on a binocular. But some hunters are willing to pay top dollar to own the best of the best. And the NL Pure is exactly that. Give it a little extra protection in rough weather, and it will show you things other hunters will never see.

#8293. Christopher Wren, Climber and Legendary Reporter, Had a “Wry Sense of Humor”

Christopher Wren at basecamp during the 1974 Pamir Expedition. In this photo, he is using a typewriter to draft the New York Times story that revealed the deaths of American climber Gary Ullin and eight Soviet female climbers. (Photo: Courtesy of Jed Williamson)

Christopher Sale Wren served as The New York Times bureau chief in Moscow, Cairo, Beijing, Ottawa, and Johannesburg. His creative life was deeply intertwined with a respect for nature, big expeditions and the many people he met on assignment. He passed at his home in Vermont on February 15, 2026, at age 89.

Wren began climbing as a student at Dartmouth, where he sometimes felt out of place, according to his daughter, Celia. A scholarship student whose parents were actors, he had little interest in fraternity life. In the outdoors, he found a bigger sense of kinship. He learned to climb with the college’s mountaineering club, practicing on campus at Bartlett Tower and on the nearby cliffs of Orford and Owl’s Head. According to Samuel C. Silverstein’s memorial in The American Alpine Journal, he once ended a public-speaking assignment on mountaineering by rappelling out of the classroom’s third-floor window.

In 1962, Wren joined the six-man team that made the first ascent of Denali’s Southeast Spur (Alaska grade 4, 65-degree ice). The expedition became the subject of his first major article for Look magazine, merging his climbing with his reporting into a career he chased around the world.

Twelve years later, while stationed in Moscow for the Times, he joined an American expedition to the Pamirs. On Lenin Peak (23,406ft), Wren and fellow climbers Jock Glidden and Allen Steck encountered members of a Soviet women’s team who had died in a storm. His reporting brought their tragedy to the Times front page, breaking the news of deaths Soviet authorities had kept secret.

For Jed Williamson, who was also on the Pamirs expedition, Wren’s contribution to mountaineering extended to his ability to tell its stories. “What he really brought to the mountaineering scene was his ability to write about it and put it out there,” Williamson said. “He had a really good sense of humor. He could turn a situation that one might not think was so humorous into one that was humorous.”

Even when faced with tragedy, Wren found a way to bring levity to dangerous moments. Celia remembered one story her father told about provisioning the Pamirs expedition. The American climbers wanted peanut butter, which he couldn’t find in Soviet shops. Instead, he packed tins of caviar for protein. “His teammates thought it was disgusting,” she remembers. “But he was a Renaissance man with an incredible sense of humor.”

Wren played guitar and banjo and wrote songs, two of which Johnny Cash recorded: Jesus Was a Carpenter and Gospel Road. “It was a fun thing that he did, and he was good at it,” Williamson said. “But he was never a chest pounder about that kind of thing.”

At home, Wren’s appetite for being outside became part of family life. During the family’s years in the Soviet Union, Celia remembered her father heading out on skis, pulling her and her brother behind him on a sled. He penned numerous books, from a biography of Johnny Cash to Walking to Vermont, an account of his roughly 400-mile walk home from Manhattan after retiring from The New York Times.

Williamson remembers that despite the breadth of his traveling and range of his accomplishments, Wren was down-to-earth.  “He wasn’t aloof or standoffish or anything like that,” he said. “He was happy to share.”

Late into retirement, he continued to ski and ride his mountain bike around the nearby lake. Celia remembered his ability to keep moving ahead. When recalling difficult experiences, he would often say, “Well, you know, that’s all behind us now.”

#8292. Montana Man Banned From Hunting for 20 Years After Bowhunters Watch Him Poach a Trophy Bull

Published Nov 2, 2026 6:36 PM EST

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

A father and son who pleaded guilty to poaching in central Montana have lost their hunting privileges for a combined 24 years. Their poaching activity goes back years, but the investigation into the men started last year based on a tip from two bowhunters, who reported a man shooting a bull elk with a rifle during archery season in September 2025.

“Lawful hunters are some of the most passionate outdoorsmen and women in existence. They’re very quick to report wildlife crimes and violations they see in the field,” Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks game warden and lead investigator Diego O’Brien tells Outdoor Life. “These two individuals, in my opinion, went above and beyond reporting the violation. They were very proactive with assistance in an area that I didn’t know very well. They proved to be incredible resources for me.”

Based on information provided by the two bowhunters, law enforcement located Billings resident Michael Letasky through a traffic stop. He matched the description of the man shooting the bull in the Little Belt Mountains, but he didn’t have the rack or any game meat. The bull was left to waste. (The two witnesses knew exactly where the dead animal was, but by then it was too late for wardens to salvage the meat.)

“The hunters that witnessed this trophy bull elk unlawfully shot during archery season were rightfully upset and immediately reported the crime to authorities,” O’Brien said in a statement. “Their quick and accurate reporting and assistance in locating evidence were crucial to this investigation. They sacrificed their own hunting trip to ensure justice was served.”

The poached 6×6 bull met the state’s trophy standards. By state code, restitution for the illegal killing and possession or waste of trophy elk is $8,000. The only animal with a higher restitution than a 6×6 bull is a bighorn ram with at least three-fourths curl, which earns a penalty of $30,000.

In addition to the poached bull, Letasky also shot a raghorn with a firearm during the 2023 archery season, and he had an unreported black bear. During the investigation, wardens also found evidence against Letasky’s son, Kolton, of Austin, Texas.

Kolton Letasky killed a Montana buck in 2024 and a Montana bull in 2022 without the proper permits. He pled guilty to two counts of unlawful possession of game and two counts of hunting without a license. His penalties include more than $3,000 in fines and no hunting for four years.

Read Next: YouTuber Poaching Bust Was a Case of ‘Wildlife Commercialization with a Modern Twist,’ Says Investigating Warden

The elder Letasky’s penalties are more severe. Michael Letasky plead guilty to two counts of unlawful possession of game, two counts of hunting during a closed season and one count of wasting game. He owes more than $12,000 in fines and can’t hunt for 20 years.

#8291. Where Did the Midweight Ski Touring Boot Go?

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

The men's Tecnica Zero G Decoy Pro, staged and ready to go for a backcountry adventure in Cooke City, Montana. (Photo: Rick Sorensen)

Overview: Midweight ski touring boots, historically three buckles and 1,300 to 1,500 grams, can handle the whole range of backcountry skis, yet the class has stagnated while lightweight and crossover boots got most of the industry’s R&D. Writer Bergen Tjossem, a former ski-shop employee, argues the next big touring breakthrough should come from the midweight category.

It’s 4 a.m. and the biting cold plunges into the open garage as I stuff my partner’s idling Forester with gear. But I stall, hovering over my collection of ski touring boots. Big boots or little boots? Neither seems right for the day. I throw my thrashed 2023 Scarpa Maestrale RS boots over my shoulder, snap on my headlamp, and lug my skis to the car. I don’t know why I still hesitate at the start of every backcountry ski day—I end up picking the workhorse boot over the specialists most of the time.

Why, then, is the industry trying to squash this midweight ski touring boot class? Even the Maestrale RS, my beloved midweight archetype, is graduating toward the next class up this season, with a fourth buckle and more heft.

Owning a quiver of boots and skis is fun; it gives you options. But if you already own a pair of alpine boots like most skiers do, one dedicated touring boot could accomplish the vast majority of your needs. Yet where backcountry skis fall on a neat bell curve of dimension and weight, the boots we can buy to pilot them are bimodally distributed: ski shapes cluster in the middle, touring boots at the extremes. The evolution of midweight ski touring boots—the ones that best serve the majority of backcountry skiers—has stagnated compared to their cousins at the ends. It’s the “missing middle” problem every ski town knows from housing.

There’s no rule or buckle count dividing touring boot classes, but allow me to split them for the sake of the rant: lightweight boots typically have two buckles and top out around 1,200 grams, like the La Sportiva Kilo. Midweight boots historically use three buckles and weigh 1,300 to 1,500 grams. Then there are crossover boots that blend touring and alpine: four buckles, around 1,500 grams, typically with a GripWalk sole compatible with tech and alpine bindings, like the Dynafit Tigard.

Ski touring dogma says the optimum backcountry quiver is two pairs of ski touring boots and two pairs of skis: one lightweight and distance-oriented, the other beefy and fun. But here’s the catch—lightweight boots struggle with big skis, especially in poor snow, because they lack progressive flex and damping. And the opposite is also true. Crossover boots are a real drag on lightweight skis. Aside from the cumbersome ROM, the added stiffness, high cuff, and heft quickly overpower lightweight skis. Yet midweights can handle the whole ski spectrum.

When I worked in ski shops in the early 2010s as ski touring took off, midweight boots were the benchmark. Dynafit’s Vulcan and the Scarpa Maestrale were the choice for skiers who wanted to climb efficiently without giving up too much on the descent. What followed that workhorse boot era was an explosion of lightweight options, as almost every company in the business invested in svelter chassis while skis got lighter and less demanding. The rise of resort uphilling and Skimo racing only fueled the growth. Lately, lightweight boots such as La Sportiva’s Kilo XTR have been beefed up to claim more of that middle segment without overtaking it completely. But lightweight two-buckle designs with sturdier components still come up short on the leverage and suspension big skis demand.

Crossovers got the next round of R&D in the name of capturing the massive resort-hybrid buyer. Scarpa’s 1,500 gram 4-Quattro XT with a legit 61 degree range of motion (ROM) revolutionized the segment in 2022. All of a sudden, boots with alpine-like skiing capability unlocked a bigger ROM, while better materials and design brought weights down to 1,500 grams per boot or less. It also introduced freaky new levels of “quiver overlap” for skiers who already own alpine boots with a walk mode.

Smooshed between the crossover and the lightweight segments is that increasingly scant boot group, the midweights. It’s not that these midweight boots don’t exist—the Scott Cosmos Pro and Fischer Transalp prove they do—but rather that they’ve gotten the shaft on R&D over the last decade. Most of the remaining midweights are just stale, longing for a refresh, a trickle-down of new tech, and a burst of innovation.

A radical solution would be to have fewer skis, and I can’t believe you’d even suggest that. I’ve got a better idea: Give me one boot that can cover the entire ski quiver: three buckles, a camming power strap, over 65 degrees of ROM, under 1,400 grams, and minimal fiddle factor. Oops, I just mostly described the Scarpa Maestrale that’s been around for sixteen years. That’s because the industry is barely competing to refine that basic formula into its state-of-the-art form.

As a skier of many setups, I can say there’s a mismatch between the boots I want and those available. Lightweights and crossovers have had their run. My hunch is that the next big touring breakthrough will be, and should be, in the missing middle. Until then, you’ll catch me clinging to my 2023 Scarpa Maestrale RS boots like the gear troll I am.

#8290. Matt Robertson Wins $1.25 Million in the Inaugural WBE The Champions Bass Tournament

Matt Robertson overcame a gauntlet of obstacles this past week to win the inaugural WBE The Champions tournament and take home $1.25 million—the biggest prize in professional bass fishing history. He bested 61 other anglers, outmaneuvering and out-fishing them in what turned into a chess-vs.-checkers matchup. Early on, Robertson chose to fish below Old Hickory Dam, and he stuck with that game plan for the duration of the tournament. He caught only two non-keepers below the dam during practice, but knew enough to gamble his entire tournament on that small stretch of water. On the final day, the gutsy call paid off again with a 20-pound, 2-ounce bag, enough to take home the top slot and $1.25 million.

One of Robertson’s biggest challenges throughout the tournament was navigating the lock connecting Old Hickory Lake and the Cumberland River. Even Robertson said he was shocked he could lock down and back all three days without issue. Normally, filling the lock with water to raise a boat to the same level as Old Hickory takes about 30 minutes. Locking down goes a little quicker. All in all, it could take about an hour for the lock to complete one full rotation. And that’s just with a small boat or two. With a barge, it could take much longer. Surprisingly, Robertson locked up and down all six times throughout the event, maximizing his fishing time at his premier spot.

Below the dam, Robertson targeted smallmouth, which must be 18 inches to keep, compared to the 12-inch spotted bass and 14-inch largemouth regulations. In three days of fishing, not a single spot or largemouth was caught below the dam. If you were going to get a bite there, it would be a smallmouth. That meant it had to be a dang good one to keep—and Robertson took advantage of his opportunities. His Day 1 bag (20 pounds even) and Day 3 Bag (20 pounds, 2 ounces) were the two biggest bags of the tournament by far.

The current below Old Hickory Dam was the magic sauce. It positioned the fish on cover and got them to bite. Robertson was fortunate to have moving water below the dam each day, which isn’t always a given. The current shifted dramatically day to day as different turbines fired at different times, but Robertson adjusted and still caught big bronzebacks.

For the armchair quarterback, it probably looked like a no-brainer to fish below the dam this week. But there was a lot to consider, and a half dozen things could have easily gone wrong and ruined Robertson’s run. But the Kentucky native defied the odds, avoided the catastrophes, and came out on top. He adjusted when the current shifted; he waited patiently to lock; he was efficient when he got bit. All of that added up to a handful of quality fish whose tails fell on the right side of the line. The end result was Robertson collecting the biggest purse in bass fishing history. And he did it in dramatic fashion.

Shaye Baker is a bass fishing content contributor for Field & Stream. He has more than a decade of experience covering professional bass fishing tournaments. Highlights Education Baker graduated from Auburn University with a bachelor’s degree in Spanish and International Trade. However, the education he nows relies on in his daily occupation came by way of working alongside many of the greatest tournament coverage professionals the industry has ever seen, learning to shoot, write, edit, and add commentary in the real world. Experience Baker spent his first few years after college simultaneously pursuing a professional bass fishing career, as well as a career in outdoor journalism in the bass fishing space. After mixed success on the semi-pro fishing trail, Baker decided that working in the industry for a guaranteed paycheck was better than fishing for a possible one. Baker’s clientele base gradually grew to the point he could transition to full-time content contribution for the likes of FLW Outoors, Bassmaster, Wired2Fis,h and several other local, regional, and national publications. He now enjoys working full-time in the industry, but has also returned to his roots, regularly participating in local tournaments with his father and friends. #8289. Secrets for Deer Hunting the Big Woods, According to a North Country Expert

Published Nov 3, 2026 10:00 AM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Hunting whitetails in the North Country forests of New England and the Upper Midwest is an undeniably challenging pursuit. Up there the landscapes are massive, think tens of thousands of acres of forest. Food sources and deer sign are more subtle. There are no edges of agricultural fields to target, and there might not even be stands of oaks dropping acorns. Lastly, deer densities are low, with some areas having maybe five deer per square mile.

It’s within this environment that Brett Joy, a member of the Just Hunt Club, has made a name for himself. Using a mix of old-school and modern hunting strategies, Joy has found success killing mature big woods bucks season after season.

I sat down with him for the most recent episode of the Outdoor Life podcast to learn his strategies for targeting mature bucks in the northwoods. Even if you don’t hunt big woods deer yourself, you can learn from Joy’s tactics and experience.

Joy uses digital maps to identify areas where two or three types of habitat converge.

“Whitetails, whether they’re in a cornfield in Iowa or on a mountain in New Hampshire, are edge habitat creatures,” Joy says. “They live on the edges, but those edges can look a lot different depending on where you are in the whitetails’ range.”

In the big woods, look for edges between hardwoods and softwoods, swamps and mature timber, mature timber and early successional growth (recently logged areas). Once you’ve identified these spots, scout them in person. Ideally, you’ll be a mile or more away from any road.

Joy believes that because the habitat is so vast in the big woods, bucks tend to have larger home ranges and core areas. They also have a variety of bedding areas — even in the early season. Whereas in the agricultural country, mature bucks tend to have only a couple woodlots and thickets where they like to bed.

“Our deer could bed on any different point of a mountain in any cut, in a swamp on any given day,” Joy says. “[Those bedding areas] could be miles apart day to day. They’re almost more of a nomadic deer … but they do have areas that they come back to year after year.”

The key is that even if you’re in a buck’s core zone, you might not see him for a week or more.

Like everywhere else in whitetail country, during the rut big woods bucks will travel between doe groups searching for does in estrus.

“But here, you may have only three does that live within 500 acres,” Joy says. So bucks have to cover more ground and do more checking. And this need to travel long distances makes rutting bucks more vulnerable.

“I like to hunt them during the rut and really focus on those areas they frequent when they’re traveling from A to B, or I hunt near one of those doe groups … and if you can find a big primary scrape or pinch point within the core area of those does, you can catch bucks going through there semi-consistently.”

Trail cameras are a critical component of Joy’s strategy because there’s essentially no visibility in the areas that he hunts. In other words, there are not places to glass from in the big woods.

“If I cared less about what buck I was targeting, I could hunt sign and not use cameras and be successful, but I really do rely on them heavily for my strategy,” he says.

Joy positions most of his cameras on large community scrapes because they serve as social gathering spots that will attract deer in vast landscapes. On top of that, Joy focuses on secluded, high-elevation areas that bucks tend to prefer.

Joy aims to run cameras from about October 15 through December 15, which gives him the full range of rut activity.

When you’re hunting the rut in the big woods, you need to have a good understanding of peak rut activity dates.

“What dictates everything is does coming into estrus,” Joy says. “And those bucks absolutely know those dates in this landscape and they will show up checking those doe groups on the same few days year after year.”

Joy conducted an in-depth trail camera survey using several years worth of his trail camera photos, plus his buddy’s photos to identify peak deer activity during the rut. He found that peak activity in his area was November 19th.

He then paired his trail cam data data with a biologist’s data on fawn conception dates in New Hampshire and he found that the peak conception date was November 19 as well.

“If I had to pick five or seven days, I’d put November 19th right in the middle of it,” Joy says.

Joy adds that he hasn’t witnessed a shutdown in activity due to lockdown. Bucks are covering the most ground during daylight during peak breeding dates.

But peak activity is different throughout whitetail country. You must examine your own trail camera photos and examine historical data to nail down the key dates where you hunt.

Read Next: North Woods Legend Hal Blood on Snow Tracking Bucks

“Now to kill deer in these landscapes you can’t just expect to hunt one weekend,” Joy says. You need probably a week of hunting and you need to hunt for the entire week, dark to dark, he says.

Joy will set up different stands within an area for different wind directions, but once he picks an area he sticks with it and does not jump around from spot to spot — even if he’s not seeing deer right away.

“Sometimes I don’t make a decision about where I’m going to sit until the day before … I’ll wait until I have all the information on a particular spot, but once I decide to [hunt there], that’s it. There’s no deviating. Once you start to doubt and jump around, you’re done,” Joy says. “The day you’re not there is the day he’ll come by.”

If you have good trail camera data and historical data on a spot, it makes it easier to commit to it for a week of hunting. Other keys to staying in the hunt long-term are: efficient access to your stand, good clothing to keep you warm, quality food to eat throughout the week, plenty of rest at night, and staying hydrated. Most importantly, you’ve got to keep the faith.

“Sitting in the cold for 11 or 12 hours a day, day after day, it really does wear on you and you start to doubt yourself and doubt your spot. You start to become negative, and once that stuff compounds … you’re not going to be there when that buck comes by.”

If you are able to stay patient and stick it out, there’s a good chance that an old northwoods buck will eventually walk by. And no matter how big his rack is, he’ll be a true trophy whitetail.

Alex Robinson is Outdoor Life’s editor-in-chief. He oversees an ace team of writers, photographers, and editors who are scattered across the continent and cover everything from backcountry sheep hunting to trail running.
