#8287. The FN Mauser Is the Best Deer Rifle that History Forgot

Published Nov 3, 2026 12:01 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

The latest for gun hunters and competitive shooters.

Hunting rifles come and go and sometimes even good ones don’t stay around. The decades following World War II saw a boom in hunters and a voracious appetite for new rifles and cartridges. This was the heyday of the Pre-64 Model 70 and the Winchester Magnums, but we no longer hear much about the many Mauser sporting rifles made by FN and imported from Belgium.

I recently got my mitts on one of these rifles, which belonged to my great grandfather, chambered in .270 Win. While this gun undoubtedly rode around in the rifle rack of Grandpa Curtis’s truck when I was a youngster, I’m looking at it anew. According to my dad and uncle, Grandpa’s brother was a gunsmith and built the rifle for him. This was after he’d raised a family in a log cabin in Colorado during the Depression and developed a taste for July mule deer. He used this rifle to shoot a lot of deer and elk.

A family heirloom like this gives me a perspective on what a quality hunting rifle looked like in the 1950s, and an idea of how well it’s held up over time. It’s also fun to compare it to the rifles we have today.

It’s common to hear or read about the many sporterized military rifles that post-war hunters adopted. These would typically be either 1903 Springfields or remnant military Mauser rifles. But these FN Mausers weren’t sporterized — they were manufactured for a couple decades as sporting-specific guns. Many, including this rifle, were imported by Firearms International Corp. and marked as such on the receivers.

They were brought in and sold by various companies and in numerous formats. An ad in the November, 1951 Issue of Outdoor Life displays the JC Higgins Model 50 — which was simply an FN Mauser and sold at Sears, Roebuck. They had the chrome vanadium steel barrel and even came with a 2.5-power scope, for $135. Another ad, from the September, 1952 issue, for the Parker-Whelen Gun Catalog, lists .30/06 and .270 FN Mausers for $137.50 without a receiver-mounted rear sight. That would cost you another ten bucks. This could be a clue to the specific origin of this .270, as the front of the barrel has markings that appear to be where a front sight was once mounted, but there is no evidence of a barrel-mounted rear sight like you’ll see on Pre-64 Model 70 rifles and others like the Remington Model 721.

Ultimately, lots of these guns were imported in various forms and were sold by companies like Weatherby, Harrington & Richardson, and Colt. Complete FN rifles, according to what little I could find, had a specific pearl edge to the checkering on the grips, but it’s likely that not all of them did. Barrelled actions were also imported and built into custom hunting rifles.

This particular rifle appears to be either one that showed up as a barrelled action — possibly with a front sight. The barrel and receiver both bear the appropriate stampings for a matched pair that left the factory in Belgium. But the 22-inch barrel appears to have been cut down and re-crowned — as these were generally 24-inch barrels. It’s stamped with the year “1951” and bears matching 2837 serial numbers.

The stock has a handsome grain and good ergonomics. It lacks any checkering, but the fore-end has a nice belly and is capped with an ivory-colored plastic cap. The grip is capped with a similar plastic cap and its vertical orientation provides a wonderful balance of trigger reach and allows a crisp perpendicular squeeze. The raised comb is, in part, made from a separate block of wood. It’s pinned atop the buttstock and shaped to match, but the seams are still visible.

The floorplate isn’t hinged on this rifle. Rather, it’s detachable and retained by a spring-loaded button at the rear and retaining lip at the front. The fitting of the stock is very precise and, despite being bedded from the tang to the cap on the fore-end, very little bedding material is visible alongside the metal. Pillars around the action screws also help create an incompressible bridge between the bottom metal and action. The precise fit of metal and wood are things we’ll only see today on custom rifles and the highest-end production guns. Factory stocks — both wood and synthetic — are either CNC-milled or molded with baked-in tolerances rather than hand fit. The workmanship on my 1954 Model 70 is good, but not to the same level.

The barrel is a pretty standard sporter taper, finishing at .635 inches. I assume it has been cut down from 24 inches to 22. It’s a heavier barrel than you’ll see on classics like the M70 featherweight and contributes to the rifle’s roughly 9.5-pound overall weight.

The action and barrel share all matching and appropriate proof marks, and remain in good shape, with the bolt sliding like glass down the slick raceways. The bottom of the bolt handle is flattened and knurled for a better grip, and is generally smoother to operate than my previously mentioned M70. The safety switch is textured on both sides. It appears to be pitting because of its irregularity, but no other parts show similar signs of corrosion.

The receiver is topped with a one-piece Redfield mount and Bear Cub 2 ¾-power scope that uses a post-style reticle. In the early days of magnified optics, this gave a sight picture similar to that of a front post iron sight — to which most shooters would be accustomed. It was fitted with a Canjar trigger — a premium aftermarket upgrade, that breaks at 3 pounds, 7 ounces as set.

To test the rifle for accuracy, I fired four five-shot groups with several different types of contemporary .270 ammo. Where we would normally aggregate these five-shot groups into a single 20-shot group for each type of ammo, It was apparent that the system was limited, in part, by the optic, so I’m just sticking with the group size averages.

I believe the rifle is certainly capable of better accuracy than this but, considering the vintage scope, it proved itself perfectly capable of hitting a deer or elk cleanly out to 200 to 300 yards. Frankly, it’s not uncommon for us to test modern rifles with high-magnification scopes that average worse. A low-power optic itself doesn’t prevent a rifle from shooting accurately either, but this style of reticle requires the correct-sized target and a lot of concentration to maintain a consistent hold. The post covers about four inches of a 100-yard target. When the barrel warmed, mirage definitely affected sight picture too. I tried both a six-o’clock hold and a navy hold (dead center), and saw some vertical stringing with both methods.

Read Next: 10 Classic Hunting Rifles Every Hunter Should Own

For as much as we hear about classic rifles like the Savage 99 and Winchester Model 70, I’m surprised that Mausers like this haven’t carried a similar reputation. So many rifles, including the Winchester, were derived from the Mauser action itself. The rifles even commanded a higher price than Model 70s at the time. While precision manufacturing, materials, and coatings have gotten better, a rifle like this one could still hold its own today.

The OL editors pick the best deer hunting rifles on the market.

Tyler Freel is a Staff Writer for Outdoor Life. He lives in Fairbanks, Alaska and has been covering a variety of topics for OL for more than a decade. From backpack sheep hunting adventure stories to DIY tips to gear and gun reviews, he covers it all with a perspective that’s based in experience.

#8286. Scarpa Golden Gate LT Review: Moderate Stack Is So Back

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Trail shoes with a moderate stack are becoming harder to find. New trail models either have inches of soft, bouncy foam underfoot (sometimes with a carbon plate), or they are minimalist models that let your feet feel every pebble. Fortunately, a few that balance protection and ground feel still exist. I’ve just discovered one: the Scarpa Golden Gate LT.

Scarpa is an Italian mountain brand based in the Dolomites. Specializing in mountain climbing footwear, elite mountaineers historically wore the brand’s lightweight mountain shoes to cross rugged terrain. Scarpa’s trail running shoes reflect that heritage; they’re known for their rugged protection and firm, surefooted ride. But many trail runners who don’t live in places like the Alps or the White Mountains don’t need an indestructible mountain running boot. Enter Scarpa’s new trail shoe line-up.

The Golden Gate LT is Scarpa’s lightweight “door-to-trail” shoe meant for a broader trail running audience who want a single functional trainer on runs that bridge varied terrain, from asphalt to gravel to rocky singletrack. I put the shoe’s prowess to the test across Los Angeles’s urban streets, steep horse trails, and sandy beaches.

Weight: 10.5oz (men’s 9, women’s 10) Stack Height: 30 – 24 mm Heel-to-Toe Drop: 6 mm

+ Handles road-to-trail transitions smoothly + Stable base + Excellent traction – Fit too narrow for wide feet – Slightly sluggish on quick turnover

The Golden Gate LT may be a departure from Scarpa’s roots in many ways, but not in style: I received a hot orange-white colorway that immediately reminded me of the Orange Crush soda can and blends right in with Scarpa’s line up of mountain running shoes and ski boots. Though the flashy look isn’t entirely my style, I’m just glad it’s not a monster truck of a trail shoe.

Most of my test runs were on the hilly, paved roads of my neighborhood. Cruising through the familiar streets, I was happy to find that while cushioned, my landings weren’t squishy at all. Instead, I noticed a small bounciness in the midsole — like I was running on a shallow trampoline. That’s likely because Scarpa blended 20% PEBAX into the EVA compound midsole to provide extra responsiveness for what I call the “road” side of the hybrid shoe’s performance.

Taking the shoes uphill, the rebound was still there but didn’t do the heavy lifting for me. That changed, however, when I picked up the pace. With some downhill momentum, my stride lengthened, and any feeling of a firm trail shoe was completely gone. At quicker paces, the bounce takes over and helps maintain speed, feeling like an uptempo road shoe. Normally I don’t like shoes with much cushioning, but the upper’s gentle TPU-reinforced support wrapped my feet so nicely that I felt confident running faster and farther.

Later, I took them out for a long run mostly on trails, connected by some roads, to see how they held up on different surfaces. On the trails, the midsole bounce was less noticeable, which I appreciated, as bouncing over unstable surfaces doesn’t make sense to me.

Compared to other trail models I’ve worn, the lugs are far more flexible, providing amazing traction across sand, dirt, and rocks. The flexibility of the outsole kept my stride smooth and stable on uneven trails and helped the shoe maintain its beginning-of-the-run feeling late into a 14-mile long run. Overall, the outsole’s efficiency felt more alive on the trails than on paved surfaces.

If you’re crazy, like me, and sprint down steep trails, you’ll appreciate the moderate, 24 mm stack under the forefoot, making toe-offs effortless, helping short, quick strides remain stable, and ensuring that tight cornering is no problem. The 30 mm heel stack, however, which contributed to the smooth cushioning on the road, could sometimes feel a bit sluggish on steep trail descents. I prefer 4 mm-drop shoes to keep my steps quick and agile and maximize the thrill of heading downhill with my hair on fire. But if you’re more sensible and take it easy on descents, then the 6 mm drop shouldn’t be a problem at all.

Back on the roads toward the end of my long run, I felt the same road-shoe ride I get on my neighborhood runs. Though my legs were more tired after battling the dusty, hilly terrain, the flexibility of the upper and the outsole encouraged me to keep my pace until the end of the run.

Durability seems mixed so far: After testing the shoe for a month of road and trail runs, the outsole has progressively felt more flexible under my feet and can take on rocks and tough objects on the trails. The edges of the lugs have retained their sharp definition from when it was new, while the upper and overall cushioning still feel just as comfortable. The midsole bounce, however, is much gentler than when it was new (for better or worse), and the bright Orange Crush splash has since faded.

Quality moderate-stack trail shoes are becoming harder to find. If your favorite model lost its way in the “space-age arms race of trail super shoes,” as our editor Cade Michael aptly put it, and you don’t like feeling every rock beneath your feet through a thin minimalist sole, this one’s for you.

Runners with narrow or medium-narrow feet who prefer a tight fit should appreciate this shoe. The heel and midfoot’s gentle padding hug my narrow feet quite tightly, and the toe box has some room for toe splay, though it’s not wide — it’s right in the middle. This close-fitting shape is useful for tight cornering and platform stability, but if you have wide feet and need breathing space for your toes, the M2C H1, an Altra, or a Topo trail shoe might be a better fit.

So, is this the lower-stacked hybrid shoe that we’ve been waiting for? With its dual personality, the Golden Gate LT certainly handles roads and trails like it’s built for both. You can also totally wear this exclusively as a trail shoe for runs of any length. Though difficult trails with demanding terrain may not be its greatest strength, this shoe provides a comfortable, energetic ride on all other terrain, achieving exactly what it’s designed for.

#8285. Old Town Sportsman PDL 120 Pro Kayak Review

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more

The Old Town Sportsman PDL 120 Pro is a beast. I tested this boat on a 6-mile fishing trip, standing, pedaling, and accessorizing the kayak to see what it can do—and I was impressed. If the name Sportsman PDL 120 Pro sounds familiar, that’s because it’s been in the Old Town lineup for some time. But this year Old Town completely redesigned the top half of this kayak and re-released it. The new model features horizontal rod tubes, a deeper and wider tankwell and cockpit, pre-set grommets for mounting motors and anchors, and more. The seat’s mounting system is different, too. Basically, everything from the water line up is different—and better. Here’s a closer look at the redesigned Old Town Sportsman PDL 120 Pro.

The top half of this boat has been completely redesigned with thinner walls and deeper wells to create more room for storage and operating space. The Sportsman PDL 120 Pro has a combined 150 inches of track, pre-cut through-hull wiring ports, pre-set holes for mounting motors and shallow water anchors, and three access hatches to get down into the hull. That means you can modify this boat however you want. Plus, the front hatch is twice as big as the previous design, and there are four horizontal rod tubes.

Old Town also redesigned the seat so the angler sits higher and has a better paddling angle. The seat sits on adjustable tracks, so you can slide it forward or back for a custom fit. Four knobs beneath the seat can be loosened and tightened from the seated position, so you can adjust the seat even on the water. A large rudder at the rear of the boat deploys with a lever to the right of the angler and is controlled with a knob to the left. Overall, the seating and controls are top-notch. The Sportsman PDL 120 Pro retails for $3,599.

I tested the Sportsman PDL 120 Pro on Thurlow Reservoir while targeting bass and catfish. I laid my bass rods in the rod tubes, with the reels to the sides of the seat. I put my tackle under the seat, my phone and keys in the little waterproof hatch on top of the PDL Drive console, and a large cooler and 14 floats in the rear tankwell.

I peddled about 6 miles during that trip, targeting bass for the first 5 hours. I liked being able to control the boat relatively hands-free with the PDL Drive while still actively fishing. I had to turn the rudder control knob, of course, when moving from spot to spot. But while fishing, I found I could backpedal if I drifted too far forward, and I could stop or correct myself when needed. The PDL Drive let me cover significantly more water than my traditional paddle kayak.

I stood up a couple of times and found the boat extremely stable in both scenarios. I was also really impressed with how sturdy and powerful the PDL Drive is. I could scoot along pretty well with this pedal drive system, and it didn’t rock back and forth like some others I’ve tried in the past. Towards the end of the trip, I baited up 14 floats and tossed them in the lake to try to catch catfish. That ended up being the most fun I had all day. As the floats started bobbing, I chased them down with the PDL Drive, giggling as I got close. I landed three solid fish and tossed them in the cooler to clean up for a buddy.

What really impressed me was how sturdy this boat is. I weigh 260 pounds, and leaning over to grab something out of the water is enough to topple many kayaks. But even when I stretched as far as I could to grab the float, the Old Town PDL 120 Pro didn’t budge, with the top of the gunwale staying several inches above the water. And, using the rudder and control knob, I was able to slip right up within inches of the floats, once I got the hang of it.

Installing the Minn Kota Kayak Terrova trolling motor on the Old Town 120 PDL Pro elevated this boat to an entirely different class of vessel—quite literally, since I had to register it at the courthouse after adding the motor. But practically speaking, the troller put this boat into a whole other league. While I’m not the biggest fan of installation projects like this, I found some great tutorial videos on Old Town’s website and dove in headfirst.

Mounting the motor itself was super easy, with pre-set mounting hardware built into the bow, specifically for the Kayak Terrova. Just line the Quick Release MKA-21 Bracket up and screw in the four bolts. This bracket is sold separately, but I recommend it so that you can take the motor on and off when loading the boat, to lighten the load. It’s also good to have it so you can detach the motor and set it in the truck or hotel room when on the road.

With the motor mounted, I bought a 6-gauge marine wire to run the length of the boat from the trolling motor to the battery—I put the battery in the stern to disperse the weight. The kit includes an optional relay board you can use to add a safety switch. I highly recommend doing this, even though it’s a little bit of a headache. The safety switch acts like the kill switch on an outboard motor and stops the Terrova instantly should you fall off.

After installing the safety switch near the seat and connecting all the appropriate wires to the relay, I was ready to hook up the battery, pair the motor to the included Micro Remote, and test it out. To test the motor, I took the boat to a local lake on a windy day. It blew 15 miles per hour, sustained throughout most of the day—the type of day I just wouldn’t have fished from a kayak if all I had was a paddle. Even the pedal drive would have been brutal. But with the motor, I could set a course into the wind and set my speed using the AutoPilot feature, or hit Spot-Lock and sit in place while I fished a point, brushpile, or dock. I even used the AutoPilot feature to slowly drift backward in strong current under the dam; I plowed my way upstream with the motor on high, then pointed my motor into the current, set it to about 40 percent, and slowly drifted backward to where I could fish without the motor raging at full bore.

The Terrova is phenomenal, plain and simple. It was a bit of a headache to install, but if I can do it, you can too. Stowing and deploying can be a bit cumbersome at first. I saw people use a rope around the shaft to lower the motor slowly and raise it back up, so I did that, and it worked well. I found my paddle to be the best tool in the boat for pushing the locking deploy/stow lever to send the motor out or lift it back up. The Lift-Assist feature also helps with deployment and stowing.

All things considered, the redesigned Old Town PDL 120 Pro is a great boat. It’s sturdy, has a fantastic layout, and the PDL Drive system is top-notch. If you’re into accessories, you can trick this boat out a hundred different ways. Stability is my biggest concern when kayak fishing, and this boat is among the most stable I’ve ever set foot in. I really value a good seat and seat positioning, too. The higher seat and better angle make it much easier to stand, stay seated longer, and fish all day. Being able to slide it forward and backward to find the sweet spot for pedaling was great, too. The bottom line is that the redesigned PDL 120 Pro is more comfortable, stable, and better equipped—which means more time on the water and more fish in the net.

#8284. There Are Over 40 Resorts Planning To Open In November—Here’s Where Experts Say Conditions Will Be Best

Mammoth Mountain opening day 2025 (Photo: Courtesy of Mammoth Mountain)

Some folks may think skiing in November is crazy: the snow is rarely good, and the mere thrill of lifts spinning often attracts crowds larger than downhill capacity should allow.

It can be difficult to know where, if anywhere, it is worth skiing in November. While resorts are making snow around the clock, the decision to open boils down to weather.

For Colorado skiers, the weather may finally be on your side. According to Open Snow meteorologist Joel Gratz, November is set to start with a “bang.” He predicts a storm arriving Sunday will drop 6 to 12 inches on nearly all mountains, with some spots seeing up to 20. Did someone say powder day?!

Several Colorado resorts are opening their lifts before Halloween is over. Arapahoe Basin opened Oct. 28, Keystone follows on Oct. 30, and Wolf Creek on Oct. 31. Snow is thin at all three for now, but their high elevations should set them up for a stronger start to November.

Breckenridge and Copper Mountain are planning to open on Nov. 6, and if the snow comes in like Gratz is predicting, their opening days could feature more than just a white ribbon of death.

A little later into the month, Vail and Eldora are both planning Nov. 13 opening dates. It’s too early to tell if temperatures will preserve the snow from earlier storms, but as long as cold air remains, these are resorts to keep on your radar for potentially decent skiing.

Neighboring Utah resorts aren’t expected to receive as fruitful a snow bounty. They’ll see the same storm as Colorado, with the highest accumulations on Sunday, says Open Snow forecaster Evan Thayer. “Cooler air will eventually lower snow levels, with some decent accumulations possible up high.”

As of the time of publishing, Brian Head is planning on opening on Nov. 6. If Thayer’s prediction is accurate, the Southern Utah resort could see “decent accumulations” on its highest peaks. Alta, Park City, and Solitude are all planning on opening on Nov. 20. It’s too early to say how these resorts will fare, but cold temperatures will be the biggest asset.

California skiers will have to wait a bit longer. Open Snow forecaster Bryan Alleretto predicts the Tahoe region’s snowy start will likely come after Nov. 10, which could be good timing for Mammoth Mountain, set to open Nov. 20. Mammoth isn’t a Tahoe resort, but it tends to share weather patterns with those to the north.

The East Coast has had a warm fall, but that could change. There’s no official snow report yet, but Maine’s Sugarloaf plans to reopen Nov. 20, likely making it the region’s first resort to welcome skiers back. Vermont’s Sugarbush follows on Nov. 21, while nearby Killington, which often opens early, hasn’t announced a date as of press time.

#8283. A Veteran Bowhunter Finds Two Bucks Locked Together Deep Into Public Land. Should He Shoot Them?

Published Nov 3, 2026 2:09 PM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Robert Denninger was in a tree saddle the afternoon of October 23 when he spotted a deer in a creek bed about 75 yards away. He’d accessed the Oklahoma public hunting area by kayak, paddling up a creek to a remote spot that he’d pinpointed the previous day.

“I decided to slide down quietly with my bow and get a better look at the deer in the creek,” Denninger tells Outdoor Life. “When I got close to the creek I spotted two big mature bucks fighting and they were locked up tight by their antlers.”

He knew he was witnessing an epic outdoor event and he shot video of the fight on his phone.

“The bucks were plowing into each other and into the creek bank,” says Denninger, a 42-year-old retiree from Dallas. “Mud was flying everywhere. My mind was racing – would attempting to harvest these bucks be a hunter’s gift or a violation of fair chase?”

It was clear the bucks were not able to separate their antlers. Denninger struggled with what to do and pondered if it would be ethical and legal to shoot the larger of the two bucks, which was a 12-pointer with a typical rack. He recalled a friend telling him a story of once finding a pair of locked-antler bucks dead in a pond. They had been killed and half eaten by coyotes.

Before deciding what to do, Denninger called a game warden.

“I spoke with a local [Oklahoma] Game Warden who assured me he didn’t have any on-call vet who could have come out to sedate the animals and attempt a safe unlocking,” Denninger says.

“The thought of letting ‘nature run its course’ and coming back in the following days to spook a pack of coyotes off two rotten carcasses or trying my best to put an ethical kill on these animals were what I believed my choices were,” he explains. “I decided to shoot the 12-pointer.”

His first arrow was deflected by brush. But his second arrow found the deer’s heart, and it quickly died.

“I watched to see if the eight point could free himself, but he only struggled more, barely able to move the weight of the harvested 12-pointer,” the bowhunter says.

Denninger had no way of freeing the deer, so he decided to shoot the second buck with his bow. Even when both deer were dead, it was impossible to unlock their antlers.

That’s when he called a couple younger buddies, who eventually arrived with a wheeled wagon.

“We tried to unlock their racks many times, and were unable to,” Denninger says. “We field dressed them. But it was a rugged haul to get the two bucks out, taking well over three hours to get them to a truck and out of the woods. It was almost midnight [by the time we were done].”

He called his Texas friend and taxidermist Dustin Moon and told him about the locked-antler bucks and his hunting tale.

“Dustin and his wife Stephanie of New Story Taxidermy drove five hours (on their sixth wedding anniversary) to where I was so they could see the bucks and help my deer processor get their antlers unlocked.”

Eventually they succeeded and the deer were separated. They will be mounted, though Denninger doesn’t know if he’ll have them in a locked-horn mount or separate mounts.

The 12-pointer is believed to be 7.5 years old and has a rough green score of 152 inches. It’s the biggest buck Denninger has taken during his dedicated bowhunting career. The 8-pointer is thought to be 5.5 years old and scores 132 inches. Both bucks have typical racks.

“I think what I did was the most ethical thing I could have done with my two Oklahoma buck tags, especially considering the alternative of having them suffer and die in their struggle, or have coyotes kill them.”

Bob McNally has been an outdoor writer since shortly after the earth’s crust cooled. He has written 12 outdoor books, more than 5,000 outdoor magazine stories (including many for Outdoor Life) and more newspaper outdoor columns and features than there are hairs on a grizzly bear.

#8282. We Need to Move Past the “Shut Up And Die Like a Man” Mentality in the Mountains

Will Gadd (left) and his friend, the late Ken Wallator. (Photo: Will Gadd)

“Shut up and die like a man!” sounds like a line from a bad action movie, but we all heard it on the radio from the paragliding competition director. The director was yelling at a terrified pilot who thought he was falling to his death. The pilot had accidentally keyed open his radio’s shoulder mic, allowing his frantic screams to be broadcast across the competition frequency.

The unfortunate pilot begging to god to not die had collapsed his wing and plummeted in front of my eyes. Twenty-one years later, the memory of this sight and soundtrack is unforgettable, and so was the director’s barking, because there was clearly no sympathy for what the pilot thought was his final, horrific ride. Miraculously, the pilot recovered his wing and flew out to land and reflect on his life choices alone.

Most pilots didn’t think the competition director’s statement was out of line for the time. Many still don’t. I see terrible parallels between flying culture and some facets of climbing’s; in alpinism especially, some see death as an attractant, or an inevitability. Over my 40 years as an alpinist and 35 as a pilot, I’ve watched climbers experience gut-wrenching trauma—then do their best to ignore it, too scared or proud to deal with the ugly, messy truth. This avoidance sends a message to younger climbers, much like the competition director’s statement so long ago: Suck it up, move on, and die with honor if things go bad.

But living with trauma doesn’t have to be that way.

When my late friend Ken Wallator was 21, he climbed Mount Belanger in the Canadian Rockies with his girlfriend Heidi. They reached the top of the difficulties, unroped, and walked along a low-angle snow ridge to the summit of the peak. But the snow ridge was actually a massive, overhanging cornice of windblown snow, and it collapsed as they stopped to take a photo. Ken somehow managed to leap to safety but Heidi fell hundreds of meters down the face.

Ken, a brave bear of a man, downclimbed the face, found Heidi somehow still alive, and started carrying her out to a distant hut. She died before they reached it.

In the aftermath of Heidi’s death, I watched Ken receive a surprising amount of blame from grieving members of the climbing community. Didn’t he know better than to walk on a cornice? Why weren’t they roped up? Ken was already wracked with guilt from the accident. When his community piled on, their condemnation lit an internal firestorm.

Thirty years later, in 2019, Ken helped me re-roof my house. He still had the strength of a bear and I watched him haul 100-pound loads of shingles up my rickety ladder. In a rare moment of emotionality, he told me how he still hadn’t gotten over Heidi’s death, or the climbing community’s blame. We talked more about trauma, and I realized only then how that day on Mount Belanger broke my friend in a way that never healed.

As two young, hungry alpinists, Ken and I didn’t know what mental “help” looked like 30 years ago, and Ken was too much a product of his culture to take it 30 years later. Despite his immense physical and mental strength, Ken died by suicide a few weeks after our talk.

More recently, Will Stanhope’s death has brought to mind this idea of “asking for help” once more. For years Stanhope had battled desperately with alcohol. He was facing various charges at the time of his death—including assault and sexual assault—while still succeeding on difficult routes as a professional climber and mountain guide.

In our last real conversation, Stanhope talked about needing to “harden up and stop letting the carnage get to me” one minute, then sobbed about the “death camp” of hard alpine climbing the next. Like Ken and me, he had lost many friends in the mountains.

“You and I [watched] our mentors and friends die, one after another, as if everyone around us was climbing their way to oblivion,” his friend Kieran Brownie wrote in an obituary. “We couldn’t return to the mountains, we couldn’t return to each other.”

Stanhope carried a heavy weight in the final months of his life, made even heavier by grief, guilt, and irreversible mistakes. After a lifetime of hard solos and even scarier roped climbs, it seemed impossible that Stanhope would ever fall off an easy 5.11. But when he did just that last April and succumbed to a head injury, to me and other friends, Stanhope’s death felt more related to the weight he carried in his head than the climb itself. His family and friends made truly profound and sometimes wrenchingly difficult efforts to help him, but, like falling, the weights of addiction and trauma develop their own momentum.

Hard drinking, hard living, and celebrating dangerous acts—usually lauded as “bold”—are hallmarks of every mountain sport I’ve ever done, from kayaking to flying to skiing to climbing. Our literature is full of stories celebrating those who climbed hard, drank hard, and died silently.

I can’t help but wonder if our literature strives to make these deaths seem somehow valiant and necessary, like dying in the mountains is a noble sacrifice rather than the tragedy it really is. The classic mountaineering texts rarely explore the trauma that comes after seeing a friend die. They barrel ever onward to the summit.

Military veterans and first responders have a trauma-treatment framework that climbers should strive to adopt. Soldiers are not considered “weak” if they are affected by bloody combat. Paramedics are not ridiculed for taking leave after responding to a grisly car wreck. These are normal human responses, and professional groups typically have protocols for helping those involved in traumatic situations. These groups have no other choice; a traumatized team simply cannot function.

Those professional protocols weren’t there for Ken, Will, that terrified pilot, or many others, including me.

When I was 19 I tried with every tool I knew to save a fellow kayaker stuck just inches from the surface in his boat. I couldn’t reach him, and he drowned in front of me as I tried to remember how to rig a better haul system. I had nightmares for years of the paddler chasing me in the dark beside that river.

Only decades later did I seek help, after a divorce and a lot of behavior I understood even less than that terrible accident. I’m lucky I survived and sought belated help. Ken and Will and many others didn’t. Many more in our community—your friends and mine—are barely standing today, carrying crippling loads. They need help putting those loads down.

The pain of trauma does not disappear with six or 600 beers. Doing dangerous climbs or flights or other high-stimulus experiences temporarily distracts from the weight, but doesn’t solve it. There is no pack heavier than one filled with trauma you can’t put down.

One of the smartest things I’ve ever heard about trauma came after we failed to resuscitate a dying man at the base of an ice climb a few years ago. A professional responder on the scene could tell I was shaken, and looked me in the eye and said, “Post traumatic stress is normal; post traumatic stress disorder is optional—if you get help. Get help.”

I see real change today, from my wife Sarah Hueniken’s Mountain Muskox foundation to the American Alpine Club’s Grief Fund, two organizations built to support mountain-trauma survivors.

But I also still see a lot of the “Shut up and die like a man” attitude, and the celebration of “bold” yet physically unimpressive climbs that are often little more than Russian Roulette. Huge, low-angle alpine routes with immense serac and avalanche hazard are not that cool, in my book. And I see many climbers who still romanticize the wrong parts of climbing, whether that’s meaningless objective hazard or the very idea of “suffering silently.”

We need to recognize that a mountain death doesn’t end with the funeral; often that’s just the start of a very long and difficult process for everyone involved. In climbing more people die on the descent after the summit than on the climb itself.

At times I’ve felt deeply angry about our outdoor tribe’s celebration of “bold” hazards, and our denial of the after-effects of engaging in high-risk sports where participants die regularly. We often celebrate the bold free solos or dangerous alpine routes where everything clicked into place. We never celebrate the dead parent who doesn’t show up for their kids’ birthdays.

But the truth is that I laughed when the paragliding competition director said his infamous line. I promised myself that if I was in that situation in the future, I’d shut up. That became my normal. Today, I hope I’d speak up on the comment, and reach out to the guy who almost died that day. Because I’ve been him, and it sucks, and I’m trying to do better.

I’m less angry today when I think about Ken, Will, or others who have left the game, and just hope that our culture continues to evolve in the same way the first responders did, and that we ultimately celebrate survival more than dying silently. We can do better, if we want to.

Finally, if, like me, you’ve been through the trauma wringer, it often takes help to sort it out. We’re not tougher than the veterans or first responders even if our culture says we “should” be—we’re just less educated about intense trauma.

The goal is to return to full function and fly in life, not get stuck in the inevitable mental dust devils of mountain death. Peace to those hurting, it can get better with help. Substances and more dangerous living may distract us short term, but long term the combo is deadly despite the romantic words we historically place on both. I write these words for the future Wills and Kens, they are me, you, our friends.

Shutting up is not a solution, because silence is death.

#8281. How to Mount a Riflescope Like a Pro. Follow This Step-By-Step Guide

Published Nov 3, 2026 4:24 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

The latest for gun hunters and competitive shooters.

When mounting a riflescope, you’re dealing with the most fragile and failure-prone point on your gun—so it pays to do it right. The process isn’t complicated, but it does require an attention to detail and some basic equipment. So in part one of our seven-part series on mastering the use of precision riflescopes and shooting to your rifle’s full potential, I’m going to dive in to how to actually get one of these bad boys mounted properly.

To correctly mount a riflescope, these conditions must be satisfied: The reticle needs to be level with the rifle. The scope must be positioned at the correct height above the bore. The proper eye relief needs to be established. And the fasteners in the rings and bases need to be tightened the right way. Before we get into detail on each of these points, here’s a basic outline of the process.

• Clamp the barrel in the padded jaws of a bench vise. If you don’t have a bench vise, you’ll need a solid gun cradle that will hold the rifle steady.

• Use a bubble level to level the rifle action. The flat on top of the Picatinny rail works. With some actions you can remove the bolt and have enough clearance on the tang (assuming it is flat) to set a bubble level as well. As a last resort you can attach the bottom half of a scope ring to the scope base and rest the level on it.

• Set the scope in the rings and lightly tighten the fasteners so that the scope will stay put but can be rotated and moved by hand. If your scope has a flat spot on the elevation turret, place the bubble level on it to level the reticle.

• An alternate method to level the reticle is to look through the scope on your leveled rifle at a plumb bob and orient the vertical crosshair with the string.

• Once the reticle is level, remove the rifle from vise and check your eye relief. Make adjustments as needed. Do this by placing the rifle back in the vise, making sure it is level, and then moving the scope.

• Tighten the fasteners to the correct torque levels with a torque wrench.

The depth of the scope rings controls how far above the bore the scope sits. The primary concern is that both ends of the scope have adequate clearance above the rifle. Having the objective end of the scope in contact with the barrel is an obvious no-no, but you want to make sure the eyepiece isn’t cramped either. Rings that are too low can limit the horizontal travel of the scope in the rings making it more difficult to get the right eye relief.

If your scope is too high, you’ll have a hard time lining up behind the rifle when shooting prone, though a stock with an adjustable cheek piece can mitigate this.

Ultimately, this is a Goldilocks situation where the scope should neither be too high, nor too low. As a rule of thumb, a gap between the objective bell and the barrel of .25 to .5 inches should be just right—but the profile of your barreled action and stock might dictate otherwise.

With proper eye relief the shooter is able to look through the scope without any part of the image being blacked out. The way to test whether eye relief (and scope height) are correct is to get set up behind the rifle in the prone position, close your eyes, rest your check firmly on the stock by taking the tension out of your neck, then opening your eyes.

You should be looking right down the center of the riflescope and have a clear view of the reticle and image without needing to move your head.

Fortunately, many long-range rifles make fine tuning this easier by have adjustable lengths of pull and cheek piece height. Rifles equipped with Picatinny rails—which most precision rifles are—provide greater flexibility with the forward and aft placement of the scope to establish good eye relief.

Read Next: The Best Scope Rings of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

Some manufacturers provide values for the fasteners in their scope rings. Many don’t. As a rule of thumb, you can tighten the screws on scope rings to about 20 inch-pounds and be good to go.

It always makes sense to check the screws on your Pic rail or scope base as well. They tend to be beefier, so you can torque them to about 30 inch-pounds without worry.

You can use a torque wrench with preset fittings, like Fix-It Sticks or the Wheeler Fat Wrench, or one with an indicator dial like this one from Seekonk Precision Tools.

Before tightening the screws, you should consider doing one of two things. Either use a sparing amount of blue Loctite on the treads—a single small drop will do—or spray the screws with some degreaser. These will help the screws acquire a more secure hold.

Tighten the screws as you would lug nuts on a truck tire. Tighten one a bit, go to a screw on the other side of the ring and tighten that a bit, and repeat as you work your way through all the fasteners.

Tighten them gradually so that the rings are applying an even clamping force to the scope tube. When done correctly, the gap on either side of the rings should be even. That’s a good sign that whoever put the scope on the rifle knew their stuff.

#8280. For Rifle-Season Elk, “Bad” Weather Is the Best

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›

If you’re day dreaming about an upcoming elk hunt during rifle season, it probably looks something like this: A wall tent set in a small clearing surrounded by aspens trying to hold onto their last bits of gold. You and your buds inside, huddled around the stove, bs-ing and making plans for the morning’s hunt. And, as long as you’re conjuring up the ideal scene, you should also picture a fresh blanket of snow dusting the meadow grasses and blanketing the slopes around you.

Weather is everything when it comes to rifle-season elk hunting, and nothing promises to put bulls on their feet like a forecast that begins with a snowflake icon. So pray for the white stuff and follow this advice.

From August through May, snow can hit the high country at any time. During October and November, waking up to white on an elk hunt is almost a guarantee, and whether Mother Nature gives you a half inch or 6 inches, consider it a gift. Weather fronts move elk, and when the storm stops, you need to be out covering ground or posted up on an elevated ridge and glassing with quality optics.

Elk, especially those traveling in a herd, typically to drop in elevation if new snow measures several inches or more. They are simply moving to where food is more accessible. Older cows know where these locations are and will rally the herd—usually consisting of cows, calves, and smaller bulls—to beeline to the new spot. Unless the snow is measured in feet and not inches, larger bulls may not make such drastic movements. Still, these elk need to eat and will shift to south-facing slopes where forage is available and is easier to get at.

New snow in the high country gives you four big advantages as an elk hunter. Here’s what they are, how they help you, and what you should do to take make the most of each.

A 600-plus-pound animal with a tan hide and dark mane really stands out against a white backdrop. When the snow hits, my elk hunting companions and I will typically climb just a little above where we think the elk are and spend hours moving from vantage point to vantage point, picking the country apart with optics. The key is positioning yourself in locations where you can see lots of ground. Don’t move from an area too quickly. Be sure and pick timber pockets apart, as these are great locations to find and put a bull or three to bed.

If you’re out burning boot leather when the snow stops and come across a set of lone bull prints or lots of tracks left by a herd, you know those tracks are smoking fresh. Don’t start following them aimlessly, though. Pull out your digital mapping app and look at the terrain. Is there an open meadow or sage flat ahead where the herd can paw down to some good forage? What about a semi-open south-facing mountainside where the sun is warming the ground? Put some thought into what the elk might do, and then make a plan of attack. When following tracks, don’t get mesmerized by them. Keep your eyes up—continually look up and ahead for a flash of tan. Each time the landscape changes, whether you topped a ridge or popped out of some tight timber, stop and glass ahead.

Nothing makes for an ultra-stealthy stalk like fresh snow. If possible, try to spot elk from above and stalk downhill to them them. Carry a bottle of wind checker and puff it often to stay in tune with fickle mountain breezes. If you’re rifle hunting with a partner or two, take the time to develop a smart game plan where if one hunter bumps elk, the others are in position to take a safe shot, or are at least in place to glass and mark animals when they more.

One big thing to remember when stalking in the snow is that you become much more visible to elk. Blaze orange is a requirement in most elk-rich states during rifle season, and that blaze orange can look like the lights of the Vegas Strip when its set against a white background. If you spot elk but the cover is too sparse for stalking or you feel the stalk is a low percentage one, simply wait those elk out instead. Set up in a good ambush spot down or crosswind of the elk, and be ready to capitalize when they get up to fill their bellies.

Another solid bonus to snow is that blood and tracks will be easy to follow if you need to trail a hit animal. This means that even with a marginal hit, you are much more likely to get a lethal follow-up shot or recover your bull at the end of what would otherwise have been a difficult, if not futile, trail job. Remember, this is your dream hunt, and the perfect elk foray ends with you sitting behind your trophy.

#8279. First Lite Uncompahgre Foundry Jacket, Tested and Reviewed

Published Nov 3, 2026 4:36 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

It’s not often that you get to hunt in an area that is the namesake for the jacket you’re wearing, but this fall, I did just that. The Uncompahgre National Forest covers almost a million acres of high-elevation backcountry in Colorado. At, and over, 10,000 feet, the wind and weather can be unpredictable. So your clothing needs to be versatile and ready for whatever Mother Nature might throw your way.

After wearing the Uncompahgre Foundry Jacket during my first-rifle elk hunt with fluctuating temperatures, driving rain, and even a healthy dose of snowfall, I will be the first to tell you that this jacket earned its name. It’s surprisingly packable, offers zippered ventilation around the triceps, and is incredibly warm. Since my elk hunt, it’s earned a spot in my treestand layering system as well. Here’s everything you need to know about this must-have outer layer.

As I mentioned above, the weather on my elk hunt was unpredictable at best. From driving rain for multiple days on end, to rapidly dropping temperatures bringing snow into the high country, I got to experience the full spectrum of temperatures and conditions. The Uncompahgre Foundry jacket was one piece of my kit that I wouldn’t have wanted to live without.

It remained durable after hiking through oak brush, deadfall, and large conifer stands, but more importantly, it kept me dry. Since I was living in a tent, my biggest fear was getting wet, and thus, staying wet with no way to really dry off given the conditions. Thankfully, this jacket both figuratively and literally had my back.

Upon returning home, I tested the Uncompahgre Foundry jacket throughout an October cold front here in Pennsylvania as well. While the conditions were drastically improved compared to the backcountry in Colorado, this jacket still fit into my kit wonderfully. Rather than wear it the entire walk to the stand, I simply packed it up into a ball and tossed it in my pack. After climbing in, I’d throw it on and enjoy my sit. It keeps me warm and surprisingly doesn’t make a ton of noise when you’re moving to grab your bow and draw back.

While I do really like this jacket, there’s always room for improvement. The first thing I noticed was the pocket design and layout. On the front of the jacket are four pockets. Two magnetic dump pockets, and just above those, two zippered hand warmer pockets featuring a warm tricot lining. Both are quite handy for different things, but I often found myself digging around in the wrong pocket due to their layout and close proximity to each other. If it were up to me, I’d leave the dump pockets where they are, and move the hand warmer pockets to a more traditional, hip-centric location.

I also had an issue, that was certainly in part user error, where the hand warmer pockets got wet during a popup rain shower. I had accidentally left the zipper open, but due to the design, the rain ran down the front of the jacket and right into those pockets. When the zippers were closed, no water intrusion occurred. User error aside, I’d argue it’s another reason to relocate the hand warmer pockets.

Where the Uncompahgre Foundry jacket shines truly is in its versatility. I was able to wear it in temperatures ranging from 20 degrees, all the way up to 50 degrees. Admittedly, 50 degrees might have been right on the edge of too hot for this jacket, it really did a nice job of ventilating when I opened up the tricep vents.

It’s incredibly windproof, waterproof, durable, and warm. Honestly, it’s an outer layer I didn’t even know I needed until I had it. And now that I have it, it’ll be accompanying me on every hunt for the remainder of the fall and winter.

As an avid hunter, I came to the realization years ago that you get what you pay for when purchasing hunting clothing. I hate being cold, and I hate being wet. Thankfully, the Uncompahgre Foundry jacket does a wonderful job of eliminating both of those concerns. If you’re hunting for a new outer layer to get you through the rut, rifle, and late season, look no further.

#8278. The Best Splurge-Worthy Gifts for the Hunter Who Has It All

Shopping for a hunter who seems to have everything? This is where you pull out the big guns (sometimes literally). Our experts have put many of these to the test ourselves—and stand behind them—so you can feel good about going a little bigger with this gift.

Thermal optics let you see heat signatures in total darkness, which makes them some of the coolest (and most useful) gear a hunter can own. The Pulsar Thermion 2 Pro pairs a crisp thermal image with multiple viewing modes and built-in recording, so you can spot game and capture what you’re seeing in the field.

If you really want to spoil the hunter on your list, it’s hard to go wrong with these Swarovski binoculars. They deliver incredible glass clarity and built-in laser rangefinding, so you can spot game and get an accurate distance without switching between two pieces of gear. They’re definitely a splurge, but once you use them, it’s easy to see why they’re worth it.

If you know a serious duck hunter, these Sitka waders would make one heck of a gift. They’re built with tough yet breathable 4-layer Gore-Tex Pro fabric, a waterproof front zipper, and a redesigned boot that’s lighter and more comfortable for long days in the water. Tip: Snag them in the badass Dark Timber camo Sitka just dropped this month for a new look this season.

For the hunter with a growing gun collection (aren’t we all?!), we recommend our very own Field & Stream gun safe. It has enough room to hold 40 long guns, along with adjustable shelves, racks, and pouches to keep ammo and other shooting accessories secure and organized.

Montana Knife Company has built a following for its American-made blades, all crafted under the direction of master bladesmith Josh Smith. This deluxe three-piece set gives you a few great knives—all made with MagnaCut stainless steel and durable G10 handles—to have on hand for everything from processing venison to making dinner.

Electric bikes have become a popular way for hunters to cover more ground, haul gear, and reach spots that would otherwise mean a long hike. The Bakcou Mule is built for rugged terrain and heavy loads, making it a major upgrade for anyone who hunts big properties or hard-to-reach public land.

For hunters who spend long days covering steep, rocky terrain, a supportive pair of boots is a must. Kenetrek’s Mountain Extreme boots—which our experts dubbed the best elk hunting boots out there—have thick full-grain leather uppers, a waterproof breathable membrane, and a supportive midsole that helps keep your feet comfortable under a heavy load.

Stone Glacier has built a reputation for making some of the best backcountry hunting packs out there, and the Sky 5900 is easily its most popular model. It’s designed to haul heavy loads over long distances, with a lightweight frame, plenty of storage, and a versatile design that works well for multi-day hunts.

We recently had a chance to test out the Meat! vacuum sealer and let me tell you, this thing is legit. It’s a heavy-duty chamber sealer that pulls a strong, consistent vacuum and creates tight, reliable seals that help keep everything from backstrap to ground venison fresh in the freezer.

We put the Goal Zero Yeti 1500 through its paces in our testing and were impressed by how well it powered everything we plugged into it, making it a great pick for hunters who spend a lot of time at camp or off the grid. It has a 1,505Wh battery along with multiple AC and USB outlets for charging everything from phones to larger appliances. Bonus: There are several ways to recharge it, including solar!

Of all the dog training collars we’ve tested over the years, this Garmin combo is by far the best. It combines advanced GPS tracking with training features, two-way communication, and inReach satellite messaging to make communicating with and keeping track of your dog in the field a whole lot easier.

A good spotting scope lets you size up game from a distance without having to get closer and risk spooking it. We tested the Maven S1.2A and loved its sharp image quality and impressive low-light performance, which make it easier to pick out details when conditions aren’t ideal.

If you really want to go all out on a gift, the Orion Modular Hunting Blind is hard to top. We tested it and were impressed with the overall design, build quality, and comfort (plus, it’s easy to set up with zero machines or tools required!). It’s a significant investment, but for someone who spends a lot of time hunting from a blind, it is well worth it.

#8277. Why Québec is the Ultimate East Coast Ski Destination

Owl's Head Ski Resort at sunset. (Photo: Cantons-de-l'Est © Cantons-de-l'Est/BBT Productions)

Nope, it’s not too much to ask: You can get great snow, both natural and man-made, wild terrain, incredible food, historic architecture, and rich cultural immersion all with just a short drive and no time zone change. That’s right. In Québec, winter is so good it feels like it should be hard to get to, but it’s just across the border.

Let’s start with the snow. Canada’s French-speaking province boasts some of the nation’s highest annual snowfall, with up to 250 inches per year. And you’ll find it in every form: deep powder, groomed tracks, and perfect corduroy, spread across terrain that varies from steep and wild to mellow and peaceful. And all that snow comes with dozens of vibrant mountain towns and more than 70 ski resorts—all within a stone’s throw of the Lower 48. (Montréal is just a 90-minute flight or six-hour drive from Boston, and New Yorkers can reach Québec City in less than two hours by air.)

Next, enjoy the rewards of going wherever the path of adventure takes you. The size of the province means you have lots of choices, but rest assured you can’t go wrong: in Québec, skiable terrain unfolds in nearly every direction. The only question is what kind of ski experience you’re looking for. Here’s what you’ll find in the four ski regions featured here—plus which resorts to hit to make the most of it

Looking for spectacular scenery? Unbelievably long runs? Buttery maritime snowpack coming in off the St. Lawrence River? Northeast of Québec City, you’ll find all three in Charlevoix, where the steep slopes of Le Massif de Charlevoix hover over the water, serving up mountain-meets-river views that are totally unique, and plunging valleys and sweeping bowls attract skiers looking to test their skills amid the serene quiet of a Québécois winter. Le Massif serves up the biggest vertical drop east of the Canadian Rockies, while Mont Grand-Fonds offers a compact layout, laid-back atmosphere, and terrain for all ability levels.

Use Québec City as your base camp and you won’t have to choose between good skiing and vibrant arts and culture. The province’s capital is an enchanting maze of European architecture and historic neighborhoods. An evening walk downtown feels like a wander through a snow-draped fairytale. The food and bar scene reflects a similar blend between time-honored traditions and modern flair. And at just 30 minutes from Mont-Sainte-Anne, it’s close enough to the slopes that you can fully immerse yourself in the true Québecois lifestyle without cutting into your ski time.

Close to Montréal, the Laurentian Mountains are speckled with charming, Alps-style villages—complete with classy accommodations, spas, bistros, and microbreweries—that support a robust après-ski tradition. Mont Tremblant offers a stunning variety of terrain, including both gentle runs and enough steep-and-deep to challenge the experts. Meanwhile, Mont-Blanc and Sommet Saint-Sauveur boast quieter settings, family-friendly atmospheres, and five-star night skiing.

The lush, forested mountains southeast of Montréal are densely packed with ski areas, making this the perfect region for some serious resort-hopping. Even better: with the L’EST GO Pass, you can nab discounted lift tickets on four of the zone’s best hills. If you like night skiing, head to Bromont, a local favorite that opens more than 90 runs after sunset. Prefer the solitude of the deep woods? Head to nearby Mont Sutton for world-class tree skiing and a far wilder feel. Laid-back resorts like Owl’s Head cater to families, while Mont-Orford’s high elevation makes it a motherlode of high-quality snow.

Each of the four ski regions featured here has its own distinct personality. What connects them is Québec’s unmistakable joie de vivre: a love of local flavours, lively après-ski, and taking fun seriously. It’s what makes a ski getaway here so full of character.

Québec isn’t far from America’s East Coast, but it feels like another universe. The province boasts a unique culture defined by its French language, historic neighborhoods, local cuisine, and a dynamic craft beer scene. In its urban areas, you’ll find 17th-century colonial architecture, complete with narrow streets, turrets, and flagstone courtyards.

Leave the urban centers, and historic brick quickly gives way to winter’s snow-flocked evergreens and white-blanket pastures. Barns and silos dot the countryside, and just beyond, mountains rear into the skyline like 5,000-foot beacons calling skiers home.

Québec’s unique combination of proximity and novelty make it one of the most unique ski destinations in North America. And yet it’s not nearly as pricey as some of the other life-list destinations you might have on your list. With the American to Canadian Dollar exchange rate, accommodations and food in Québec tend to offer a strong value on a complete ski trip, especially for U.S. travelers. To make the most of that value, explore ski packages and resort offers across Québec on maneige.ski to find the right getaway for your next winter adventure.

Between its vast and varied terrain, deep snow, rich culture, easy access, and affordable prices, Québec has everything skiers need to squeeze more adventure out of winter. Whether you’re looking for more terrain, more culture, or more discovery, you’ll find it here.

Ready to take your ski adventure further? From breathtaking mountain views and exhilarating runs to vibrant après-ski and charming resort villages, Québec offers much more than great skiing. Explore the regions and plan your winter getaway with Bonjour Québec.

#8275. Vanja Matijevec Gave Up His Own Everest Summit to Save Three People

Vanja Matijevec on the Lhotse wall during his 1981 Himalayan expedition (Photo: Aleš Kunaver, kept by the National Museum of Contemporary History of Slovenia)

Vanja Matijevec belonged to a generation of Slovenian alpinists who pushed onto some of the biggest walls in the Himalayas, but one of the defining moments of his climbing life came when he chose not to summit.

On his legendary 1979 expedition to Everest, Matijevec gave up his own planned summit attempt to help Stipe Božić, Stane Belak and Ang Phu, who had become stranded above 8,000 meters during their descent. Božić later remembered Matijevec’s selflessness as helping him survive after he lost a crampon high on the mountain.

Born in Ljubljana on October 14, 1946, Matijevec first encountered the Slovenian mountains as a child, tending cattle on pastures above Tržič. He came to alpinism later, after meeting climber Jože Hočevar through his field work, and began training as a mountain guide in 1975. In 1979, Matijevec, Lado Vidmar and Blaž Oblak made the first ascent of Lucifer (WI4+), a roughly 200-meter frozen waterfall in Gozd Martuljek. The climb, completed with equipment Matijevec later remembered as rudimentary, helped usher in the era of modern ice climbing in Slovenia.

But Matijevec’s ambitions stretched far beyond Slovenia. In 1981, Matijevec and Franček Knez climbed to the rim of Lhotse’s immense South Face, then considered one of the great unsolved problems of Himalayan alpinism. Over the course of his life, Matijevec accumulated more than 30 first ascents, including a direct new route up the West Face of Trisul in 1987. Despite his achievements, his peers remember his kindness more than anything. Fellow Slovenian alpinist Viki Grošelj, who had known Matijevec since their early climbing days, remembered him after his death as a distinctive personality and, simply, “the right man in the right place,” he told Slovenian newspaper Delo.

#8274. I Hike With a Flip Phone. Here’s the Tiny Camera I’m Bringing Along.

Over the past few years, I’ve learned I’m much happier when I don’t have my smartphone on me—I’m not sure the human mind evolved to have 24-hour access to all of the Internet’s information on demand. In an effort to disconnect and be more present, I took a page from the Gen Z playbook and started carrying a flip phone instead. It’s been great—except for the camera.

A while ago, I started testing a potential solution in the Life Camera S168, a thumb-size digital camera built to compete with the Kodak Charmera. How did it actually perform on the trail? Check out this video to see what kind of photos and footage this $30 gadget is capable of turning out and read our full review for more.

A while ago, I swapped out my smartphone for a flip phone. I was getting tired of how distracted I was—doomscrolling, checking my emails—and I wanted to simplify things. This has really done the trick. On the trail it’s pretty much everything I need. It can send messages, make calls, if I need to get a hold of 911 in an emergency, it can do that. It has an MP3 player, so I can listen to podcasts at night, and it even has a rudimentary mapping app, although I’m not sure I’d trust it, I always bring a paper map and compass as backup.

However, it does have one big shortcoming: the camera on this thing really sucks. The pictures are grainy, blurry, and usually blown out. It’s not how I want to remember my trips. I often find myself hiking with my smartphone just so I can get better pictures and video. I’ve been looking for a solution, since that kind of defeats the purpose of ditching the smartphone, and I think I’ve found one.

This is the Life Camera S168. It’s part of a crop of new thumb-sized digital cameras that are designed to appeal to the retro crowd, they’re kind of like old digital cameras or old film cameras, you know, the disposable you used to take to summer camp with you. The most familiar one is the Kodak Charmera, you may have seen that in stores.

However, according to a lot of online reviews, the Life Camera’s photos and video quality is significantly better, and it has, from what I’ve seen, a fairly decent camera, you’re not going to confuse it with an iPhone or anything, but it may be enough for my purposes.

So, is the Life Camera a gimmick or a game changer? Well, that depends on you. If you’re like most hikers and you have your phone in your pocket most of the time, it’s definitely a gimmick. Your phone can do anything the Life Camera can do, and probably in better resolution.

If, however, you’re part of the small subset of hikers like me, who find they’re happier when their phone is off and in their pack, or if they’re just carrying a flip phone, you might give the Life Camera a try. No, the resolution isn’t anything to write home about, but it can capture your life on the trail in adequate detail, and if you don’t mind that retro vibe, it’s kind of fun. I’ll be carrying one on my next hike.

#8273. Go Further in Québec’s Winter Wilderness

Snowshoeing in Gaspésie. (Photo: Gaspésie © Gouv.Qc / I. Roberge)

Let this sink in: More than 92 percent of Québec is public land. Come winter, those millions of acres of woods, trails, and open glades get absolutely buried in snow, turning the province into a sprawling winter playground where opportunities for ski touring, Nordic skiing, and multiday snowshoeing abound.

All that wild landscape would be nothing without a trail system to match—which is why it’s a darn good thing that groomed trails and skintracks cover the province, courtesy of Québec’s adventure-minded culture and infrastructure. Cozy rustic huts dot the high country, Nordic centers pepper the lowlands, and there’s an extensive network of designated ski-touring areas across the region.

Behind Québec’s extensive network of winter trails and refuges lies a long tradition of winter travel and exploration.

Long before winter travel became a recreational pursuit, Indigenous peoples used snowshoes and knowledge passed down through generations to navigate the territory now known as Québec. Today, these snow-covered landscapes offer countless opportunities for exploration, from Nordic skiing and multi-day snowshoeing to backcountry adventures.

Today, Québec boasts 28 national parks and dozens of Nordic and cross-country centers. It also boasts plenty of grassroots backcountry ski areas, each complete with trail maps and designated runs. There’s no avalanche mitigation at these sites—they’re wild at heart—but the effortless parking, signage, and basic infrastructure make them a perfect stepping stone between sidecountry and true backcountry. Always remember to come equipped with the appropriate training, equipment, and avalanche awareness. And if you’d rather explore with a qualified guide, you can find businesses certified through Aventure Écotourisme Québec’s Quality-Safety certification program, which sets recognized standards for risk management, guide training and service quality.

Looking to do a little bit of everything? Try Vallée Bras-du-Nord. This all-season adventure center maintains both groomed cross-country ski trails and designated backcountry terrain. Its varied slopes and jaw-dropping views guarantee an unforgettable outing, while a collection of yurts and cabins make it a true ski-in, ski-out getaway. You won’t find a backcountry experience like it anywhere else in North America.

For a more homegrown vibe, head to Sommets du Fjord, a blues-and-blacks zone just beyond the charming village of Petite-Saguenay. The town sits right on the edge of the legendary Saguenay Fjord National Park—yet another ski touring and snowshoeing epicenter—which makes it an ideal multisport base camp.

Want to turn a great day into a great week? Treat yourself to a fully immersive multiday traverse through Québec’s snow-draped winter landscapes. Robust hut systems in national parks like Mont-Tremblant and Monts-Valins make it easy to plan linkups via Nordic ski or snowshoe, and village-to-village trips in the Laurentians like those along Les Routes Blanches offer chances to discover culture and cuisine alongside the stunning landscapes. Simply choose a trail to one or more of the parks’ remote refuges and use them as stopover points to cook, relax, and connect with your adventure buddies—and recharge by a blazing woodstove before hitting the trail again the next day.

The adventure doesn’t end when the skis or snowshoes come off. Beyond the trails, Québec’s welcoming villages, local flavors, and cozy inns offer the perfect setting to unwind and reconnect. Share a well-earned meal, raise a glass of a local wine or brew with your fellow adventurers, and relive the day’s discoveries. Because sometimes, going further isn’t just about the distance you travel, it’s about everything you experience along the way.

Your next winter adventure starts here. Whether you’re seeking powder-filled backcountry descents, multi-day Nordic ski routes or peaceful snowshoe expeditions through snow-covered forests, Québec invites you to explore further. Discover inspiring winter experiences and start planning your next expedition with Bonjour Québec.
