#8262. How I Got Benighted (Twice) on Yosemite’s ‘Lost Arrow Chimney’

In the first installment in our Benighted series, Shino Jomoto shares with Climbing the weird and spooky tale from her night in the chimney on September 17, 2023—and what all climbers can learn from her epic.

With over two decades of climbing experience, Jomoto specializes in epics, which she defines as getting sandbagged on adventure multi-pitch climbs and big walls that take far longer than anticipated. But her biggest epic of all occurred in the storied chimney route (5.10a) up Lost Arrow Spire in Yosemite.

Earlier this week, a Yosemite Climbing Association (YCA) newsletter detailed the history of the Lost Arrow Spire, including the chimney route. First ascensionist John Salathé himself bailed near the top in 1946. The next year, he came back “for an all-out effort” that took over five days. “Pushing through the claustrophobic shadows of the Lost Arrow Chimney, Salathé and [Anton] Nelson endured searing heat, dehydration, and brutal physical exertion,” the YCA shared. “They spent four bivouacs dangling from crude hammocks tied to pitons driven into the wall.”

The Lost Arrow Chimney is also believed to contain a human skeleton. On March 19, 1961, 17-year-old Irving Smith died in a rappelling accident from the top. An American Alpine Club trip report shared that Smiths’ body remains in the chimney: “While a ranger and volunteer rescue party was preparing to attempt the difficult and dangerous removal, Smith’s parents and Park authorities determined that no further life should be risked, and that the body should remain at rest where it lay.”

A comment on the Mountain Project page of Yosemite’s Lost Arrow Chimney (5.10a) foreshadowed what was to come: “Don’t let the moderate grade fool you. After pitch 7, you are halfway done.” The Lost Arrow Chimney is 10 pitches.

Poor fitness, dehydration, and sleep deprivation conspired, and by pitch eight we needed headlamps. Too tired to continue, we did the only sensible thing: slept inside the chimney.

I started climbing in 2005, mostly out of a hatred for my corporate job. That led to years living out of a station wagon, trying to figure out how to rock climb. Fast forward decades later, I’m in the business of going on epics—a lot.

Jim Herson said you could write an entire print edition on just my epics alone. I’ve had near-death epics like lightning and hypothermia on a big wall. But I’ll put it this way: I can climb El Cap faster than I can climb the Lost Arrow Chimney.

The reason why I wanted to share this is that nine out of ten climbers will have an epic on the Lost Arrow. You might be able to climb 5.13, but try to climb 10 pitches of old-school chimney—see if you can still call yourself a 5.10 climber. I think everyone goes in with the confidence of the grade. Then they just get gut-punched by the old-schoolness of the climb.

On my Lost Arrow Chimney epic, we weren’t in danger. We never called YOSAR (Yosemite Search and Rescue). You’re just humbled in a silly way because it’s such a silly grade.

Aside from the likes of Chuck Pratt or old-school climbers, I don’t know anyone who’s ever redone this route. When you do a climb, you usually redo it. You want a redpoint or you go back again. Nobody is dumb enough to redo this climb. We’ve done it three times, so it really goes to show either how incredibly stupid we are, or how memorable of an epic it was that we just needed to clear the record.

The lore that Jim Herson shared with me was he knew a guy who climbed the Lost Arrow Chimney and then never rock climbed again. The reality is he went to med school and gave up climbing. But that was his last-ever climb. It just embodies the spirit of the Lost Arrow Chimney.

The first time John and I did Lost Arrow Chimney in 26 hours on October 5, 2019 as a party of three, and we were actually in decent shape.

The time we slept in the chimney a few years later, we were a party of two. We thought we were fit. But we did all the classic gumby moves. We got up too late and got lost on the approach. To get back on route, we had to rappel. It’s obvious on a topo where you should go, but at four o’clock in the morning, you get lost. And we didn’t bring enough water.

On the climb, we started losing daylight. My boyfriend started dry heaving from dehydration and lack of fitness. He stopped mid-pitch in a chimney—he couldn’t go on.

There’s nothing you can really say in the dark. We’re not Rocky Talkie people. We have too much pride for that. So we just had to communicate with a rope. Finally, I was on belay. I went up to him. We were mid-chimney—this wasn’t even a belay station.

John was like, “I can’t. I can’t do this anymore.” And he’s a 10-times better climber than I am. So I was like, “All right, I’ll go.” He was like, “Are you sure?” I was like, “We can’t sleep here. We can sleep in a lot of places. This is not a place to sleep.”

It’s always scary when a very experienced person says, “I’m scared.” John rarely says he’s scared. It takes courage to say that. When you’re in the dark, there’s nothing you do. You can’t start yelling and placating, you know? You just realize in that moment like, it’s a serious climb. And you’re still having to reconcile that with 10a.

So I went questing and found this chimney that was adjacent to the climb. It wasn’t a chimney you go through on route, but everyone goes by it.

We were two pitches from the notch. Should we suffer for six hours, then rappel and call it a day? Or suffer through the whole night? You make those calculations. We decided we might as well stay put, rather than burden resources to call for YOSAR or any sort of search and rescue. I think that’s the number one thing: Can you self-rescue?

We had brought a salad that we thought we were going to eat at the base. So we ended up at the bivy with a salad, but no water. It’s kind of hard to eat a salad without water. So all of my swear words were salad- or foliage-related. It doesn’t matter if you have a whole buffet, if you have no water, you don’t want to eat anything. So we were just staring at this salad in the chimney. It’s one of those things with the Maslow’s hierarchy—if you don’t have water, you can’t do anything.

We laid out both climbing ropes so that we were a little bit insulated from the ground. We did the bivy dance. It was flatter than most bivy spots I have slept on. We were really depressed, just waiting for daylight.

Back sleeping was impossible, so we were relegated to side sleeping for the next six hours. There was no way to sleep besides big spoon, little spoon. The walls were very cold. I put a giant sad face in chalk where I was. Another group went and did it later and said, “We knew where you bivvied ’cause there was a giant sad face.”

But we were so thirsty, the epic wasn’t over. We could hear Yosemite Falls. Our brains went: Maybe we can just hike over there. Another lesson is you’re not rational when you’re having an epic. So we lost another half day going to the falls. We were sitting in a pool of water that we couldn’t drink. And we realized we couldn’t cut over. So we had to go back. A day and a half later, we got back to the car.

Finally, on June 2, 2024, we got our redemption. We did it in a day and tagged the summit where people do the Tyrolean. It still took us all day—and we didn’t even free it. We had to pull on gear. It makes you respect the history of the first ascensionists—the lineage of people who have tried it and who have bailed. There’s an insane amount of really, really old bail slings.

You’re in there and it’s a vortex. It’s spooky. I’m not a mystical person, but there are hexes that have been kind of swallowed by the rock. It’s a freaking spooky museum of gear. When you’re in there, you have an appreciation for who climbed this before you and the style in which they climbed it, because it is terrifying.

I feel like I’ve gotten my chimney badge in Yosemite. There should be a club for it: the Lost Arrow Chimney Support Group. If you can summit the whole climb and rappel in a day, I would have mad respect. More people climb the Nose than the Lost Arrow Chimney. Anyone who’s dumb enough and adventurous enough to sign up for that level of masochism will resonate more with me than if you’re C1ing a 30-pitch climb.

If you survive nine or ten pitches of chimneys with your partner, you will be bonded forever, for better or worse. They’ve done all these studies about reality TV shows, like for love matchmaking. You put people in intense situations and they confuse their endorphins as romance, but it’s really just adrenaline. Part of it is trauma bonding. Some couples are more willing to climb the Lost Arrow Chimney than go to couples therapy.

The beauty of epics is there are way more fun memories than sending. Every sending story is so ephemeral. But when you’ve been sucker-punched so hard by something scary, or that requires lack of sleep, or incredible amounts of suffering, you remember those experiences for decades.

If you don’t have some delusional optimism, you will never get off the ground. That delusion will catch up to you at some point. But you have to have a little bit of fuel. As long as it’s not over your head or dangerous for you and others. Can you live well and safely enough to live another day? Go do it.

Delusion meets reality at some point, like when you’re having an epic. Benighted is a subcategory of epics—it’s in the taxonomy. There has to be some darkness involved, generally speaking, but you don’t need to have slept.

The easy way to know is when you end up at the parking lot, you see your best friends, and they’re like, “How was it?” The face doesn’t lie. You actually don’t need to say words. They see your face and they’re like, “That was an epic.”

John and I have an epic grading scale. It’s the reverse GPA.

Every time we finish, we rate them. The Lost Arrow Chimney was like a 5.0.

As told to Maya Silver. This story has been edited for length, structure, and clarity.

#8261. New Research Finds That Short Workouts, or Exercise Snacking, Are as Effective as Traditional Strength Sessions

When life gets in the way, it can be tough to stick to your usual workout routine—but new research suggests you might not need to try to cram in your typical hour- or hours-long workout schedule.

The study, published in the Journal of Exercise Science and Fitness in October 2026, found that exercising in short bursts throughout the day—a practice sometimes called “exercise snacking”—can be as beneficial as one long, continuous workout. In fact, exercise snacking may be more fun for some people, which could lead them to exercise more often.

“The idea behind fragmented resistance training [or exercise snacking] is that there’s more of this feeling of autonomy when you’re achieving things on a regular basis,” Craig Pille, MD, a sports medicine physician at NYU Langone, who was not involved in the study, told Outside. “I think that changes the psychological burden of exercise.”

Here’s what to know about exercise snacking and how you can adapt it into your own workout routine, whether you’re just trying to stay fit or prep for your next outdoor adventure.

The authors of the new study recruited 45 male college students at Tongji University in Shanghai, China, for involvement in the research. The students were put into one of three groups: a traditional resistance training group, a fragmented resistance training group (the exercise snacking group), or a control group. The participants in the two resistance training groups were asked to work out three days a week for eight weeks.

Those in the traditional resistance training group completed their workouts by doing three sets of 20 squats all in one workout session, while those in the exercise snacking group performed one set of 20 squats at three different points throughout the day; they had at least a one-hour block of time between each squat session. During their final training session, participants filled out a questionnaire asking how much they enjoyed their workouts.

“The cool thing about this study is that it shows that both groups had benefits. The results show that both [training plans] get you fairly equitable outcomes,” Dr. Pille said. In other words, both groups saw comparable improvements in muscular strength compared with those in the control group. “But the difference was in an enjoyment scale survey,” Dr. Pille continued. “The fragmented resistance training group scored a little bit higher.”

There are a few limitations to note. “This is a pretty small sample size: 45 kids who already had some experience doing weight training,” Dr. Pille said. “Also, the authors only looked at one real test, the back squat.” The researchers also pointed out that because women weren’t included in the study, the results may not be as applicable to them.

But while we don’t have enough research to say that exercise snacking is a good solution for everyone—or even most people—it’s certainly safe to try if you’re looking for ways to fit more movement into a busy schedule, Dr. Pille said.

When you find yourself with ten minutes to spare, any kind of movement is better than no movement, he added. You could climb a few sets of stairs in between meetings to loosen up before a hike, do a set of ankle and hip mobility exercises before you head out for lunch if you’re prepping for an upcoming run, or do some lower-body sessions in short bursts during your strength training days ahead of your next bike ride.

“The idea here is what we preach all the time in sports medicine: movement is medicine. We want you to move your body,” Dr. Pille said. “Exercise snacking makes this a little more achievable for people.”

#8260. The 7 Items That Got Me Through October (and the Rest of Fall)

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Oh October, the month of mystery. Here in Boulder, Colorado, it’s when you wake up in the dark not knowing if it will be warm, cold, raining, or windy. The only thing you do know every morning is there will be even more much-larger-than-life-sized skeletons poking out of peoples’ lawns. (Why has this become a thing? As my friend Clare said on a run the other day, “people are desecrating their lawns with plastic trash!”)

Anyway, it’s a tricky time of year for running. Head out the door overdressed and you will end up a puddle of sweat that, depending on the weather, ultimately makes you cold. Leave underdressed, as I did for a tempo run two weeks ago, and your limbs will feel like they’ve been cursed by a witch who’s turned them to immovable ice.

But tricky conditions can be solved with treats. My trusty associate editor is, in his words, “going to the desert to do something stupid.” (Go Cade!) That leaves just me to round up our gear of the month. Here are the five items I kept packed in my Janji Ultrahauler (another piece of gear I can’t live without!) so I was ready for whatever I woke up to:

Kilian Jornet’s fledgling shoe and apparel company has stuck to relatively technical alpine equipment—until now with the Nnormal Cadi. This do-everything trail shoe is exceptionally comfortable thanks to a padded heel collar and tongue and a cushy midsole with 37 mm stack in the heel, 31 mm in the forefoot. It’s got a nice wide toe box (an obsession of mine as I work on my foot strength and toe splay). And with a Vibram Megagrip outsole it’s tacky on all terrain and in all conditions. I also appreciate the mesh upper, which is breathable on hot days and dries quickly on wet ones. It’s the only shoe I brought on a trip recently, which means I found myself wearing it for a 12-mile run around the Charles River in Boston—definitely not as energetic as your typical road trainer these days, but it got the job done just fine. It’s just a solid, dependable shoe.

It’s rained A LOT in Boulder this month. And by a lot, I mean more than zero times. I know I’ve lived here for too long because I’ve gotten soft and the only thing that got me through more than zero very dark, very wet mornings was this rain jacket from Arc’teryx. That’s because it’s actually waterproof. But it’s also super lightweight and breathable, meaning you don’t incinerate in your own body heat and end up wet anyway. Plus one for the cinch on the hood so you can actually keep it on your head while you’re running and another bonus for the vents under the armpits, which help moderate body heat. I know $450 is an obscene amount to spend on anything, but this is definitely a case of you get what you pay for.

When it comes to running pants and tights I am very, very picky. They can’t suffocate my waist, but they also need to stay put. They can’t bunch around the knees, but they also can’t be so baggy that the pant legs rub into each other. The Janji Altas Multi Pant is one of the few pieces that passes my stringent test. They are supremely comfortable thanks to a wide elastic waistband, and a drawstring lets you dial in the fit. They’re loose enough to allow for full range of motion, but they’re streamlined enough that I can wear them for harder efforts without getting annoyed. Why I really love them for this time of year is they are lightweight and breathable, providing just the right amount of insulation. And even better, they have nearly knee-length ankle zips so I often wear them for the warm up and zip them off for intervals—no shoe removal required.

There is something so comforting and luxurious about tucking into a comfy vest for a fall outing. Enter this fleece-lined vest from 7Mesh. It’s super breathable yet cozy thanks to a soft, woven outer layer paired with the light and ultrasoft fleece lining. I’ve been loving it for colder runs when a jacket feels like too much but a long sleeve isn’t quite enough. And I’ve also been loving it on the bike—especially because the vest folds into itself via a big back pocket, revealing little straps that let you fix it to your bike frame when you’re not wearing it.

Not too cold and not too warm, snug but not tight, these gloves are  a shoulder-season star. They’re so lightweight that I don’t think twice about wearing them for the start of a run before the sun rises and stashing them in a pocket as I warm up with the ground. I can use my phone with them on, carry my ballot (the midterms are on Tuesday!), as well as maneuver zippers and, if desperate, tie shoes. Plus the colors and patterns instantly boost my mood. (They came in so many fun options!)

One-star review for the name. Zero stars for the logo branded on the top of the collar. And yet, five stars for these socks. They are just that comfy and moisture-wicking. I am pretty skeptical of overengineered gear, but CEP has me thinking maybe there is something to developing stuff in a lab. These socks provide a gentle amount of compression and arch support while also being ventilated in all the places you want it. In other words: they stay put, and they keep my feet comfortable for a wide range of temperatures—perfect for fall running. Most importantly, my feet do not slip in my shoes. I repeat: no slippage here. My friend saw me running in them the other day and he said he also loves these socks so much that he ordered five pairs. Oh and they come in approximately one billion colorways.

I know, I know, it’s a crime to spend more than $50 on a hair product—much less two products. But hear me out: Colorado is savage on my wavy hair. When left unchecked, the dry air and harsh sun leech out every last drop of moisture, turning my hair into a wiry mess. Add in the rainy days of October (or my annual pilgrimage to Hawaii) and in years past I am ripping out chunks of matted hair every time I shower. Enter this fancy shampoo and conditioner. I am not exaggerating when I say this stuff has revolutionized my hair’s life. For the first time in 13 years since I moved here, my hair feels soft. And I can actually get a brush through it when I get out of the shower! You better believe I will be buying it again.

#8259. The Gear That Backpacker’s Editors Loved in October 2026

With spooky season behind us, we’re into fall’s final stretch. Here at Backpacker, we made the most of it: A month ago, our editors got together to backpack a stretch of Wisconsin’s Ice Age Trail, then spent October exploring the forests of the Pacific Northwest, strolling our local trails in Vermont, and even notching a few early-season ski days in Colorado. Here’s the gear that helped us do it

I know: How brave of me to pick what must be the most commonly-used sleeping pad in existence. But some things are classics for a reason, and this folding closed-cell pad is one of them. Consider: It’s unpoppable, a big deal when you regularly go backpacking in the desert like I do; it doesn’t need to be inflated or deflated, which eliminates one task from both your nighttime and morning routines; and it’s light, with a regular running just 14 ounces.

Is it comfortable? Opinions on that vary. I’ll admit that it may not be the supportive option available for side sleepers (or, with its R-value of 2.0, cold sleepers) but I’ve found its egg-crate-style design to be comfier than flat closed-cell models like Walmart’s roll-up Ozark Trail. Anyway, if you’re not tired enough to fall asleep the minute your head hits the ground, you could always just try hiking farther. —Adam Roy, Editor-in-Chief

This poncho is the answer to a dilemma I’ve faced since starting to backpack with my dog. I worry about keeping her warm on chilly nights, but a dog-size sleeping bag never seemed like the best solution, and she’s too big to crawl in with me. The Palisades Sleep Poncho from Ruffwear is the first wearable sleeping bag I’ve seen available; it offers more full-coverage warmth than a dog jacket, stays put better than a blanket, all while being less confining than a sleeping bag. Featuring a ripstop shell and packable synthetic insulation, the poncho slips over the dog’s head and drapes over their back so they have the freedom to move around, curl up, roll over or sprawl without compromising coverage.

A cinchable neck baffle keeps in warmth, and soft, adjustable leg loops eliminate slippage (it’s also easy to bundle up the rear of the poncho with a button for potty breaks). On an October night camping in Washington’s Mt. Baker Wilderness, temps dipped below freezing. My dog, who is usually restless in the tent, slept soundly all night curled beneath the Palisades Poncho. Her water dish was frozen solid when we woke up, but she was cozy and content all night long. Paired with a pup-sized foam pad, this poncho makes for a doggy sleep system I can feel confident in. Bonus: It’s extremely cute. —Zoe Gates, Senior Editor

I should have mentioned the price of these hiking pants in the video, but I forgot to. So I’m going to lead with it here: $430 for a single pair of pants is a little outrageous no matter how you spin it. That’s about the same cost as weatherproof snowpants. But the Charge Trousers from Thrudark are exceptionally well made, thoughtfully designed, and built with premium materials (some of which I’ve only ever seen in packs and tents). There are three main things I like about these pants. First, the layout is exceptional. There are six pockets (all on the front), but they don’t look like cargo pants. The ankle cuffs have snap-button adjusters to tighten or loosen them depending on preference and what you’re doing. The hips have Velcro adjusters built in, so you can dial in a perfect fit to your waist, and despite that feature, Thrudark still included belt loops. (Some brands don’t do loops if they have the adjusters, and that drives me nuts.)

My second favorite thing is the materials that these pants are made with. Thrudark used a high-tensile cotton and a Dyneema-Cordura blend that is both highly durable and lightweight. The knees are reinforced with that blend, so you can kneel in a bed of nails and would probably be just fine (at least the pants would be). The rear panel has a four-way stretch material over the butt, which offers a lot of freedom of movement. Third and finally, they’re just comfortable. I can’t say that about every brand’s hiking pants. Where do they fall short? The price, obviously. There’s also the question of how well the cotton elements would hold up if exposed to too much rain (or ungodly perspiration from the wearer). Maybe I’d ask Thrudark for one more pocket on the back, but then again, who on Earth needs seven pockets? —Will Brendza, Associate Editor

Polartec, a well-known fabric company that supplies much of the outdoor industry with its fleece, just released two new versions of its popular Alpha fabric that you’ll be seeing in big-name and cottage brands this winter. One of them is Alpha Wool, a fabric that uses a wool base weave with tufts of Alpha polyester insulation on the outside.

Our very first sample is a crew pullover from cycling brand Ornot. It’s not quite as featherlight as pure Alpha, but at 8.5-ounces in medium, still lighter than micro-grid fleece. Because of that base wool layer, it’s totally stink-free. It’s also slightly more wind-resistant, softer, warmer, and more durable than regular Alpha. —Benjamin Tepler, Senior Gear Editor

#8258. After Testing 122 Pieces of Gear, We Found the Best Climbing Gear of Fall 2026

Gear testing above 12,000 feet on the golden granite of Chamonix's Aiguille du Midi. It's a hard job, but someone's got to do it. (Photo: Anthony Walsh)

Rock climbing season doesn’t end when snow hits the high country. Some of the best conditions of the year are right around the corner: cool temps, ample shade, and just the right amount of humidity in the air. Unless you’re sharpening your ice tools, don’t give up on the rock (or plastic) season just yet—with the right gear, you’re in for the best season of your life.

Climbing’s gear-testing team has spent all summer sweating it out with the latest and greatest so you don’t have to. We tested 28 harnesses, 27 pairs of climbing shoes, 30 pairs of approach shoes, 9 ropes, and 28 backpacks—a healthy mix of new items and longtime favorites. Some of the gear was good, some was great, and a lot of it missed the mark: bruised hips, sore feet, exploding packs—it’s all part of the gear-testing game.

2026 was the year of the hyper-specific shoe. Although notable all-arounders made it onto our list, the real highlights were the shoes who didn’t try to do too much. One shoe felt about as stiff as a crampon, with its new-age carbon insert, and powered us up numerous vert testpieces; another had about as much support as a woolen sock (but, like, in a good way!); and the best shoe I’ve ever used for offwidths is absolutely terrible for finger cracks. Perhaps 2026 is the year of the shoe quiver.

The harness is the one piece of gear that will make or break your day on the wall. In an effort to find the best climbing harness available, we put everything from fast-and-light alpine G-strings to beefy big-wallers to the test this year, taking them on trips from the cold Canadian alpine to the steep walls of Devil’s Tower to overhung sport routes at The Red.

Unlike this year’s crop of rock shoes, my favorite climbing packs worked hard to serve multiple niches. One versatile alpine-climbing pack carried anywhere from one to four days of mountain kit with ease. And a new haul bag might just be the last pack (and airplane carry on) a rock climber will ever need.

The best climbing ropes are a tough category of gear to review because, these days, almost all are well made and perform great right out of the package. It’s only after hard wear—climbing pitch after pitch in rain, snow, and ice, coiling and uncoiling on dirt and sand, and taking some big whippers—that a rope reveals its true colors.

Helmets are our best defense against rockfall and weird whippers while climbing outdoors. And after years of writing accident reports—often of climbers who took a seemingly benign fall, before something weird happened—I regularly note how fortunate the climber was to be wearing one. When shopping for a helmet, take the time to find one that’s comfortable, lightweight, breathable, and fits properly—because actually liking your helmet makes you far more likely to wear it.

#8257. 17 Campfire Recipes to Make Your Next Outdoor Gathering a Hit

At the end of a long day, there’s nothing like sitting by the campfire, watching the flames dance and hearing the wood crackle (as long as the fire’s made safely and legally, of course). The only way to make it better is savoring a Michelin-star-worthy meal while sitting fireside. When preparing your menu, it’s easy to opt for a go-to hot dogs and s’mores combo, but there are so many more delicious meals out there. With these revolutionary campfire recipes, you won’t want to settle for anything less than all-plates-scraped-clean delicious. All you need is a burning campfire and a rumbling stomach.

This hearty combo tastes even better in the woods than it does at the diner. Whip it up over a campfire, and you’ll not only impress your buddies—you’ll have a no-pot meal with zero cleanup (eat right out of the bag!).

Got a relaxed morning? Make this tasty combination of sweet pears and crunchy granola.

Drizzle these fluffy pancakes with maple syrup for breakfast or top with chives and sour cream for a savory dinner.

“Just like Mom used to make,” says our editor of this simple, not-too-sweet pastry that’s perfect for breakfast or a healthy dessert.

A few simple spices elevate your already-delicious, fresh-caught trout to sublime, says Charlie Borrowman, Washington-based cooking instructor.

Pizza at camp? We’re in. This prep-ahead pie is an easy crowd-pleaser.

With fresh, handmade pasta in your repertoire, you can go as far out as you want without ever leaving behind the taste of a home-cooked meal.

Spice up this classic Turkish dish with shelf-stable Spanish chorizo, roasted right on your campsite coals. Best part? Eat straight out of a zucchini, so there are no dishes to clean.

Prep these at home for a delicious first-night treat with south-of-the-border flavors.

Take your fireside fish skills to the next level with this savory salmon recipe.

Apple pie is a classic flavor for a reason. The mixture of ripe apple and warm spices (cinnamon, cardamom, and ginger) work as well on warm summer nights as on chilly fall ones.

Hear us out on this one. All Backpacker editors have an opinion on what cheese works best in a s’more (mine is a Dubliner cheese). Try it out and find out for yourself.

This camping-friendly take on a classic Italian confection is so good, you’ll probably dream about it.

Craving ice cream? This take on a frozen classic is the next best thing.

This decadent treat is a welcome change from typical backcountry desserts, and requires almost no clean-up.

Throwing a campsite party? This treat satisfies any sweet tooth. Tip: In place of the English toffee bits, you can use four chopped 1.4-ounce chocolate-covered toffee bars (or plain toffee). Don’t overfill your cones or they won’t melt properly.

To turn this Thanksgiving staple into a portable treat, use a combo of graham crackers, instant sweet potatoes, marshmallows, and fall spices. The result delivers all the flavor you love in a outdoor-friendly package.

#8256. How Joe “Stringbean” McConaughy (Finally) Broke the John Muir Trail FKT

Joe McConaughy thought he would probably start a bit slower than François D’Haene when he went after the Frenchman’s record on the John Muir Trail (JMT) this September. He guessed he’d be maybe 20 or 30 minutes behind in the early miles.

But when McConaughy got to Kearsarge Pass around mile 40, he was an hour off of D’Haene, who ran the Fastest Known Time (FKT) on the 223-mile trail through California’s Sierra Nevada in 2017, just months after winning UTMB for the third time.

“That was definitely a bit of a crack in the armor,” McConaughy told Trail Runner. “But I told myself that maybe he went out at more of a race effort, while my pace was better for a multi-day FKT.”

McConaughy, known by his thru-hiking trail name, “Stringbean,” has more than a few multiday FKTs to his name. He’s set records on the Pacific Crest Trail, Appalachian Trail, Long Trail, and Arizona Trail. And he had two prior record attempts on the JMT, one of which earned him an unsupported FKT.

“I thought my experience could help me beat him,” McConaughy said.

As he chased the ghost of the JMT’s past, McConaughy drew from his many multi-day FKTs and races. All of the miles and mistakes, successes and failures, and lessons and growth along the way helped him ultimately establish a new FKT of 2 days, 16 hours, and 15 seconds, taking nearly three and a half hours off a time that had stood for nearly a decade.

In rock climbing, climbers talk about “flashing” a route. It’s when they successfully climb the whole thing on their first attempt—without any practice or “beta” to help. McConaughy’s JMT effort was pretty much the opposite of flashing. The 33-year-old Seattle-based endurance coach was incredibly familiar with every mile of the JMT. Prior to his record setting attempt this fall, he’d covered the trail four times—the first in 2014—including the two prior FKT attempts. He’d also spent five summers guiding backpacking trips in the Sierra.

So when McConaughy ended up in a blizzard on Muir Pass with snowflakes landing in his eyeballs, it didn’t really stress him out or slow him down. If anything, it helped him move faster as he wanted to get up and over to warmer ground.

“I’ve seen the worst that the Sierra can throw at you,” he said, citing thunderstorms, blizzards, and rugged terrain. “I didn’t have to do a bunch of mental gymnastics, worrying about things I hadn’t experienced before. Instead, I could devote all of my energy to things that actually were issues.”

Most of McConaughy’s issues during the record attempt were ones he expected to occur, was prepared for, and could handle. “The long climbs were long climbs and some of the descents take decades,” he said. But after numerous JMT attempts he knew “it could feel much harder.” A little over a day into his attempt he was two hours ahead of D’Haene’s splits.

The JMT is far from the only goal for which McConaughy’s persistence has paid off. He took seven swings at earning a Golden Ticket into the Western States 100 before clinching one at the Black Canyon 100K on his eighth try in 2025. He’s also raced the Cocodona 250 three times and has a trio of Barkley Marathons starts.

“I like to think I’m more fun than a project-er, but when I look back, that’s pretty much my entire running career,” he said. “I feel like it gives me purpose. I want to do routes that inspire me and motivate me and take what I’ve done wrong, or what I feel like I could improve on, and continue to experiment, tinker, and optimize.”

He’s not as intense as a rock climber going after a seemingly impossible objective like the Dawn Wall, he swears. Rather, it’s about finding the sweet spot where he’s pushing himself to grow but having fun doing it. He’s not training to be the best at any given race or record attempt; he’s training to be the best version of himself for years to come.

“I get a lot of joy from sticking with the process, training with a smile, putting in the work to make a difference, and looking for opportunities to rise like a phoenix and perform the best that I can,”  McConaughy said.

Caroline Himbert, who is coached by McConaughy and set her own unsupported FKT on the JMT this July, helped pace McConaughy on the JMT this fall. “He goes back to things he’s failed at and tries to continuously learn and grow; he loves the science and spreadsheets and takes things seriously,” Himbert said. “But at the same time, he doesn’t take things too seriously and he keeps things fluid and fun.”

As evidenced by the fact that it stood for nine years, the JMT record was stout. D’Haene is known for bringing a newfound level of professionalism to FKT attempts, with a full support staff, set of pacers, and film crew. But rather than seeing the competitive level of the record as a deterrent, McConaughy saw it as part of the draw.

“It’s the granddaddy of FKTs,” he said. “More people have attempted the JMT FKT than pretty much any other premier route that exists—and the fact that François [D’Haene] and Darcy [Piceu] were the [previous] record holders is an ode to the level of attention and competitiveness that it’s gotten.”

On his first attempt in 2022, McConaughy set an unsupported record of three days and one hour. But Jeff Garmire beat it by 13 minutes just 25 days later.

McConaughy knew he could do better, so he tried to reclaim the record in 2024. But he hallucinated in the final miles and wound up off-trail on a class-four scramble, much closer to life-and-limb-threatening risk than he’d anticipated. It was a wake-up call for McConaughy, who always considers what he’s asking of others when he chases a big goal. He’s now the father of a 6-month-old and knew he couldn’t end up in a similar situation—or worse—if he went back.

“That experience made me really rethink what the record meant to me and ask myself if I wanted to do it again,” he said, adding that it felt reckless to go for another unsupported record. But after much reflection, and many conversations with his wife Katie, he decided he had to go back.

“I knew I couldn’t exist as an athlete without trying to put my stamp on the JMT,” he said. “This was my third time [attempting the FKT] on this trail and I wanted to give it my all, and use my best tips and tricks from every other effort to get the record.”

McConaughy showed up with a 12-tab spreadsheet and 12 years of beta to guide his effort this fall. He thought some of the greatest opportunities for improvement lay in fueling, pacing, and recruiting an all-star crew to help him out. In his unsupported-style attempts, he’d had to carry all of his own food and gear with no supply restocks along the way.

At Cocodona in 2025, McConaughy hit a wall that no amount of carbs could fix. He thought he knew how he needed to fuel to compete for the win. He’d done sweat testing and was experimenting with high-carb fueling. But he ended up with GI distress and struggled to breathe. He still finished in a respectable fourth place, but it was far from the finish he wanted.

He started working with nutritionist Meredith Terranova, who suggested he was likely hypernatremic—too high of blood sodium concentration—during Cocodona. He wondered if trying to optimize his performance through a data-driven approach with high carb fueling and sweat tests meant he’d stopped listening to his body.

So on the JMT he turned to real food like trail mix, purees, and waffles, especially on the big climbs—of which there is no shortage with 38,000 feet of elevation gain to cover. He also used recovery drink mixes and fat- and protein-based fuels from his nutrition sponsor, Näak.

“I feel like sticking to more whole food was the biggest learning and the biggest difference maker in my performance,” he said.

He also made up ground through a smarter sleep strategy. In his 2022 attempt, in which he finished six hours behind D’Haene’s record time, McConaughy slept for six hours. He knew there was an opportunity to trim down time spent resting while still sleeping enough to avoid dangerous hallucinations.

He settled on taking a mere 40 minutes of sleep beneath a pine tree on Bear Ridge—around 28 hours in. He thought it might be prudent to get at least an hour but he decided to push it a little with 40 minutes, figuring he could always nap later if he needed it. When he got to his third night out on the trail he was still running strong, cracking jokes, and appreciating his surroundings, Himbert said.

“You could tell he was having a good time and he was a ball of energy,” she said. “I was with him more towards the end, and he was still moving so well. I think that’s the key with this trail; it’s so challenging but if you can still move well towards the end then you can crack these times. I think Joe really nailed it, and it went close to perfect.”

McConaughy’s crew was one of his greatest assets. He learned some things about crewing the JMT after his crew missed him at Kearsarge Pass during his Pacific Crest Trail FKT in 2014. The PCT overlaps with the JMT for about 170 miles. He had to keep going on the PCT for two days with no sleeping bag, only a half-day’s worth of calories, and nothing warmer than a thin windbreaker. “We didn’t really know what we were doing,” he said. Hence the 12-tab spreadsheet this go-around, which was largely for the benefit of his crew and the complicated logistics of supporting a record-attempt on the JMT.

Part of the beauty of the JMT is that it offers an uninterrupted tour of backcountry wilderness. The trail only crosses the road twice over the course of the entire 223 miles. That’s also what makes it a bear to support. Meeting McConaughy on the trail required hiking several miles and thousands of feet of climbing to deliver food and gear. Pacers ran monster sections—usually around 40 miles at a time. But his crew of pacers was up for the challenge, with a collective résumé that boasted JMT FKTs, podium finishes, and 200-mile runs.

“Tara Dower talked about being a vessel on the Appalachian Trail, and I certainly had a similar experience on the JMT,” McConaughy said. “I was able to appreciate the beauty of where I was and the excitement of doing this absurd endurance thing because my crew was always filling my cup instead of making me pour things out to keep going.”

One thing that McConaughy has learned time and time again, is that he runs best when his cup is full.

“Gratitude and joy are the greatest performance-enhancing drugs,” he said.

While he was running, he thought about Katie, who was home solo-parenting so he could acclimatize to the altitude and run for 64 straight hours. He thought about his parents, who enabled him to get outside and run cross-country from a young age. He thought about the people who have supported his running career, and the friends who traveled to the Sierra to help him through the 223-mile journey. And he thought about the Sierra themselves, the mountains that have kept him coming back time and time again for the last 12 years.

“I run my worst when I’m thinking about how far behind someone’s splits I am,” he said. “When I caught myself doing that on the JMT, I thought, ‘This is doing more harm than good. You need to move forward at your own pace, and focus on the things that really matter.’”

After shaving over three hours off such a long-standing record, McConaughy hopes that he’s reached an end with his JMT FKT attempts. With all of the time and effort he has dedicated to the JMT, it feels a bit like a fairytale ending: “The princess was saved,” he said.

Now, he’s ready for a new goal, one he’s ready to chase to fuel his performance and fill his cup

“It’s one of those moments where I realize I’m maybe more capable than I thought I was,” he said. “And that makes it exciting to go back to Cocodona, or Western States, or another FKT, or any number of things to see what I can do.”

#8255. A Conversation Between Alex Honnold and Jim Morrison on ‘Everest: The Other Side’

At first glance, it might not seem like Alex Honnold’s free solo of El Capitan has much in common with Jim Morrison’s first ski descent of Everest’s north face, which is documented in Jimmy Chin’s new film Everest: The Other Side, which releases today, October 30.

But in a conversation during a live recording of Climbing Gold in May, it became clear that several parallels exist between these historic firsts:

Despite their shared sky-high risk tolerance, both Honnold and Morrison also agree with the general public on one thing: They consider each other “crazy.” Morrison called Honnold’s ropeless ascent of El Cap “totally insane.” Meanwhile, Honnold struggled to identify the line one might ski down Everest’s north side in a photo. Once Morrison pointed it out, Honnold declared: “That seems like death.”

The Hornbein Couloir on the northern Tibet side of Everest has taken the lives of several climbers, including the snowboarder Marco Siffredi who attempted to make the first descent of the couloir in 2002; his body has never been found.

Two Americans, Thomas Hornbein and Willi Unsoeld, made the first ascent of Everest’s north side in 1963. The north side’s first ascent came just 22 days after Jim Whittaker became the first American to climb Everest via the south side. The 9,000-foot couloir they took to the top was colloquially known as “Hornbein’s Avalanche Chute.” Jimmy Chin also attempted an ascent of Hornbein’s in 2003, but was caught in a near-deadly avalanche.

At the age of 50, after two failed attempts and the staggering loss of Hilaree Nelson, his partner in life and mountains, on Manaslu, Morrison skied down Hornbein’s Couloir on October 15. He pulled it off just four months after undergoing a partial knee replacement. Before Morrison’s ascent last fall—which included a 12-person team of Sherpas, Ecuadorian fixers, and filmmakers—no human had successfully ascended the line since 1991.

Honnold’s conversation with Morrison about his historic ski descent was part of the first-ever live recording of Fitz Cahall’s and Honnold’s Climbing Gold podcast. The interview took the stage at Outside Days on May 31 in Denver, CO. The podcast episode dropped today, alongside the release of the film. You can watch an excerpt above, and read on for Honnold’s and Morrison’s thoughts on grief, the question they dread most, and risking their lives for sport.

Morrison conceived of the goal to ski down Everest’s Hornbein Couloir with Hilaree Nelson. The two ski mountaineers met on Makalu (8,463m) in 2015 and fell in love.

“We were on a tear,” Morrison told Honnold and Cahall, “ticking off these dream runs all over the planet.”

The two had been trying to get to Everest to attempt their ski descent. But COVID delayed their plans, making it impossible to get to the Chinese side of the mountain. To stay in 8,000-meter-peak shape, in 2022, they headed to Manaslu (8,163m) where Morrison recalls they “had a pretty incredible day all by ourselves up on the mountain.” He started skiing down first; Nelson followed, but when Morrison stopped to wait for her, she never appeared. She had set off a small avalanche. “What ensued was a multi-day, horrific rescue of her and trying to find her,” he said. “And it changed my life.”

At first, Morrison wanted to hang it up—never ski or head into the mountains again. But eventually, he began to realize “this is part of me, this is in me.” And he returned to the goal they’d started together. “I wanted to do it for her, and her legacy, and us.”

On the summit, Morrison spread some of Nelson’s ashes. “It was a really emotional moment for me, looking off at mountains I had skied with her, Lhotse and Makalu,” he reflected. “I really felt like she was there.”

In 2011, before losing Nelson on Manaslu, Morrison’s wife, daughter, and son passed away in a plane crash. While he has experienced unfathomable loss, he continues to try to push past the grief to keep living. On stage, he shared a metaphor he uses to grapple with loss:

I’ve described grief as a big heavy wet blanket that gets put on you. It’s just really hard. You go through a process of losing a loved one or spouse or child and it’s a really heavy weight. I like to think over time you take that blanket and you dry it out and you begin to fold it up. And eventually, you put it in a backpack and you carry it with you.

After free soloing El Cap, Honnold said his life became “a crazy whirlwind.” A week and a half later, he was on an expedition in Alaska. Then the film came out, thus marking his “six month deployment to Hollywood” of screenings and award ceremonies.

The effect was that his memories of free soloing El Cap blurred with the scenes from the film as he watched himself on the big screen, again and again. What he’d set out to do for himself became a messy, public experience. As Chin releases his film, Morrison may undergo a similar experience of distorted memories and mayhem.

Honnold also recalled the dreaded question punted at him on his Hollywood deployment: What’s next?

Morrison received the same question after his Everest descent and gave an answer Honnold wished he’d come up with years ago: Isn’t this enough?

“I just achieved this 10-year life dream,” Honnold joked of receiving the “what’s next” question. “I don’t have another life dream lined up on the back burner.”

Morrison called achieving his Everest ski descent goal an “incredible journey” and noted that he appreciated the team that supported him throughout the process.

Cahall teed up his last question by warning that “some of this is triggering to some people.” Meaning, this talk of visualizing fatal falls, of risking it all for the goal. But, Cahall wondered: Are we mistaking complacency for safety?

Morrison said that he doesn’t really see it as complacency versus risk. It’s not an either/or situation. “This is what I’m drawn to and this is what my life’s goals have been centered around,” he said. “I’m not going out there to make a mistake and not come home.” He added that while his ski descent might seem like a “horrendously risky thing,” it was the culmination of extensive planning and preparation, just like Honnold’s El Cap free solo.

“It’s really hard to look at you climbing El Cap without a rope and rationalize it and understand it and be able to relate to it because it is so totally insane,” Morrison said. But at the same time, he said he held “deep respect” for all of the preparation and focus Honnold put into ticking the goal.

“Without taking some amount of personal risk, you just can’t lead a rich and fulfilled life,” Honnold added. “People watch the film Free Solo or a film like that and they’re like, ‘Well, that’s crazy!’ Yeah it’s unusual, not the sort of risk taking you normally see, but it’s still making smart choices in their life in order to lead the most fulfilled life that they can.”

#8254. An Oregon Deputy Rescued a Missing PCT Hiker After Following Bare Footprints in the Snow

A deputy saved a lost PCT hiker after discovering a set of footprints in the snow, with one foot bare. (Photo: Marion County Sheriff's Office)

An Oregon sheriff’s deputy rescued a missing and hypothermic hiker along the Pacific Crest Trail after following a set of bare footprints in the snow, the Marion County Sheriff’s Office said.

According to the department, the deputy was patrolling near Breitenbush Lake on the PCT (Mile 2039.4) on the afternoon of October 30 when he came across the footprints and realized that while one of them showed the outsole of a shoe, the other appeared to have been made by a bare foot. The officer, who was “concerned for the individual’s safety,” followed the tracks for almost five miles to Forest Service Road 4220, where he discovered a man in a sleeping bag.

“Thanks to the quick actions of our Forest Patrol Deputy, the man was located and immediately transported to Detroit, where medics were able to treat him for exposure to the elements,” the sheriff’s office wrote. The hiker, who had been lost for 4 days, is being treated for hypothermia and frostbite.

<span data-mce-type="bookmark" style="display: inline-block; width: 0px; overflow: hidden; line-height: 0;" class="mce_SELRES_start">﻿</span><span data-mce-type="bookmark" style="display: inline-block; width: 0px; overflow: hidden; line-height: 0;" class="mce_SELRES_start">﻿</span>

The Salem-based Statesman Journal identified the deputy who made the rescue as Derrick Ramseyer, a 19-year veteran of the department.

The sheriff’s office said that Ramseyer had “likely saved the man’s life, and called the incident “an important reminder to always be prepared when heading into the wilderness.” The office urged hikers to carry an inReach or other emergency communicator and keep a close eye on weather conditions, which can shift rapidly at higher elevations.

The northern stretches of the Pacific Crest Trail are experiencing freezing temperatures with the onset of late fall, especially at higher elevations. On October 30, the Boulder Creek weather station, which is located roughly 13 miles from Breitenbush Lake and 2,000 feet lower, recorded a low of 31 degrees Fahrenheit.

While it’s not entirely clear how the man came to be partially barefoot, hikers losing shoes in snow or deep mud is a surprisingly common occurrence during the shoulder season, and can leave them frostbitten and trapped outside in inclement weather. In April 2023, three separate groups of hikers had to be rescued on Colorado’s Quandary Peak in the span of a single week after losing their shoes in soft snowpack.

#8253. The Best Ski Boots for Wide Feet—From Resort to Backcountry

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

A lineup of alpine ski boots clicked into skis on snow. (Photo: Re Wikstrom)

Overview: Wide feet often need a high-volume ski boot, meaning a last of 102 millimeters or wider, though some wide-footed skiers do fine in medium-volume boots with lasts of 100- to 101 millimeters. We highlighted seven boots with lasts from 100 millimeters to 103.5 millimeters, including men’s and women’s options and one backcountry touring boot.

Wide feet are a problem for skiers. Take it from someone whose bootfitter once called hers “platypus feet.” My forefoot is wide, I have basically no arch, and my heel, ankle, and calf are skinny. That wide forefoot points me toward a wider last and “high volume” boots, but my flat foot swims in them, with way too much room between my instep and the boot ceiling and around my ankle and calf. So what do I do? I stuff my platypus feet into low-volume boots that keep them snug, then work with a bootfitter to stretch and grind out the toebox.

For skiers with more typical wide feet (a wide forefoot, a higher instep, and proportionally bigger ankles and calves), the fix is usually far simpler: try on a few boots with a last of 100 millimeters or more, either a generous mid-volume or a high-volume model, and see what fits.

Why do so many of these boots all have BOA dials, you ask? Because whether you like them or not, you can’t argue that BOA makes it easier to fine-tune the fit and wrap above the instep. Here are our testers’ favorite boots for skiers with wide feet, high insteps, and thicker calves, all available in multiple flexes for men and women. And remember: boot fit is highly specific to your foot shape. To find the best boot for you, visit your local ski shop and work with a professional bootfitter.

Sizes: 24.5-29.5 Last: 102 mm Flexes: 120, 100

Pros and Cons + Convenient entry and BOA lower closure + Performance on par with stiffer boots + 100-flex version offers big value – Fit out-of-box was more snug than expected

One tester called it the best 102-millimeter-lasted boot ever made, and the fit balance explains why: secure and pinch-free through the rearfoot, roomy up front without going bucket-wide. A new lower-shell BOA dial lets you fine-tune the wrap across your forefoot and instep, and entry is among the easiest around. The reworked R-Go Fit liner grips just enough to hold your heel, snug at first but relaxing after a couple of runs. The 120 flex skied like several 130s, so if you like a softer boot, look at the Rossignol Hi-Speed HV BOA 100.

Sizes: 23.5-30.5 Last: 102 mm Flexes: 85-130

Pros and Cons + Lots of room, everywhere + Very square toebox shape + Foot feels planted for good edge control – Potential for quickness requires high volume foot and leg

Plenty of wide boots drift toward medium width or ski like the box they came in. The Premio BOA doesn’t. It averaged a 5 (roomiest) across all eight fit zones testers scored, and its toebox is the most noticeably angled they’ve tested, letting toes spread out for comfort, warmth, and grip. Stance angles and shell construction keep the foot planted flat through every edge angle, even on lower-volume feet. The only knock was quickness, which a thicker, higher-volume foot should close by filling the boot out. Available in flex options ranging from 85 to 130.

Sizes: 22.5-30.5 Last: 100 mm Flexes: 130, 120; 115, 105 (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Extra room in toebox, forefoot, instep and calf + Performance snug in heel and ankles + Double BOA offers fine adjustment to an already good fit – Testers said DD might stand for difficult donning

A true medium, the 100-millimeter-last Speedmachine 3 still has room for higher-volume feet to pack in and feel secure, with the performance payoff of a snug fit. The shell follows the foot’s natural shape while the liner cushions the wider, bony spots. Once your foot settles in, it’s held firmly, with just enough breathing room left in the toebox, forefoot, instep, and calf. A strong rearfoot hold keeps narrower, pressure-sensitive feet happy too. Entry takes more effort in the tested 115-flex DD (dual dial) than in the 105-flex model with buckles up top and BOA below.

Sizes: 23.5-30.5 Last: 101 mm Flexes: 120, 110; 105 (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Flawless medium fit for average feet and legs + Particularly good shin and toebox fit + Skied as strongly and accurately as 130-flex models – A bit difficult to get on

The Veloce Space Dual’s 101-millimeter last runs a smidge wider than true medium boots but fits just as snug for average and wider feet alike. Its cabrio design keeps things friendly for higher insteps, and testers praised the snug shin fit and just-right toebox. Dual BOA entry can be a cable-tangled hassle, but testers called it worth the cover charge. On snow, it handled icy groomers to crud with ease, even outperforming stiffer boots. Available in two flex models for men, one for women.

Sizes: 24-31.5 Last: 101 mm Flexes: 130, 120, 110; 105, 95 (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Easy on, easy off + Extra room over top of foot and through instep + Skis predictably with good stability – Might be too high-volume for skiers with low insteps

A 101-millimeter last makes the Nexus 130 BOA a higher-volume boot that balances comfort with performance, and the shape works for wider feet and higher insteps alike. The ankle break sits high and slightly forward, which accommodates higher insteps, and heel hold is excellent on genuinely high-volume feet. Even a low-volume skier barely noticed slop once the heel was driven into the pocket. Mid-entry means you lift the spine lever and step in hands-free, yet it skied like a true 130 flex, with a lively, springy rebound.

Sizes: 22.5-31.5 Last: 102 mm Flexes: 130, 120, 100 (men’s); 105, 95 (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Accommodating fit + Comfortable + Skis more powerfully than expected – Might not be high-volume enough for some

Salomon’s wide-fit answer isn’t a soft, cavernous compromise: it skis like a performance boot. A 102-millimeter last gives wide-footed skiers plenty of space through the forefoot and instep, with ample cuff room for thicker calves. Once the BOA is dialed in, tension feels smooth and even from shin to toe, and even mid-volume testers felt locked in rather than sloppy. It’s plush inside yet quick, lively, and efficient edge to edge, scoring on par with narrower, more technical boots. Truly wide feet may need a bootfitter to tune the heat-moldable Custom Shell.

Sizes: 22.5-31.5 Last: 103.5 mm Flexes: 120 (men’s); 120 (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Flex is progressive, you never feel the “brick wall” + 60° range of motion has almost no friction + New Vibram sole extremely grippy on rocky terrain – Wide last will be too cavernous for some

A touring boot for wide-footed skiers who want one boot for big missions, the mid-weight Radical Pro walks well and skis hard. The forefoot and heel pocket run wide, and our tester kept the scaffo clamped a bit to snug them up, so narrow feet should beware. The instep sits low enough to hold the heel even on a skinny-footed skier, leaving toes cozy and the descent locked in. On multi-day tours and a three-day Eastern Sierra traverse, the progressive flex muted vibrations in wet, manky snow, and the walk mode pivoted freely.

Fit makes or breaks a ski boot, and wide feet make it harder to get right. Expert skiers vetted and tested every boot here, but the best one for you depends on your own feet. A professional bootfitter is still the fastest way to narrow the field. Until you get there, here’s what to know.

Boot width is listed as the last: the internal width at the forefoot, in millimeters, measured on a size 26/26.5 shell. The number also hints at overall volume—the height over your instep and the room around your lower leg in the cuff. Narrower boots generally have a lower instep and a snugger cuff, while wider boots have a higher instep and a roomier cuff. Boots sort into three groups:

Not always. Some skiers with wider feet are comfortable in a medium-volume boot. Everyone’s tolerance for a snug fit differs, so try several widths at a ski shop and go with what your feet tell you.

Feet and legs come in too many shapes for one tester to speak for everyone. A boot that feels custom-made on one skier can feel punishing on another. That’s why we partner with professional bootfitter Mark Elling, who leads the Masterfit/America’s Best Bootfitters annual ski boot test. Every brand, large or small, is invited to submit models. Over two weeks, 10 expert testers—evenly split between men and women—skied 50 boots, averaging three runs per boot across a range of conditions.

Mark Elling has worked full-time in the ski industry for more than 35 years as a writer, a level 3 PSIA-certified instructor, a snowcat skiing guide and a professional bootfitter. He runs a year-round specialty bootfitting lab in Bend, Oregon (BootRX.com), and is a former board-certified pedorthist. Elling coordinates Masterfit’s annual boot test, and he’s the author of The All-Mountain Skier: The Way to Expert Skiing.

#8247. 31,000 Miles, 28 Years: Karl Bushby’s Walk Around the World by the Numbers

Karl Bushby walks through a park in Peterborough, England, on October 22, 2026, during the final leg of his 28-year Goliath Expedition. (Photo: Leon Neal/Getty Images)

On November 1, 1998, Karl Bushby left Punta Arenas, Chile, and began walking north. Ahead of him, the 29-year-old British former paratrooper pushed a modified golf trolley filled with supplies and gear that he dubbed “The Beast.” His goal: to walk as far as a person could in unbroken footsteps on Earth, without using anything but his own hands and feet to make forward progress. His planned route for what he called the Goliath Expedition would take him from the southernmost tip of South America to his hometown of Hull, England, a journey he estimated would take him about 12 years.

Exactly 28 years and one day later, Bushby arrived back in Hull’s Queen Victoria Square to cheering crowds at shortly before noon on November 2, capping off a journey that was much longer—and far more complicated—than he could have imagined when he began. Along the way, he navigated shifting ice floes across the Bering Strait and swam the Caspian Sea to dodge geopolitical tensions and the English Channel after Eurotunnel refused to let him walk through the service tunnels connecting France and the UK. Not all the obstacles were physical, either: Bushby decamped to Mexico to regroup after his sponsorships dried up in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis and spent 10 years crossing Russia, stymied by visa requirements and an entry ban. (He finally received the permission he needed in 2014 after walking 3,600 miles across the United States to Russia’s embassy.)

All of that added up to something larger than a hike—a journey that ended up taking almost exactly half of the 57-year-old’s life. (It demanded a commensurate sacrifice, and not just from him. Bushby has a son, now 36, who he’s only seen a handful of times since leaving, and a 12-year-old granddaughter he had never met until finishing his trek; he also had and lost two long-term romantic relationships during the journey.)

For all that, the man behind the Goliath Expedition isn’t inclined to brag. When Backpacker writer Bill Donahue caught up with Bushby in Mexico in 2012, at what would turn out to be the halfway point of his walk, Bushby downplayed his own achievements.

“I’m an average guy,” Bushby said. “I’m less than average. I’m an underachiever. All I’m doing is putting one foot in front of the other.”

Here’s what Bushby’s big walk looked like by the numbers.

The approximate distance that Bushby walked from Punta Arenas, Chile, to Hull, England. That’s equivalent to 14 thru-hikes of the Appalachian Trail, 1.25 times the circumference of the globe, or roughly 13 percent of the average distance from the Earth to the Moon. That distance took him through 30 countries, according to the Associated Press.

The total distance Bushby had to swim during his trip. That included roughly 179 miles across the Caspian Sea in September and October 2024 and 21 miles across the English Channel in October 2026. Bushby did both of those swims in stages, resting on a support boat at night and returning to the coordinates where he had gotten out of the water in the morning.

The amount of time Bushby spent in jail after crossing borders without authorization. That includes 18 days in Panamanian custody after he crossed the roadless Darién Gap from Colombia and 58 days in Russian detention following his crossing of the Bering Strait from Alaska.

Bushby’s average pace across his entire trip. While far slower than other long-distance hikers—the small group of people to have hiked 10,000 miles in a year all had to knock off roughly 28 miles per day—the legal and financial hurdles Bushby faced, as well as his refusal to use transportation to bypass complicated terrain, meant that making miles was significantly more difficult for him.

The number of carts that Bushby used to carry his gear during the Goliath Expedition. The first, the Beast, survived three years before breaking down in Nicaragua. He used its replacement, the Beast 2, for the remaining 25 years. In an interview with The Guardian, Bushby called the cart “my Wilson,” referring to Tom Hanks’ famous volleyball and conversation partner from Castaway.

#8246. Is Yellowstone National Park (Back) in Its Wild West Era?

A crowd waits for Old Faithful geyser in Yellowstone (Photo: Grant Faint / Getty)

I was sitting on my tailgate, listening to the sounds of songbirds and car honks, when a scuffle broke out in a nearby picnic area. Shouts echoed from the woods as a crowd swarmed two dudes who were shoving and swinging at each other.

Welcome to a hot summer day in Yellowstone National Park. The tussling group seemed to be a motorcycle club, based on their headwear and matching T-shirts. Given their sweaty disposition, I’m not sure “staying hydrated” was listed in the bylaws.

“This place is nuts,” said my wife, returning from the restroom as the two dudes were separated. “What happened here?”

“Fist fight at the Old Faithful corral.” I shrugged.

Then we embarked on a long trek through the semi-apocalyptic parking lot. Frantic drivers whipped around corners, cutting each other off. Exasperated families double-parked and hurried away. Frustrated sightseers returned to their blocked vehicles and laid on the horn. Finally, my wife and I breathed a sigh of relief as we reached the safer confines of the world’s most active hydrothermal zone, the scalding Upper Geyser Basin.

Yellowstone seems to be having a moment as the poster child for rising threats facing the National Park Service (NPS), including bad visitor behavior. While the parks attract record-setting crowds, the Trump administration simultaneously gutted the workforce, cutting NPS staff by nearly 25 percent since 2025. Interpretive signs about important topics like Indigenous displacement and slavery were torn down and replaced by nationalistic propaganda. More trash than ever was recently pulled from Yellowstone geysers, including strange stuff like fidget spinners, fake nails, and a baseball cap displaying the words cowboy hat.

For outdoor enthusiasts watching these disturbing events, it can feel like there’s never been a worse time for national parks such as Yellowstone. My wife, who’d never been there before, was shocked by the wackier things we saw during one high-season day. I arrived better prepared, having come to Yellowstone a grand total of TWO times. My first visit happened 20 years before, when some young whitewater paddlers and I came through on a cross-country road trip. The park felt somewhat calmer back then, but by no means sane. There were about 3 million visitors that year, instead of about 4.5 million now.

Back then, occasional thrill seekers with camcorders chased wildlife, while today’s park paparazzi are influencers with smartphones. Then, like now, I saw a few tourists hopping off boardwalks and stepping across dangerous thermal crusts. I don’t think I’ve ever witnessed anyone stick their fingers in toxic waters, but I’ve definitely seen videos on Tourons of Yellowstone. Each time I’ve gone, we talked about the poor souls who fell and the impulsive daredevils who flung themselves into acidic hot springs, where they were fatally burned or entirely dissolved.

After my first visit, I mostly gave Yellowstone a wide berth. Later, I returned to the mountains and canyons of Wyoming, exploring real places and stories from the Wild West era for a book, Discovering the Outlaw Trail. That’s how I learned that Yellowstone National Park never saw any “good old days,” though some periods have been better or worse for various reasons.

In 1872, when President Ulysses S. Grant signed the first national park into law, word had already spread in the East. Yellowstone was a landscape like no other, filled with abundant wildlife, erupting geysers, and plunging waterfalls. For ages, it was home to nomadic and resident Native peoples like the Mountain Shoshone. Now this volcanic plateau in the Rocky Mountains was threatened by westward expansion of the United States.

For a decade, no more than roughly a thousand visitors made the long and jolting stagecoach journey. Yet the bad behavior started immediately. Seeking souvenirs, vandals hammered away at mineral deposits. Poachers slaughtered countless bison, elk, and bears for their hides, leaving fields of carcasses. Squatters built illegal cabins within the boundaries, hoping the park law would be repealed. Tourists tossed trash, timber, and soap into geysers like Old Faithful. When the erupting fountains sent foaming debris sky high, onlookers cheered. The handful of park staffers watched on, horrified.

After the railroad arrived in 1883, things only got worse. With growing crowds came petty pickpockets, horse thieves, and gunslinging outlaws. Bandits hid behind bends in the road and robbed the passing tourist wagons one by one. The largest stagecoach robberies in U.S. history were said to have happened in Yellowstone. Not once, but three times.

The reason for the mayhem? During the lean federal budgets following the Civil War, Congress had been willing to establish the park, but they weren’t willing to fund it. With limited rules and near-zero enforcement, Yellowstone developed a reputation as a fun place to get away with things.

During our summer day in Yellowstone, my wife and I managed to break away from the crowds. To start, we took a six-mile hike through quieter parts of Upper Geyser Basin, which reminded us why this is a special place worth protecting.

We watched the angled eruption of Daisy Geyser with maybe a dozen fellow visitors. Then we walked past Punch Bowl Spring to a unique feature that few visit, Black Sand Pool. Under our feet, the ground tremored with loud thumps, the result of steam implosions happening beneath the pool’s surface.

During our hike, we met a friendly Oregon family that ranks Yellowstone among their favorite parks. To avoid the craziness, they devised a unique itinerary, staying a few nights each at several park lodges and hiking outward during the quieter mornings. In most ways, this family resembles the majority of parkgoers. Hikers who love the parks, follow the rules, and appreciate the rangers. While poor behavior may be increasing again, such offenders remain a highly visible minority of visitors.

That said, without a few key decisions made during the fading days of the Wild West, Yellowstone might have gone bad altogether.

Tucked away in the woods bordering Norris Geyser Basin, there’s a log building overlooking a small river. Today, this old Army post ironically holds the Museum of the National Park Ranger. Inside, a bronze bust depicts Harry Yount, a legendary figure from Yellowstone history. If the frontiersman’s face looks particularly tired, well, there’s a reason for that.

In 1880, as this nascent national park was being overrun by poachers and miscreants, the meager budget was enough to hire exactly one game warden. He was expected to single-handedly patrol over 3,300 square miles of parkland. Instead, Yount quit in protest after 14 months, reporting that one guy couldn’t do a job that required a well-funded ranger service.

And guess what, the government listened! It just took 35 years. In the meantime, they tried pretty much anything else. They invited some vigilante cowboys, offering them half the collected fines. Naturally, these volunteers avoided the gunslingers and targeted wealthier tourists. So, the U.S. Army was sent in. For decades, half-hearted soldiers chased outlaws beyond park boundaries. The soldiers went back to their posts and waited until the villains cartoonishly returned.

In 1916, the National Park Service was established. Finally, professional rangers assumed responsibility for management, interpretation, and enforcement within an improving park system. Disorder gradually decreased across the West and in Yellowstone, but not entirely. The national parks went on to become a beloved feature of the U.S.

The story of Yellowstone’s destructive early days, and its first park ranger, offers a cautionary lesson that’s easily forgotten: when crowds increase and park budgets and staffing decrease, lawbreakers rise again. We’re seemingly back where we started, with Yellowstone in its Wild West era again.
