#8205. 45 Years Ago, One Kids Book Series Taught A Generation How To Make Bad Decisions

Imagine if you could tell Bilbo Baggins to leave the ring behind for Gollum, have Leslie not swing on the rope to Terabithia on that rainy day, or remind Jonas to pack warmer clothes at the end of The Giver. Most fiction is concrete, with the authors dictating what happens next. But that changed when two writers figured out a way for the reader to control a character because the reader was that character. We’re talking about Choose Your Own Adventure, of course. The first published installment arrived in 1979, with The Cave of Time — though as we’ll see that wasn’t really the first book. For decades, Choose Your Own Adventure was an atypical experiment in literary determinism that resulted in one of the most-read book franchises ever created.

For a generation, these interactive novels transported readers through space and time to form their own stories, putting them in the cockpit of planes, the gi of a judo master, or even the fins of a shark. By the end of the 90s, CYOA closed the chapter on its story, but nearly twenty-five years later, the company is back in action. Here’s how it all began, ended, and began again.

A few variations of the cover to “Sugarcane Island,” the first ever CYOA book

Interactive books weren’t a completely new idea before Choose Your Own Adventure (CYOA), but its predecessors weren’t mainstream popular. There was a romance novel from the 1930s, where the reader decides which suitor the protagonist marries, with dozens of possible endings. Several high-concept stories arrived by the 50s and 60s, like Raymond Queneau’s surreal Story As You Like It or Robert Coover’s explicit and unsettling The Babysitter. Celebrated for their uniqueness, none of these caught on beyond their novelty and were purely adult fare. It wasn’t until a lawyer teamed up with a young writer to find a way to bring this idea to bookshelves across the country.

Edward Packard came from a family deep in the legal business, but practicing law was never something he truly cared about. While his passion was writing, Ed’s children's books were never picked up by publishers. His fate changed one evening in 1969 while making up a bedtime story for his two daughters about a character named Pete. Struck by writer's block, Packard couldn’t figure out how to progress the tale and asked his kids what should happen next. When both girls answered differently, he realized Pete was never the protagonist – it was his kids living those adventures firsthand in their imaginations. Immediately, Packard knew he was onto something.

Ray Montgomery had just started Vermont Crossroads Press in 1970, after cutting his teeth writing roleplaying scenarios for Clark Abt, a pioneer in educational games. The Yale and NYU grad had aspirations larger than his employer and ventured out to make a name for himself in publishing. When Packard walked into his office with a draft of Sugarcane Island in 1976, Montgomery saw great potential that perfectly aligned with his interests. “I Xeroxed 50 copies of Ed’s manuscript and took it to a reading teacher in Stowe,” Montgomery said in an interview from 1981. “His kids — third grade through junior high — couldn’t get enough of it.”

Sugarcane Island became the best-selling book of the upstart publisher, moving over five thousand copies, but they were still an unknown entity in a crowded landscape.

It was this point where things started to get messy for Packard and Montgomery. Both writers saw a potential for larger success beyond the small Vermont publishing house, and the two pursued greener pastures, independent from each other's ventures. Packard published two CYOA-style books in 1978 under the Harper imprint, Lippincott. Meanwhile, Montgomery’s agent managed to obtain a six-book deal from Bantam in 1979, and the two writers came together to officially launch the CYOA experience as we know it today.

Similar to the origin story of Sugarcane Island, Packard turned to his kids for story ideas. His daughter, Andrea, told him about her summer escapade, spelunking, and her desire to wander solo to explore more. She imagined a tunnel that could transport her to another time or place, and her dad loved it! Andrea scribbled more notes and ultimately ideated the first published CYOA book, “The Cave of Time.”

Interior from “The Cave of Time” with two of the multiple endings available to readers

While hiking through Snake Canyon, you come upon a cave you’ve never noticed before. You step inside and can potentially travel to medieval times, a prehistoric era, the Ming Dynasty, and other periods. Along the way, you can find your fortune through a foolish king, dine with cavemen, battle the Loch Ness Monster, try to escape the sinking Titanic, or any number of unpredictable possibilities. Some endings are bittersweet, others hopeful, and some are just plain grim.

A fortuitous mistake resulted in Bantam overprinting this inaugural entry, and the publisher remedied its overstock by donating 100,000 books to schools and libraries throughout America. This charitable act guaranteed their target audience would have no problem discovering the book, transforming CYOA into a household name practically overnight.

50 books later, readers returned to the cave for another adventure, making it one of the few retro CYOA titles to have a sequel. For her efforts, Andrea received a credit in the book and a percentage of royalties that still come to her mailbox decades later.

The opening page of every CYOA book warns readers they are responsible for their own fate. There’s no backtracking allowed (in theory), creating a flexible narrative where the outcome changes each time a page is turned. More often than not, the wrong turn leads to fatal consequences. But, really, who hasn’t flipped backward to reconsider a choice?

Few books offer the chance to be the master of a protagonist’s destiny, have wild adventures in a pocket-sized format, and combine those parts with the element of risk and uncertainty from a single decision. Some books have as many as 40 endings, and that finality could happen as early as the first ten pages. While most readers sought the happily ever after conclusion, others found pleasure in seeing how many ways they could fail in the grizzliest way possible.

Nope, this is definitely not going to end well. Don Hedin illustration from “The Forbidden Castle.”

“My philosophy was that it should be like life,” Packard once said, with the intent of including moral realism in the reader's experience. Smart choices were typically better than impulsive, haphazard decisions, but morally virtuous ones weren’t guaranteed to be the wisest, and you often paid for heroics with self-sacrifice. Cheating was discouraged, but technically, if you didn’t take your finger off the page, it wasn’t a final decision.

There was one time when being mischievous paid off, and that famous case was the twelfth book, Inside UFO 54-40. This is the only book in the series that explicitly rewards cheating. In order to find the secret alien planet, the reader must forego the typical CYOA patterns and stop playing along. Only by reading the book straight through would they stumble on a page unmarked by any choices to discover this paradise. “You did not make a choice, or follow any directions, but now, somehow, you are descending from space—approaching a great, glistening sphere.” The lesson was ambiguous, but a valuable one - sometimes, disobeying the rules is its own reward.

Stacks of CYOA books are common in any library or bookstore no matter where you live

CYOA books dominated stores around the world during the ’80s and ’90s, with hundreds of millions of books sold in 38 languages. But as the new millennium approached, Montgomery and Packard found themselves at a crossroads with no page to turn.

Video games were taking over, as screen time replaced reading. Sales dwindled until the company flew the white flag in 1998, ending with book #184, Mayday, which Packard co-wrote with the person responsible for the very first title in the franchise, his daughter Andrea.

In 2003, Montgomery and his wife Shannon Gilligan (who met while working on an Atari game based on the CYOA books) bought the rights to the franchise and revived it through Chooseco. Montgomery passed away in 2014, writing Gus vs. the Robot King, but Gilligan has kept the brand thriving as CEO while bringing it to new places.

Cover to Murder at the Old Willow Boarding School

Today, CYOA sells an average of a million books annually, evolving to reach a more inclusive readership and touching on issues that affect modern society. Their bestseller remains a four-pack filled with Classics, but Chooseco transitioned into graphic novels like Eighth Grade Witch and offers longer CYOA books with titles like Time Travel Inn and Murder at the Old Willow Boarding School, which introduced their first nonbinary character. Readers ages 5 to 8 can dip their toes into the Dragonlark series, and even younger ones can start their adventure with the adorable board book The Abominable Snowman, with lethal endings absent from these kid-friendly editions. There are also board games, a math book, an upcoming Tarot card set, and a proposed book series for nostalgic adults with more mature themes — but nothing too explicit.

Packard wrote a trio of books in the CYOA style under the name U-Ventures in 2010 and continues to write fiction while maintaining his blog.

Montgomery always hoped the CYOA series would be a stealth reading program to excite kids into becoming voracious bookworms. Years later, his dream continues to be a reality and may soon rekindle that same love within adults who grew up on these books.

There are surprising plans beyond the traditional format that Gilligan couldn’t divulge in 2023, but even as technology evolves, nothing beats the experience of reading a physical book and not knowing what awaits the reader when they turn it over.

At Toy Fair 2023, Shannon Gilligan said: “Touching a page and moving it makes the brain think you’ve been somewhere on some super subtle level.” And even though she said Choose Your Own Adventure is at the “dawn of a relaunch,” the truth is, we’ve all been on this adventure for years.

This article was originally published on Jan. 5, 2024

#8204. Parents Of An Only Child Deserve To Feel Stressed Too

Parental. Stress. Is. Valid. For. Everyone.

“Do you have any more kids or just the one?” It’s a question I’ve been asked countless times by fellow parents at various birthday parties or school pickups while we stand around watching our kiddos play. And my answer is always the same: “No, it’s just my son. He’s an only child.” The question has always seemed innocent enough and without any detectable judgment. But there’s just something about that phrase “just the one” that’s always rubbed me the wrong way. As if one, by itself, isn’t enough or less than what it should be.

As an only child myself, I never thought of it as anything to be ashamed of. But now that I’m a mom, I'm much more aware of the stigma surrounding the “one-and-done” mentality. No one is ever directly rude or insensitive, but subtle remarks like “just the one” or assurances that “there’s still time” to have another suggest my life — and my child’s life — are lacking in some way. It’s as if to say our family isn’t whole just the way we are.

It can feel a little isolating at times. In fact, there have been moments when I’ve hesitated to open up to other moms about my own parenting struggles or concerns because I only have one kid, whereas many of them have multiple. I’ve found myself wondering, How can my problems compare when I’m dealing with one kiddo and they’re juggling two or three or even four? It can make me feel like I don’t have a right to complain or vent about my child’s latest tantrum because they are dealing with those things on a larger scale than I am.

It’s worth noting that no parent has ever said any of this to me directly. But it’s an underlying worry that always creeps into the back of my mind. In many ways, society (and social media, a viral extension of society) has conditioned me to think that way. If you don’t have any kids, you’re made to think your life is incomplete. If you have one kid, you’re encouraged to give them a sibling or they’ll be lonely. It feels like it’s never enough. But I’m done allowing myself to feel that way. It ends now.

These days, I keep reminding myself that I have just as much of a right to vent as parents of multiple kids. It's not a competition, and parental stress is valid regardless of how many kids you have. Full stop.

That’s not to say that I don’t appreciate the added struggles and responsibilities that come with having more than one child. Taking family trips, juggling sports schedules and school drop-offs, not to mention dealing with a revolving door of colds and other ailments, are challenging enough with one kid, let alone multiples. But you never know what someone might be going through that could make caring for one kid much harder than it looks.

One glaring example that comes to mind is the whole concept of having a “village” to lean on in times of need. Many parents with multiple kids might have grandparents or extended family nearby who can help at a moment’s notice, while some parents with one child might not have any loved ones nearby. Support (or lack thereof) can make a huge difference when it comes to caring for little ones. And, of course, you have no idea what each parent is going through emotionally, physically, or even financially, which can all contribute to a rise in stress levels, regardless of how many children you have.

But honestly, even if you do have a ton of family close by who are ready and willing to help, that shouldn’t automatically mean you need to have more kids. Parents of only children shouldn’t need to explain themselves to anyone or be made to feel like they are doing something wrong. Every family, both big and small, deserves to take up space in the world.

Being a parent can be the most rewarding thing in the world. But it’s also a full-time job with zero breaks and very little appreciation given in return. Every mom and dad is a superhero in their own way and deserves the right to complain or feel all the feelings. I don’t want to take any credit away from parents with multiple children. I simply want to feel like my own struggles and grievances deserve a seat at the table too.

Kelly Schremph is an entertainment and lifestyle writer with bylines at Us Weekly, Refinery29, Bustle, Romper, Scary Mommy, and more. She lives in California with her husband, their son, Chris, and their yellow lab, Luna, who still acts very much like a puppy. When Kelly isn’t watching TV (or writing about it), she’s usually chasing after one of them.

#8203. Here Are The Rules To 19 'Bluey' Games Straight From The Show

From “Keepy Uppy” to “Work,” and everything in between, here’s how to actually play Bluey games from the show with the whole family in real life.

Raising kids is a daily learning experience, but Chili and Bandit make it look so easy in Bluey. Sure, they have their tough times, like Bandit’s failed attempts at making a duck-shaped cake for Bingo’s birthday, or the Sticky Gecko incident with Chili (which she prefers we don’t talk about), but they overcome and make us want to excel at parenting as much as they seem to be. Much of that parenting and resolution comes from play — Bluey games that show good parenting and good fun can go hand in hand. Who knew animated anthropomorphic dogs would be our parenting inspiration, but here we are. But how do you play the games from Bluey in real life? What are the rules of the Bluey games?

We can’t all reach the same level of playtime excellence that Bluey’s Mom and Dad constantly achieve. But you can recreate wonderful games. We’ve rewatched every episode of the show with attention to the games, and then we tried them at home with our kids. Did they all work as perfectly as they did on screen? Not exactly. But in general, did we have a good time? Are Pomeranians a hardy breed? Exactly. Here’s a list of 19 specific Bluey games that come straight from the show into your living room — a guaranteed good time for the whole family.

From Bluey Season 1, Episode 5, this game is best played in a wide-open field on a bright day with fluffy clouds looming in the sky. So, this one isn’t an everyday affair. Your kids hide under the shadows cast overhead, then run, jump, and scream into the next nearest shadow. Touching any part of the ground the sun hits means you’re out. It’s also a good way to stretch your budget on sunscreen.

This game comes from Season 1, Episode 25, “Taxi.” Destination unknown, as your living room becomes a taxi, and your kid — the driver. Set up some chairs and a makeshift dashboard, and into traffic, you go! Watch out for pedestrians, other drivers, or whatever other hazards will get in the way of making your arrival on time. There are plenty of variations you can do with this game, changing the vehicle from a cab to a plane, train, starship, sandworm, or whatever imaginary vessel you want.

Watch “Taxi,” Bluey Season 1, Episode 25 on Disney+ here.

The game of “Raiders,” comes from Episode 16 in Season 1, which is called “Yoga Ball.” If you’ve got a Yoga ball in your home, you’re ready to play Raiders! The goal is to grab a lost treasure hidden behind obstacles you set up. Once they snatch it – you come after them and roll the ball down the hall to recreate that iconic movie scene. Really, though, if you’ve ever seen any Indiana Jones films, you can make up other gambits to chase your kids with. Even after the game ends, you can still teach them about monkey brains at dinner.

Watch Bluey Season 1, Episode 16, “Yoga Ball,” right here.

I’d say who doesn’t love The Grannies on Bluey, but if your kids become half as exasperating as Janet and Rita, you will definitely have your hands full. This one comes from Bluey Season 1, Episode 28. The “rules” are simple: Your children dress up and act like octogenarians, turning mundane tasks into elderly-inspired chaos. If you’re daring, combine Grannies into any of the other games on this list, and watch the madness unfold.

Watch Bluey, Season 1, Episode 28, “Grannies,” right here.

This game comes from Bluey Season 3, Episode 14, which is called “Perfect.” It’s a solid diversion if you’re at a gathering with other adults, but your children still want to play. Gently lob your kid in another direction and let them spin and twirl to their heart’s content. Then, like the game’s namesake, they return back to you, ready to be thrown again. Minimum effort on your part, but maximum fun for the little ones since they’re really the ones in control of how wild the boomerang is!

Watch Bluey, Season 3, Episode 14, “Perfect,” right here.

From Bluey Season 2, Episode 3, it’s all about “Dance Mode.” Did your kids know there’s a switch on your back? If they find and flip it, you turn into a dancing machine – no matter where you are! If you’re coy, you can convince your children they also have a button that turns on their best jitterbug. This game is not for those who embarrass easily, but if you’re ready to show your kids how committed you are to playtime, Dance Mode turns everywhere you go into a boogie-down good time.

Watch Bluey Season 2, Episode 3, “Dance Mode,” right here.

We all might think we know the game of charades, but Bluey Season 2, Episode 5, “Charades,” takes it up a notch. This is the only game on the list that requires investing a bit more into your game, but it’s worth it. Use a pack of Charades cards that don’t require reading and have pictures on them, then act out the image until someone guesses it correctly. It’s a lot of fun seeing how children interpret the world around them, you’ll be surprised how enjoyable this game can be with little ones. Nana Heeler plays this with the kids, so this is a good way to get grandparents or older relatives involved in playtime that won’t involve sprinting around the house.

Watch Bluey, Season 2, Episode 5, “Charades,” right here.

From Bluey Season 2, Episode 14, “Fancy Restaurant,” we get a classic make-believe game with a new hilarious twist. Why go out for a dinner date with your significant other, when you can stay home and be served by your kids? They can be the maître d’, the waiter, the chef - or if they are feeling villainous, the lazy exterminator – and give you a night out you’ll never forget. I’d suggest setting some ground rules about what you’ll eat before you start playing. Otherwise, you’ll feel exactly like Bandit did at the end of that episode. Poor guy…

Watch Bluey Season 2, Episode 14, “Fancy Restaurant,” right here.

From Bluey, Season 2, Episode 3, “Bad Mood,” is sort of what it sounds like. Intended as an exercise in emotional regulation, the concept of the game makes it exceptionally fun for any situation. Bandit plays this with Bingo when she’s in a bad mood, climbing onto his feet and controlling her limbs as they smash into things, much to Bingo’s excitement. Even without a bad mood, your kids will love piloting a parent mech. Viking hats sold separately.

Watch Bluey, Season 2, Episode 3, “Bad Mood,” right there.

In Bluey Season 1, Episode 31, everyone gets down to business in “Work.” If you’re a remote worker, you already know the struggles of trying to stay afloat at the job while having kids scamper underfoot. The kids can interview you for a profession of their choice, and turn you into their employee to boss around. If you play your cards right, you might be able to distract them with the paperwork of their own to let you sneak in some actual work time. Try not to get fired - ideally from BOTH of your jobs!

Watch Bluey Season 1, Episode 31, “Work,” right here.

In Bluey Season 1, Episode 36, everyone gets the travel bug with “Backpackers.” But, the trick here is nobody is actually going anywhere! Save money on a vacation to hike around the Alps or the Appalachian Trail, and instead backpack through Europe in your own home. Your children call the shots here, as they create the exotic locations and give you commands about what to do and say while on your excursion. Remember – as much as you wish you were, you are not a cartoon dog. Unless you’ve been doing your deadlifts, don’t wear the kids on your back if you want to be able to bend over when you’re older. What they can do instead is fill an actual backpack with household objects you’ll use on your trip instead of the items you’d actually need. Who needs a passport when you can hand Customs a toilet brush instead?

Watch Bluey Season 1, Episode 36, “Backpackers,” right here.

This one comes from Bluey Season 2, Episode 10, “Rug Island.” Find the biggest rug or carpeted space in your home, drag some potted plants or couch cushions onto it, and transform your living room into a deserted island in the middle of the sea. Bluey and Bingo used felt markers to make all the objects in their little haven by the shore, but anything goes on the rug so take whatever you like and pretend it’s the essentials you need to survive. Imagination rules above all else, so immerse yourself in the mind of a child and drift away to simpler times when an island could just be a rug.

Watch Bluey Season 2, Episode 10, “Rug Island,” right here.

This comes from Bluey Season 2, Episode 2, “Feather Wand.” When Bingo discovered a feather on the ground, she quickly realized it was a magic wand. Whenever she pointed it at something or someone, she exclaimed “Heavy!”, and made it weigh a ton! You haven’t lived until you’ve cleaned your teeth with a floor toothbrush. Much of the fun happens when the objects are disenchanted, and suddenly become their original weight as they abruptly fly at your face once the struggle is over.

A variation on this would be from the episode “Magic Asparagus”, where your child transforms you into different animals by zapping you with an enchanted vegetable. Bluey used asparagus, but a sturdy carrot or parsnip would do the trick, too. Nothing leafy, unless you like cleaning up sprigs of supernatural broccoli from your dining room floor.

Watch Bluey Season 2, Episode 2, “Feather Wand,” right here. Also, watch Bluey Season 1, Episode 49, “Asparagus,” right here.

This game comes from Bluey Season 2, Episode 25, “Double Babysitter.” A brilliant game to wear out your young ones, this game works best at night time when it's darker. Your child is the cat, trying to catch the “mouse” AKA the beam from your flashlight or laser pointer. Bluey and Bingo were elated to play this with their babysitter, and it will quickly become a favorite with your little kittens, too.

Watch Bluey Season 2, Episode 25, “Double Babysitter,” right here.

Not every game on this list requires the parents to break a sweat. I’m throwing you a bone here. This one comes from Bluey Season 2, Episode 8, “Daddy Dropoff.” And, it’s a game you can easily play on your back in bed, while your kids have a romp with your frisky feet. Whatever is below your knees becomes the animal of your choosing, and your kids can play and take care of them. When you get tired of playing, just remind them of how stinky your feet are, and that should be enough to send them running.

Watch Bluey Season 2, Episode 8, “Daddy Dropoff,” right here.

As the day comes to a close and you are all winding down, Favorite Thing is a fantastic way to interact with your kids at mealtime that doesn’t wind them back up. This comes from Bluey Season 2, Episode 7, “Favorite Thing.” The rules are simple: Everyone takes turns sharing what their favorite thing was that happened to them today, and you discuss it and turn their singular experience into a moment everyone enjoys. This a sneaky way to get your kids better at their conversational skills and having etiquette at the dining table, while also creating fun family memories that will last a long time after the plates are cleaned up.

Watch Bluey Season 2, Episode 7, “Favorite Thing,” right here.

This game comes from a classic Bluey episode: Season 1, Episode 8, “Fruit Bat.” It’s typical to read a book to your kids at bedtime to help them sleep, but it’s a bit unusual for you to fall asleep while reading their book. Try as you might, you just can’t stay awake, especially when you get to the exciting parts. Your kids can try to wake you up, but you’re having such a hard time keeping your eyes open! Whether you finish the book, or flop onto their pillow for a nap of your own, is up to you.

Watch Bluey, Season 1, Episode 8, “Fruit Bat,” right here.

This comes from Bluey Season 2, Episode 46, “Octopus.” Chloe the Dalmation learned this game from Bluey, who explained Dad is the octopus behind their couch, and the two kids are fish trying to steal his treasure. The octopus tries to stop them with his tentacles, swinging them at the fish and trapping them in his suction cups. Simple enough, and easy to play.

The dilemma is, when Chloe brings the game back to her home to play with her dad, it isn’t the same experience. Every time one suggests something, the other felt like their ideas were being rejected. Instead of turning the other person down, they decide to say yes to everything and remake the game to fit the way they play.

The lesson Chloe and her dad learned is when it comes to games, there are no rules. Playtime with your kids is like improv comedy. It’s best when it’s “Yes, and –“because saying no grinds the scene to a halt. There are still boundaries that must be respected, but let your imagination go as far as they can reach to make playtime a truly enjoyable experience for everyone involved.

Watch Bluey Season 2, Episode 46, “Octopus,” right here.

The game that started it all! From Bluey Season 1, Episode 3, this game is essential. Blow up a balloon, toss it to your tiny ones, and let the havoc begin. As long as the balloon never touches the ground or pops, the game continues! If it does land, throw it back in the air and start again.

This article was originally published on Jan. 13, 2023

#8201. Bethany Joy Lenz: "The Easiest Thing To Do Is Believe The Person Asking The Least Of You"

The One Tree Hill alum sat down with Scary Mommy to talk about her first novel, The Betrayal of Cora Wexford, and why the Victorian era isn’t as far off as we’d like to think.

Bethany Joy Lenz didn’t just write The Betrayal of Cora Wexford. That art on the cover? She painted it, which feels especially fitting for a novel about a woman who is an artist in that very medium. Lenz is a longtime hobby painter (she does it for the joy of “slapping around on a canvas”), not a portraitist of the dead like her heroine, but she says the process gave her a window into Cora’s head: getting lost in meticulous work, where every stroke matters.

That attention to detail runs through the whole book, Lenz’s first novel after her bestselling memoir Dinner for Vampires. Set in 1888 London as Jack the Ripper terrorizes Whitechapel, it follows Cora, 38, single, childless, and running from her past, as she’s commissioned to paint the forgotten women whose deaths the city keeps shrugging off. All the while, her own relationship with a charming stranger named Miles starts to hint that darkness could be closer to her door than she even imagined. The Ripper may dominate the headlines, but Lenz is just as interested in the unspoken violence happening in living rooms everywhere, and in the people who look the other way.

When Scary Mommy caught up with the One Tree Hill alum, she opened up about everything from gaslighting and the psychology of looking away to why 45 feels like the most settled she’s ever been.

Scary Mommy: Which came first, Cora or the Ripper? How did you land on telling the stories of these "invisible" women against the backdrop of Ripper lore?

Bethany Joy Lenz: Cora was first, absolutely. The only reason I set it in Victorian times is because every time I thought about the story, that's the only way it would manifest itself in my brain. Probably because one of my favorite suspense films is Gaslight with Ingrid Bergman and Charles Boyer. So I wanted to set something in that world that maybe is like a companion to Gaslight. It's not the same story, it's not derivative, but it lives in that world and there are a lot of similar notes and themes. Once I realized that's where I wanted to set it, I actually picked 1888 because I wanted it to be around the World's Fair and the construction of the Eiffel Tower. Then I realized there's no way I could set a story in London in 1888 that's a suspense and not talk about Jack the Ripper.

I had to recalibrate and then realized, actually, I think this is perfect — I can parallel the heightened, feverish fear that everyone was experiencing around being a potential victim of physical violence while psychological violence was happening in living rooms everywhere, all over London. I mean all over the world, really, but for the purposes of this story, I just wanted to look at why is that so? Why is everyone wrapped up in the fear and fascination with just the physical violence when we're made up of so much more as human beings, and why doesn't the psychological violence and emotional violence get the attention that it deserves?

SM: Cora toes the line between authenticity and survival, which is what most women did then. How much of that tension felt distinctly Victorian to you, and how much kind of bleeds over into 2026?

BJL: You know what's funny is I thought that I was going to be discovering so many things that shocked me that were so different. They're not. I really thought, like, OK, so maybe we're not institutionalized now because we are experiencing fluctuations of menopause. Maybe we're not shut up behind closed doors because we might be eccentric or forced to be looked down on by society if we choose not to have children or be unmarried... I just don't think much has changed, unfortunately. So the more that I wrote, the more I researched, the more I was like, Oh, we're still here.

I think that's why I was also drawn to putting this in a time period that wasn't modern, so that it didn't feel threatening for readers to feel like it's too close to home. I think as they read, they're going to realize that it is close to home. I'm hoping that people will discover that as they're going — that things maybe have not changed as much as we would like to think that they have. But the thing is, it's timeless. These issues have existed for as long as we can imagine, and that's important to realize and remember.

SM: You've described what happens to Cora as a kind of murder in itself. And while this is a big genre leap from your memoir, Dinner for Vampires, those same traces of manipulation surface. Was fiction freeing in a way? How did it feel different for you?

BJL: It felt different writing fiction in the sense that context could be adjusted. I could take things and put them anywhere and any time and really craft the most succinct version of an amalgam of experiences that I've had, that women I know have had, and be able to tie it all together because the truth is these narcissistic personalities are so unoriginal ... It's funny because they believe that they're the most original, wonderful person that's ever existed. And they're so special that they're the most basic and beige and uninteresting people that have ever existed because they don't exist. They don't have a person within themselves to exist as.

SM: One thing that frustrated me most while reading, because I understood where Cora was coming from, was how much truth was sitting right in front of everyone and they just refused to see it. That feeling of am I crazy? really got to me. I feel like that a lot these days. Why was it important that the danger wasn't just Miles, but a whole community looking away?

BJL: Thank you for mentioning that. I think you're right; it is very prevalent today. And what I've learned from being around this personality type for so many years of my life and seeing how the community tends to respond to the victim and the perpetrator, I think human nature just never changes, and we're always looking for the low-hanging fruit and the easy way out. The easiest thing to do is believe the person who is asking the least of you, which is always going to be the abuser or the narcissist in this scenario.

It's hard to ask people to consider that they were wrong and that they got something so wrong — that they could believe that there's this person in their community who is wearing a mask and presenting something completely false to everyone and legitimately fooling everyone, and to think that I got fooled.

It sends people into a whole well of introspection. That's the requirement in order to decide to believe a victim. You have to believe that you also have been hoodwinked, essentially, and understand that. That's really hard on the ego. And I don't mean to say it from a place of feeling judgmental because I've been in that situation too. I've been asked to believe something that I didn't see evidence for when I was much younger. I was just like, "Look, he's never been mean to me. I don't know. I don't want to get in the middle of it." And I regret it, but I had my own life. I was busy. I didn't know. So I'm hoping that this will help make people aware and help people feel safe to go ahead and explore those parts of themselves because it's OK to grow.

SM: Absolutely. We’ll switch to something a little lighter now: If we’re dream casting, who plays everyone if this becomes a series? You were my Cora, btw.

BJL: Oh my gosh. Yes, I would love to play Cora in some sort of live version of it, whether it was TV or theater. I mean, I would love to see this on Broadway with a super cool rock soundtrack like Florence + The Machine. And I've recently been listening to some Agnes Obel, Lizzy McAlpine, Tame Impala. Let's just pile it all in there, make a super cool, dark, gothic, Victorian musical.

Dreamcast, I really haven't gone there in my brain. I guess I kept kind of picturing in my mind ... she's a redheaded actress... She's the redhead in The Forsytes, the modern version of it, not the Damian Lewis version. I think of her as Helen in my brain.

I feel like Miles could go so many different ways. Gosh, if Mads Mikkelsen was 35, I'd be up for that. I’d love to play Cora. Is Pedro Pascal Armand? I don't know. We need some super hunky Arabic man for Armand.

SM: Speaking of new chapters, One Tree Hill just turned 23. It’s like a baby that’s gone off to college and graduated. After Drama Queens and your memoir, on the other side of it all, it feels like you’ve come to this place where there is just so much happiness. You turned 45 this year and just seem so much like yourself. Is that an accurate read?

BJL: Absolutely. I feel so much more settled than I have in years. There's just a lot of stability in my life in a way that is so beautiful and comforting. And whether I'm traveling or wherever I'm living or whatever I'm doing, I think it's the sense of self-acceptance and self-forgiveness and compassion and all those things that we just work really hard to achieve within ourselves, and finding that connection for me with God and my faith and just feeling like I don't have all the answers and that's OK.

When I was younger, I felt like I needed all the answers in order to feel safe and secure. And I think there's actually a lot more comfort now in not knowing exactly all the things and being OK with it, just exploring and listening and learning. It's better.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

#8200. Are We All Boomers Now?

While we may actually be Millennials and Gen X, it’s become clear that the kids think we are … old.

As I lay on my bed with one of my teens next to me, laughing over a Reel before we forward it to my mom, I find myself suddenly the butt of a joke. “Why do you poke your phone like that, mom? You’re such a Boomer. That’s so unc.”

I paused, hovered over the sharing airplane, and looked at the seemingly normal (to me) way that I am tapping my phone. Was I acting like an old lady? Was I “unc,” the new gender-neutral uncle-derived slang term the teens currently use to describe anyone annoyingly older than them?

After a moment of denial, I settled into the belief that my kid was actually right: I am old. No, not as old as my parents or as old as most U.S. politicians, but when it comes to the benchmarks that define age, I am decidedly more crotchety than I was five years ago.

Today, as I sit in my dining room typing this missive on the morning of my 43rd birthday (Yes, I am an geriatric millennial), I am faced with two important thoughts: Why is my neighbor’s car engine so loud, and what kind of bird is chirping in the tree outside of my window?

I pause to send my friend a recording of the bird. She replies that it is a mockingbird (likely mocking me, like my children) and I get back to work. She’s a Boomer now too, I assume. She recently invited me over to learn about plants — and take a few clippings. Wild times for the Real Housewives of Pittsburgh as we all work remotely from our messy homes.

I begin to mentally list the things that now piss me off: Overhead lighting, too many people talking at once, small talk at professional events (or anywhere), pants with a waistband and shoes without good arch support. I am furious that every movement in life requires a new app, deeply concerned about the safety of e-bikes and gas station drugs and the state of our local roads, and trialing my fourth set of cooling bed sheets. I also list the things I do not care about any longer: fashion trends, what anyone else thinks of me, and the well-earned lines and wrinkles on my face.

It’s a weird juxtaposition when you’re parenting in middle age, raising kids that are on the cusp of adulthood. In many ways I feel like I’m in the prime of my life. I’ve whittled down my friend group to the besties who can stand me, my career is satisfying and moderately successful, and I’ve finally found a hairdresser who gets me. Some days I walk down the street feeling like a million bucks — only to be cut off at the knees by a side-eye at my shoe choice from my teen daughter.

I ask my friends, my comrades in aging semi-gracefully, if they feel the Boomerness creeping up on them, too.

“For sure,” one friend tells me, “Or like how my boyfriend always talks about how we used to be able to get a hamburger for $5 or what the cost of gas used to be.” I remember… it was under a buck the day I got my license.

Another friend says her kid dissects the “unc-ness” of her text messages. Emoji choice is a dead (☠️) giveaway, apparently. So are the television shows and movies we reference as “recent.” Hold hands while I tell you this: The final episode of Parks and Recreation aired well over a decade ago; ten whole human years ago. Don’t even get me started on the OG version of SATC.

So I’ve chosen to accept my fate. In many ways, we are becoming the Boomers now. Not literally — generations are fairly well-defined, and Boomers were born between about 1946 and 1964. But in the funny, small ways that matter, many of us Elder Millennial and Gen X parents are showing our age.

After some soul-searching in my backyard inflatable hot tub, which helps with the aches and pains of old age we’ve barely touched on, I’ve decided this isn’t such a bad thing.

So I am worked up enough about e-bikes to briefly consider a run for town council? That’s because I care about the safety of kids in our community; call me Karen. I’m frustrated with the condition of roads or schools or public infrastructure? I won’t apologize for being old (or mature) enough to realize civic engagement matters. If we want to live in a thriving and bustling community, we are the adults that must create that now. We can’t decry the loss of a village if we aren’t willing to get out there and make one.

We’ve also, as a group, taken healing quite seriously. I am proud of us for this, more than anything else about our generation. While we might bitch about the cost of everything or the state of the world in those Boomerish ways, we are also a generation that is serious about breaking cycles, building new patterns, and parenting conscientiously.

We talk about our therapists in ways that normalize taking care of our mental health. We find mental health help for our kids when they need it, too. We mess up with our kids—and we apologize. We try, we screw up, we try again. Our hips and back and knees may be less flexible than they once were, but I am proud that we are trying to keep our minds flexible. Our Gen Z and Alpha kids poke fun at us and insist the way we dress is awful, but I choose to believe that they see we are working so hard.

So, to my fellow Millennial-and-Gen-X-Boomer-but-not-really-moms, pull up a supportive chair and join me. Bring your latest craft project, your current book club read, or your stack of political postcards that you need to get out before the midterms. Bring your comfy soft pants, your persistent chin hair, and your achy lower back. We will turn off the Big Lights, skip the small talk, and bitch about hot flashes while our kids make fun of us in the next room. Honestly, I think we’ve earned this.

Meg St-Esprit, M. Ed. is a journalist and essayist based in Pittsburgh, PA. She’s a mom to four kids via adoption as well as a twin mom. She loves to write about parenting, education, trends, and the general hilarity of raising little people.

#8199. All The Banned Or Censored Bluey Episodes — And Why They Were Given The Boot

Bluey is the most beloved show on the planet. But you can’t see all the original versions in the United States.

Bluey has become not only the biggest kids’ show on the planet but one of the most popular TV series worldwide. Period. First airing in its homeland of Australia in 2018, the realistic portrayals of parenting combined with the zany wholesome hijinks of a pair of adorable animal sisters means the show is loved equally by kids and adults.

But. Not every single moment of Bluey is available in the United States. A handful of episodes were eliminated by American censors and/or Disney. Some episodes have also been heavily censored and/or altered for American audiences. Why would a kids’ show be censored or have episodes banned? It’s a reasonable question and the easy answer is: it’s complicated. Sometimes it’s because a word has a different connotation in the U.S. than it does in Australia. Other times, there’s an innuendo, or topic U.S. censors have deemed inappropriate.

Across all seasons of Bluey, references to Australian-specific things were localized for American audiences, so we won’t spend too much time discussing those unless they were explicitly censored for serious implications (as serious as Bluey can be, anyway). Likewise, certain bits of dialogue were altered through the series for various reasons, and unless it was something provocative, this article will also glance past those changes.

So, without further ado, here’s a full list of censored and banned Bluey episodes as of May 2023, including one very recent body-shaming moment in Australia.

Update! This list now includes 2024 Disney+ versions of Season 3 episodes!

The good info about the first season is currently no episodes are banned in the U.S. anymore. However, a few notable changes were made to them, some of which were censored and altered outside of Australia.

What was censored and why? A fairly wholesome and hilarious episode, this episode and two others from the first season, “Shaun” and “Teasing,” along with “Flat Pack” from Season 2 were censored due to the use of a racially-insensitive term that could refer to Aboriginal people. The ABC apologized and claimed it was not intended to refer to that abhorrent use of that word. “Daddy Robot” and the other episodes now use a nonsense word to replace the derogatory phrase.

Update: “Teasing” was restored on Disney+ when Bluey season 3B was added, replacing the offensive phrase with “Shoobi-doo-wop”.

What was censored and why? A scene where Bluey is playing “Penguins” in the bathroom was cut from the U.K. and the U.S., although it’s still referenced in the episode. The cut scene has Bluey sliding around the room, something that could be dangerous for a kid to do on a wet tiled floor.

What was it censored and why? The episode ends in the U.S. with Bandit finally boarding his imaginary airplane, only to realize the reckless cab driver is also his pilot. However, the original version continues after that realization, with Bingo’s character pretending to throw up on Bandit’s lap. In the U.S. version, there is no vomit, and that’s why the episode ends earlier here than in the original one.

What was censored and why? As the girls are looking for a way to use some cash, they meet a unicorn handler (actually a pony with a horn on her head). Bluey is excited at this idea but learns only one of them can have a ride on her. Their disappointment quickly disappears after the unicorn drops a huge turd on the grass, leaving the kids fleeing as they scream their heads off. The turd does not exist in the Disney+ version.

This horse and her owner were seen again in the Season 3 episode “Pass the Parcel,” only this time the horse had already relieved itself. In the original version, her feces can be seen in a wide shot where the kids are playing the game, but the American version has an alternate version with the poo pile missing.

What was censored and why? At one point in the episode, Bingo asks her dad how babies get into mom’s bellies. This line is cut in the U.S. version. Apparently, Disney doesn’t want pregnancy discussed in-depth in a show aimed at preschoolers.

The second season brought a few new challenges to the show that needed resolutions, including one episode that will probably remain in the Disney vault until the end of time.

Why was it banned? Similar to “Daddy Putdown,” this one is even more focused on pregnancy and carrying babies. The episode does not exist on Disney+ and in the U.S. at all. In it, Bandit (the dad) simulates what it’s like to give birth. The entire episode is banned as a result.

Will it be unbanned? Most likely never. Unlike “Family Meeting” (aka “the fart episode”) it appears this one is not coming to Disney+ anytime soon.

Why was it changed? Jack seems to act like a child with ADHD. Although he is too young to comprehend the way his brain understands the world around him, he knows it works differently from others.

In the original version, Jack tells Rusty “There’s something wrong with me.” It was later revised to “There’s something going on with me.”

Why was it censored? Bluey hands Conductor Bandit something when he asks for her ticket that she instructs him to rub all over his face. In the original version, imaginary poop was passed to her dad. In America, the line was changed to transform that invisible heap into a slug.

Why was it censored? We already discussed earlier how this one was hit with the same racially-insensitive insult heard in “Daddy Robot,” but there may be another reason this one was controversial.

The core of this episode is a whirlwind examination of the cycle of life, rife with metaphors and silliness to keep it light. However, this episode does include a part that can be interpreted as an afterlife, and it’s also possible to see this plot as a baby’s first look at evolution.

Currently, the episode is available on all platforms in the U.S. with only the derogatory term removed. If you haven’t seen it in a while, it’s a deeply moving six minutes worthy of a rewatch.

The release of this season has been split into several batches of episodes. At the time of publication, Australia is about to get the third part of the season, with no plans on when it will come to the United States.

What was censored? The episode opens with Bandit looking unhappy about the results of weighing himself, grabbing his sides remorsefully. Chilli shows similar dissatisfaction when she does the same. Arguably one of the biggest chunks to be edited out of this show, “Exercise” turned into a huge divisive battle immediately with accusations of fat-shaming, and concerns centered around body dysmorphia in children and adults. Ultimately, the first minute of this episode was removed across all global distributors due to these concerns, instead starting in the backyard with Bandit beginning his workout routine and no discussion on the shape of his body. To be clear, this episode has not even aired yet in the US.

Why was it censored? In one flashback, Bandit is playing “Boomerang” with Bluey while having a conversation with Fido. In the original version, the conversation seems to be about getting neutered, or in human terms having a vasectomy. When it arrived in the U.S., it was changed to be about having Bandit’s dog teeth removed.

Why was it censored? In a scene where Bingo and Bluey teach Bandit how to use a swing, the girls intentionally position him so it hits him in the crotch, causing him to cry out, “My groin!” That word is eliminated in the U.S. version.

Also in S3, the word “groin” is edited out of the U.S. version of “Chores” when Bandit complains about hurting his groin after attempting to do Bingo’s “Bee-yoop” silly walk.

Why was it censored? When Bingo proves to Bluey she’s annoying too, only in a different way, the younger sister tapes her nose back and puts fake teeth into her mouth. Bluey says she looks “crazy” in the Australian version. The word “crazy” does not appear in the U.S. version.

As opposed to an abrupt cut to hide something like Bandit’s groin hit in “Born Yesterday,” the cut is not noticeable at all and adds to the element of surprise once Bingo reveals herself.

Why was it censored? While having an imaginary drive with Bluey that starts to take a turn into madness, her stuffed cat Agatha threatens to pee on the curtains. In the censored version, Agatha instead tells them she’ll scratch their curtains.

What was censored? When Muffin goes on a rampage and tries to escape from her dad while still on the call, she runs around the house, eventually smashing into the bathroom, which Trixie is using. In the original version, Trixie can be clearly seen on the toilet, forced to cover herself up. The American edit crops this out, instead keeps the shot tight on Muffin’s face so as not to reveal the scene behind her.

Update: As of the summer of 2023, “Faceytalk” has been restored to the original version, with Trixie easily seen seated in the bathroom.

Why was it censored? Unicorse is using his best moves to get on Chilli’s good side in the worst way possible. While showing off his sweet moves, Chilli remarks about the chili sauce stain on his body. Australians heard Unicorse respond with, “Wanna’ lick?” The American version has altered this to “Want a bit?”

Why was it censored? Twice in “The Decider,” the two families of sports fans tease each other by saying their team will “flog” the opponents. A term more commonly used with Australian sports fans than Americans, Disney+ viewers will instead hear “beat” due to the violent implications of what the other word means.

Why was it banned? The obvious reason is the sheer volume of references to passing gas. There isn’t any real potty humor here, but the impetus of the episode is based around a silent but deadly affront to poor Bluey’s nose.

Why was it banned? In the opening moments of "Relax," Bandit calls the kids "Super Troopers" in the US edit. However, in the original Australian version, he refers to his girls as "Dingle Berries." What's so controversial about a nonsense word? Turns out the phrase has more than one meaning, and while many know it as a way to insult someone's intelligence, it stems from something more fecal. Apparently, when it comes to Disney Plus, bathroom humor and Bluey mix like cereal and windshield washer fluid, so those berries were better left where they belonged.

If you’re looking to find all the episodes closer to how they looked when they initially aired, the only way is to get the DVD of Season 1 and Season 2, which is region-specific to the United States. There are also other ways to find Bluey episodes, but even the hardiest of Pomeranians wouldn’t dare look in those dark corners of the web. Occasionally, the ban does lift on an episode, but so far, that’s only happened once or twice.

Non-banned Bluey episodes air on Disney+ in the United States.

This article was originally published on March 27, 2023

#8198. Karla Souza Talks Narrating The New 'Thomas & Friends' Special, Mom Guilt, & More

The HTGAWM star and mom of three talks narrating the new Spanish-language Thomas & Friends special, and how she’s leaning into her latest parenting era: minivan life.

Karla Souza has accomplished a lot in her career. She famously played a law student covering up multiple murders in How To Get Away With Murder. She won two International Emmys for producing and starring in Dive (La Caída). She’s built a filmography that fluently bounces between Hollywood and Mexico. But it took a little blue engine to impress maybe the most fickle audience of all: her three kids, ages 8, 6, and 2.

Souza is the Spanish-language narrator of Thomas & Friends Railway Stories: Really Helpful Engines, a 30-minute special that kicks off a new era for the beloved franchise through refreshed character designs, three original songs, and a story about friendship, teamwork, and helping others. She’s also, as she learned after signing on, the first woman — and first Mexican woman — to narrate Thomas & Friends.

Scary Mommy caught up with the charming Souza to talk about the special, why “balance” is a myth, officially surrendering to minivan life, and more.

Scary Mommy: Your kids are 8, 6, and 2, which is prime Thomas territory. Were they Thomas fans before? Do they have a sense of what you’re doing?

Karla Souza: This is actually the first project that I'm able to watch with them, so it was very special. I was definitely chomping at the bit, wanting to be able to share something for the first time with them. They were very confused as to why I wasn't making the train sounds and why that was somebody else. There was a lot of confusion with that part of it, but I love this new chapter of being able to share these kinds of things. And it was the first thing that I did for that kind of age range.

I just find it so special to think that maybe, when they have kids, they'll be able to show old Grandma… there’s something to be said about doing projects that can live on for generations.

SM: What does it mean to you that kids can hear Thomas in Spanish, told by a Mexican narrator?

KS: I wasn't aware that this is the first time that a woman and that a Mexican woman is the narrator of Thomas and Friends. I am so honored, and I'm very excited that female voices get to guide these new generations in seeing women in these kinds of positions.

I love how Thomas and Friends has content that isn't in overdrive, as a lot of the kids' content nowadays is extremely saturated with, I don't know, stimulation is just being thrown at you. I find that this type of content is not only going to provoke imagination, but it's also going to turn on their hearts how to be a better person, how to work as a team, how to learn from mistakes in a calmer way. So it's been a great thing to watch with my 2-year-old as well as with my 6- and 8-year-old. That doesn't really get to happen as much, so I'm really grateful for that.

SM: Three kids, a career as an actor and producer, you split your time a lot between two countries. What does balance actually look like for you, or is that nonexistent?

KS: Yeah, it's not possible. I think that word is thrown around as if it were possible to have a balanced life. I mean, anyone who's near my life is like, "How do you do this?" I think the trains have systems; they're on the tracks. There are times when the train leaves. If there's a delay, there's an announcement to all the people that there's a delay. It's the same. If I didn't have all these systems and a community of people around me to support me, my husband, my family, our nanny, the school, everything, we would not be able to do this. My mom didn't work, per se, so I never saw what that would look like. So it's been a learning curve for me to understand how to juggle all of it.

There's a lot of mom guilt still there that, every therapy session, I'm trying to get to why I still feel that way. It's real, it's hard, but I will say that also the ability to see my kids watching me do something that I love, watching me impact society in a way, watching me live out my purpose, is as important as being with them 24-7.

SM: Such a good reminder that we’re not alone; we all feel like this in a way. Your youngest is 2. What difference strikes you the most about parenting your third compared to your first?

KS: My 2-year-old started saying words that were like, "Where did she hear that?" I'm like, "Obviously from us; there's no other place. This word isn't going to magically appear in her mouth. That is why she is saying that word." It's funny how you're in denial of, like, "I don't do that,” but surely we do.

I think having children is a great mirror for who you are and the work you have to do on yourself, because they call BS so quickly when we try to teach them about, like, breathwork. And yet when I get frustrated, I'm not practicing what I am trying to teach. So as much as I try to think that they aren't as perceptive, they are. They just absorb so much of how we live our lives, of what we do.

Whenever I've noticed that working on myself is actually the best way to show up for them and to model it, that's how I see it with my 2-year-old and my 8-year-old — my 2-year-old is an imitator of everything she sees from my 8-year-old. Whatever my 8-year-old wants to do, whether it's gymnastics or staying up late or reading a book, my 2-year-old goes off and does it. It just shows you how interaction and who you surround yourself with really is very important at this stage in their lives.

It’s an interesting sort of case study on life and how we are as humans and what makes us feel like we belong.

SM: Yeah, it is fascinating how it shows up like that.

But yeah, the 2-year-old obviously is the queen of the household, and my 8-year-old is as well, but the 2-year-old is coming in like a storm. She's a spitfire. So we do what she says. My 8-year-old is a great sort of... I try to not put the caretaking role on her as much because a lot of people try to have the older kids kind of become the caretakers, and I don't want to do that. But I will say she has a lovely pull towards taking care of her baby sister.

I love having that separation of years, but yeah, the 2-year-old's my last one. We just bought ourselves our first minivan, so I've given up. That's it; I'm a mom of three. I've never had a minivan in my life, and we just got one. I'm like, "All right, that's who I am now."

SM: We rented a minivan for a girls’ trip a few years ago. Five moms driving up the coast in a rented minivan; it was hilarious. But it was the first one I drove as well, and I was like, “You know what? There’s something to this. It’s super comfortable.”

KS: I know. The kids just get in and they get out, and it's just so comfortable. I feel more powerful driving it than I thought I would be. I'm like, "This is actually cooler than I thought." But yes, I've given up on the cool, sexy cars now and I'm like, "All right, I'm going to embrace it."

SM: As you should. Let's make minivans cool and sexy.

KS: Yes. Hey, you did it on a girls' trip! That's hilarious.

SM: Pivoting a bit, I saw you post that How To Get Away With Murder just marked 12 years since its premiere. Does the ending hit differently now that you’re a mom of three?

KS: Man, I am in awe of Laurel being able to be a mom at that period of her life. I'm still shocked. And I'm shocked that I, as a human being, was able to... I think I was pregnant when I did that scene on the elevator where she's having these contractions and there's a potential stillbirth. Nowadays, knowing so much more, I'm like, "I don't know how I could do that today." But I will say that at least playing to be a mom definitely prepared me in the smallest of ways, but it did prepare me to be a mom. It kind of gave me that vote of confidence because I never thought I could be a mom.

I didn't grow up with that faith of I can do it. I was like, "I still feel like I'm a child and I'm trying to parent my own child, my inner child every day." But that's why I thought I wasn't sort of made for motherhood, and look at me three kids later: here I am.

So for all the moms out there, all the women out there, who feel like they wouldn't be able to do it, I was that person. I was definitely thinking, "How can I still have a career and do what I love and travel with my friends in a minivan? How can I do all these things and still have kids?" It's possible. Does it all look the same as when I was single? No, it doesn't, but it is possible. It's tough, but that's the caveat. It's the silver lining, but yes.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

#8196. One Controversial 'Bluey' Character Isn’t Actually All That Bad

There are always characters in TV shows that viewers loathe, whether it be for legitimate reasons or personal preferences. The same goes for kids’ entertainment, and that sentiment persists even in something as wholesome as Bluey. If you were to make a tiered chart of characters from this popular Australian kids' cartoon on Disney+, chances are a high percentage of fans would rank these two characters at the bottom – Muffin and Judo. We’ll save the Heelers’ Chow Chow neighbor for another day, but Bluey’s cousin Muffin is a divisive one among its audience.

Muffin’s fiery temper has landed her in some hilarious situations, but it’s also made Bluey fans leery of her. Brash, spoiled, and tantrum-prone, many have compared this member of the extended Heeler family to Angelica Pickles from The Rugrats. It’s easy to take Muffin at face value as a prima donna, but she’s another case of Bluey showing kids and parents in a more realistic light.

Despite her behavior, Muffin is the prime example that no child is irredeemable, holding an uncomfortable mirror up to expose some unpleasant truths about raising kids, and certainly worth a deeper look at why she’s really one of the best in the show.

Muffin’s debut in “BBQ” proves what happens when the immovable object meets the irresistable force

Even from her first appearance in season one’s “BBQ,” Muffin was a chaotic force of nature. She’s like a wild pony, unable to be tamed no matter how hard anyone tried unless she took the reins for her own sake. There are plenty of examples of Muffin’s bratty tendencies across the series, making it understandable why this kid has such a rough time getting fan support.

She was mildly antagonistic to her older cousin in “Horsey Ride,” being a know-it-all when her younger sister Socks was nomming on Bluey’s special toy. Season two showed us how demanding Muffin could be in “Charades” and “Library,” and she was just plain bonkers in “Sleepover,” but there’s no culprit to blame on that other than lack of sleep.

No shortage of episodes display the negative traits of this character, but many show her as a precocious child who just likes to have fun. Muffin was following Bluey’s play pattern when it came time to defend their nail salon in “Stumpfest”, the same as she did in “Backpackers.” She’s also genuinely well-mannered in the Christmas episodes, unrelated to Santa visiting their home, and has been a good big sister with her sibling, even helping the pup hold an ice pop in “Charades.” Even in season three’s “Pizza Girls,” Muffin was more about anarchy than she was about disobedience and stirring up trouble.

Chaos, thy name is Muffin Heeler! Still from season three’s “Faceytalk”

Muffin’s turning point occurs in season three’s “Faceytalk,” which is about the Heeler children virtually playing together on tablets. The episode begins with Bluey’s mum, Chilli, reminding Bluey not to hog the screen from Bingo, “because we know what happens when you hog.” While this may seem like a simple lesson, it falls into the deeper message of the episode as the plot progresses.

Muffin wants to finish drawing a hat on the Faceytalk screen before turning the tablet over to her little sister, Socks, and resists the boundary Stripe places on her screen time. Trixie, meanwhile, has washed her hands of the situation because she has “somewhere to be.” Remember, Muffin is around four years old here and is testing the limits of what she can and can’t do. There’s no intent of malice on her part since, in her mind, all Muffin wants is to doodle her pink cowboy hat. Stripe gets in the way of her finishing that task, but has difficulty being firm and following through with what he says. After Muffin absconds with Stripe’s phone, a wild chase through the house forces Trixie’s involvement and leads to a standoff with her husband instead of her unruly daughter.

“Faceytalk” isn’t just about Muffin’s problems with sharing, because the root of the problem starts with her parents. From the onset, the couple had communication problems regarding how to handle their kids and being on the same page with each other. In the last act of this episode, it all comes crashing down into the event that permanently changes who Muffin becomes.

The running theme through this story was “hogging” things, and Stripe felt like Trixie hogged the kids when it came to discipline, and undermined him, while Trixie felt Stripe wasn’t doing things the way she wanted and was therefore inferior to her decisions. In the end, the pair find unity in their parenting, and in doing so, start a cascade effect on Muffin that begins to see the character make some changes of her own.

This granny is about to find out what happens when you mess with Muffin

A few episodes later, “Granny Mobile” brings us the threequel to the Granny series. This story marked the first time Muffin appeared since “Faceytalk,” and the difference in her personality is immediately noticeable.

The Heelers, with Muffin joining them for a playdate, visit their neighbor Doreen’s yard sale. After seeing a mobility scooter for sale, the girls decide to play Grannies, with Muffin playing the part of Gladys the “grouchy granny.” After spending some time as this character, Muffin tells Bluey she isn’t enjoying being so mean but is unsure how to play the part differently.

As Doreen struggles to not be such a pushover during her yard sale, a real grouchy granny shows up demanding to buy the scooter for a fraction of its actual price. Muffin, so lost in her elderly persona that Daniel Day-Lewis would be impressed, grouches back to the actual octogenarian, and uses her Muffin powers for good instead of evil, helping Doreen get four times the asking price for the vehicle.

Muffin’s good deeds showed her there was a time and place for her authoritative voice, acting as positive reinforcement that it’s possible to still follow the boundaries set by her parents while also maintaining her inner self. If anything, this proved Muffin can stand up for others the same way she used to for herself, advocating for the voiceless in whatever situation may occur. How this realization will be used in future stories remains to be seen, but the evolution of Muffin is clear now, and the road ahead is starting to look much less bumpy than her wild ride in “Sleepover.”

Muffin might be pure unbridled chaos, but we wouldn’t have her any other way

It’s important to remember that Muffin is only around four years old by the end of season three, so her emotional development is still in flux as she learns about boundaries. If her behavior was like this as an adult, it would certainly be a call for alarm, but this is relatively normal for a preschooler.

Outgrowing this phase will naturally happen through her mum and dad collaboratively parenting their child, and supporting each other. It won’t be easy and there will likely be more disagreements as they figure things out, but seeing how quickly Muffin changed in season three, it proved it’s never too late to make positive changes that will enhance the attitude of their kid while improving communication with each other.

While some parents may fear their children reenacting the negative traits of Muffin, or others may label her “annoying,” watching someone like Muffin grow onscreen is vital for kids and adults to observe. It took some time, but Muffin is learning about the consequences of her actions while her parents strive to become better at their jobs as caregivers. If there are two things Muffin taught us, it’s that coconuts have water inside them, and it’s never too late to make a change.

#8194. 10 Questions Worth Asking At Your Annual Physical After Age 40, According To Doctors

They want to talk to you about prevention, prevention, and more prevention.

Between work, kids, kids’ extracurriculars, family obligations, and everything else, it’s easy, as moms, to let our own health fall by the wayside. If nothing’s bothering you, of course your annual physical is the first thing to get canceled in a week loaded with other appointments and to-dos. But doctors agree that while moms are often the last people to complain about feeling tired, rundown, or off, they also tend to wait too long to bring their concerns to a medical provider, as Scary Mommy previously reported. So, this is your sign to keep that annual physical and use it to talk to your doctor about all the health concerns that come with aging. While you might be fine now, your doctor is eager to tell you how to keep it that way.

“Cardiovascular disease is the number one killer in the United States for both men and women. In order to live a long and happy life you need to understand your risk for developing cardiovascular disease and how to combat and lower your risk,” says Dr. Colleen Reidy, DO, is a family medicine physician at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center.

“This is the blood work that I recommend for most patients,” says Reidy. “CMP will evaluate electrolytes, kidney function, and liver function. A CBC will look into your blood counts. Ferritin level will screen for iron deficiency, which can be the first sign of colon cancer. Lipoprotein a and LDL/lipid panel can give us insight into your risk for high cholesterol and cardiovascular disease. If you are obese or have a family history of diabetes, you might want to consider getting your A1C checked to rule out pre-diabetes or diabetes.”

Make sure you discuss any family history of cancer with your primary care provider while you’re at it. “Age-based cancer screening allows for early detection of certain types of cancers and reduces cancer mortality,” says Dr. Jacqueline Jepsen, family medicine physician at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center.

Your family history may influence when screening should begin and how frequently it should be performed, according to Dr. Harold Jaimes, board-certified internal medicine physician and owner of Jaimes Medical Group in Chicago.

“Always tell your doctor about any family history of cancer, especially when relatives were diagnosed at a younger age. This can significantly change screening recommendations,” he says.

“Routine colon cancer screening now begins at age 45 for most people, rather than 50. Be sure to tell your doctor if anyone in your family has had colon cancer, particularly at a younger age,” Jaimes says.

You might be at higher risk of colon cancer — and therefore require screening at an earlier age — if you have a history of radiation to the abdomen, inflammatory bowel disease, or certain types of polyps, according to the American Cancer Society.

“Age 40 is the year to start doing routine yearly mammograms. If you have dense breast tissue, then you might qualify for follow-up ultrasound,” Reidy says.

Women should stay current with cervical cancer screening, including Pap smears and/or HPV testing, as appropriate for their age and medical history, Jaimes adds. New guidelines allow for women to self-swab the vagina at home to be screened for HPV. If you’re someone who struggles with annual well woman visits, talk to your OB-GYN about this option.

Keeping up with the recommended vaccine schedule is an important part of disease prevention that boosts personal immunity and herd immunity, Jepsen says.

“The average age of menopause in America is 51 years old. However, the perimenopausal phase can last a few years and can look different in everyone. It’s good to talk to your doctor about what to look out for,” says Reidy.

Women, especially after menopause, are at risk of decreased bone density, Reidy points out. As Scary Mommy previously reported, you can maintain bone density with exercise, like strength training two to three times per week or adding walks, and even dancing, into your day-today. Bringing up osteoporosis with your doctor allows them to talk to you about any potential risk factors too.

“You might want to talk to your doctor about any chronic conditions, like celiac disease, or long-term use of steroids that might put you at increased risk of osteoporosis and warrant earlier screening,” Reidy says.

Exercising isn’t just about your weight; it turns out that your muscle mass is the best indicator of your longevity and quality of life as you age.

Most doctors recommend 150 minutes of moderate intensity exercise per week, but it’s important to talk to your doctor about what that means for you, Reidy says. Make a plan with your provider that takes into account your unique medical history, risk factors, and lifestyle.

“As we age, certain hormone levels change, and this is normal,” Jepsen says. “It is important to discuss with your doctor what signs of aging you should expect and what symptoms are ‘red flag’ symptoms, meaning you should reach out to your doctor to discuss further.”

“I remind my patients that many serious medical conditions develop silently, long before symptoms appear. Annual visits give us an opportunity to identify problems early, address risk factors, and hopefully prevent more serious illness down the road,” says Jaimes. “After all, we wouldn’t think twice about maintaining our cars to keep them running for years. Shouldn’t we give our own bodies at least the same attention?”
